product_title: Love Notes: A Musical Romance Boxed Set
review_body:
Pieces of Me
This book follows the main character, Peyton, through a a full year of ups and downs and massive changes in her life. During this journey, she suffers a lot of blows, but always ends up a better and stronger version of herself. We get to walk in the shoes of a girl who is in essence a social outcast - she is overweight and the target of constant abuse at school, and then she meets him.

What I liked
1. Peyton - Peyton was an interesting character. We meet her when she has essentially hit rock bottom, and we get the pleasure of struggling with her and getting to be part of her metamorphosis. But, did she really change or rather did she allow her real self to emerge? I think it was a little of both. She learns to love herself and her circumstances and along the way, other people want to love her too.

2. Peyton\x27s friends - Peyton was blessed with a great group of supportive friends. She wasn\x27t always honest with them, but they always had her back and they constantly tried to push her out of her comfort zone so that she could grow.

3. The author understood that this kind of growth and self-actualization takes time. There were no instantaneous rewards for Peyton. She gets a guy after a lot of work and time. She goes from an overweight, plain jane after a myriad of steps and a lot of time. I like that we had to wait patiently and we got the cheer and hope for Peyton.

And if that\x27s not enough for you and you love a good LifeTime movie, you will love this story. There is a LOT of drama. I hope to learn more about Jace in the next book. I feel as though we just scratched the surface there, but overall, a great read where I was able to root for the underdog and watch her come out on top.

review_headline: Holy mind blowing books batman!!! This book is awesome!
review_body:
5 DARK, DAPRAVED & DESOLATE STARS

**I received an ARC for an honest review.**

I have literally just finished this mind blowing book. So this review is fresh off the presses.

I wasn\x27t sure how I would feel about getting more personal with Ryan\x27s character. I just didn\x27t want the author to make me feel anything for him and actually want him to have a life. product_title: The Amazing Colossal Apostle: The Search for the Historical Paul
review_body:
Dr. Price raised so many points that will raise the question if Paul the main proselytizer of Christianity actually the one who wrote the epistles. He scrutinized the only account for a historical Paul and concluded that it was not Luke who wrote the Acts of the Apostles and it only appeared in historical records until the second century. Next, the conversion story of Saul has the pagan parallels like that of Buddha and Euripides\x27s Bacchae as well as OT parallels like that of Moses. Then he did a commentary on each epistle and pastoral letters; chapter by chapter, to show the problems within these works, their contradictions to each other, contradictions to the gospels, derivations from he gnostic sources like the kenosis hymn, the lack of historical value, the silence of Church fathers until Irenaeus, and the Marcionite influence.

My only problem with the book is the lack of geographical analysis as to why Paul of the NT never existed, as to why Paul never left any trace that he had been to places like Corinth, Galatia, etc. Nonetheless, I highly recommend this book and will probably buy the print version next time.

review_body: That was a marvellous ride! My first with Gordon B. Hilton, who has been writing fiction and creative non fiction since the 1990s.  His debut novel Biddy Debeau Rides for His Life is very well written and keeps you engaged with the story right through. It gives an insight into the dark underbelly of the life or maybe strengthens the stereotype of an American biker, giving you glimpses from the movie `Easy Rider\x27. Being a rider myself, certain portions of the book I could identify with, which is proof enough that there are certain things which are common to bikers all over the world irrespective of nationalities. Nothing in the book seemed fake. It all rang true, including the surreal drug induced scenes or the highs that a rider gets while on a ride and the mind wanders. The author must have been a rider himself to uncover the workings of a biker\x27s mind. Yes, it is different.  It is definitely a must read whether you are a biker or not, just for the sheer adrenalin pumping action scenes of across the border adventures that have been plotted and woven beautifully. It does have a retro feel to it and maybe would have been a vrooming success if it was published in the 90s or maybe earlier.  Not an author to be written off. Look forward to more of his wonderful work!  This book was received by me from Story Cartel, as an advance reader copy, in exchange for my unbiased review.

product_title: Pulse: (#2 The Beat and The Pulse)
review_headline: 4.5 stars for a gal who fights for life and love
review_body:
Ren has had a rough year. Her mother died, she had to seek out the father who abandoned her at the age of five, for his other family, and he\x27s not so keen to see her again. Nor is his daughter, Monica. Relegated to closet bedroom at her father\x27s gym, Ren learns to channel her rage by training in mixed martial arts. She strikes up an uneasy friendship/sex buddy relationship with Ash, the disgraced boxer her father once trained. The more they interact, the more Ren begins to trust that she won\x27t always be alone.

Banned from the UFC, Ash fights in an underground fight club, and Ren joins him. Well, until Thunder, a title contender, tries to take out Ren. Ash and Thunder both disappeared that night six months ago, leaving a bloody mess of the training gym, and Ren with a broken heart.

In PULSE, Ren is fighting in both the UFC qualifiers, and the underground, needing the brutality of the ring to dull he sense of loss. Then she learns what truly happened between Ash and Thunder, and she\x27s initially furious. She suspected Ash had killed Thunder, and he\x27s currently under house arrest, but the story is more complicated.

Thunder is rotten to the core, and there\x27s only one way Ash and Ren can take him down...in the underground cage fighting championship. Ren and Ash both get the chance to step into the legitimate ring, as UFC fighters, but to do so would scrap their plans for revenge.

It\x27s a well-told erotic romance, though the romance is a bit back-burnered for the vengeance plot. Thunder makes a perfect villain, antagonizing Ren during her matches, taunting Ash every chance he gets, but he\x27s not the only problem. Secrets are being kept that could influence the rest of their lives, and no doubt cause a good bit of conflict.

product_title: Legitimate Lies
review_body:
After reading the author\xE2\x80\x99s first book, Hush in the Storm, I was eager to dive into Legitimate Lies.

Once again, this book is well researched. It has to be as the topic of both of the author\xE2\x80\x99s books tackles first a disturbing current social problem and then the world of witness protection. Without the poignant research, these books would have fallen flat.

What is fascinating is that it approaches the new issues in this book very creatively. Within this highly suspenseful story, the pull-push of romance is weaved in. As in the first book, the involvement between characters feels very real. This is most likely due to the author once again having researched the psychological affects of being in such highly stressful events.

Yearnings and reality collide in Jen\xE2\x80\x99s new world from the very first page. The tension builds rapidly and stays that way for the remainder of the book. Surprises and action scenes are peppered throughout. There is always one question. Who can she trust? As she battles with that, magic happens and her faith walk is challenged and embraced bit by bit. All very realistic and not over done.

Julie Cosgrove, has me hooked.

Both of her books in this series are ones that should be read and once done, the reader might be like me and be amazed at how often the stories, the characters, and the issues come to mind. This is a good thing, as we need to be aware of what is happening around us concerning human trafficking to even being more sensitive to the emotional wars within hurting people around us.

Hushed in the Storm and then Legitimate Lies guides us there.

product_title: The Abbot\x27s Agreement (Hugh De Singleton\xE2\x80\x99s Chronicles Book 7)
review_headline: My favorite in Master Hugh\x27s Chronicles
review_body:
Mel Starr never ceases to impress. His 7th book in The Chronicles of Hugh de Singleton, Surgeon, The Abbot\xE2\x80\x99s Agreement, just might be his best novel yet. Starr is the master of creating a puzzling mystery set in Medieval England. I highly recommend this book for lovers of mystery fiction, whatever the setting.

Hugh de Singleton, bailiff for Lord Gilbert Talbot, is on his way to purchase a Bible in Oxford. Accompanying him is the loyal and physically dominating groom, Arthur, a handy person to have while traveling the roads of England in the 14th century. But before they travel very far, they discover the remains of a novice at the local abbey, and the old and frail Abbott persuades Hugh with the promise of a free Bible to stay and find the felon. Hugh, ever mindful of his growing family and his decreasing purse, agrees.

There is a lot to love about Starr\xE2\x80\x99s mystery series. His characters are always believable and well-drawn. Hugh is especially complex. An intelligent man, bound by the culture and wisdom of his day, he endeavors to find truth in his cases and also in his understanding of God and man. Medieval England comes to life as seen through Hugh\xE2\x80\x99s first person narrative. Hugh may be constrained by the limited scientific knowledge of he day, but he makes up for it with his wit and inventiveness. In The Abbot\xE2\x80\x99s Agreement, Hugh cleverly discovers the how and where of the crime, yet the who and why remain a mystery. In this, human behavior becomes the main focus of the investigation.

Master Hugh is also a man of deep faith. He longs to read the Bible for himself, rather than having others tell him what it says. His study of the Scripture leads him to an understanding that bordered on what those of his day believed heretical. I loved Hugh\xE2\x80\x99s explanation of Jesus\xE2\x80\x99 atoning sacrifice, an idea that many today struggle with as well. Other heretical ideas are also explored \xE2\x80\x94 ideas that still seem alive and well in today\xE2\x80\x99s modern world.

While The Abbot\xE2\x80\x99s Agreement can be read as a standalone, I recommend that you start at the beginning. Hugh is a wonderful character and this mystery series is one of the best I have read.

Highly Recommended.

Audience: Adults.

(Thanks to Kregel and Lion Hudson for a review copy. The opinions expressed are mine alone.)

review_headline: Wonderful! Horror with a side order of ribs...
review_body: Horror stories are without a doubt Carole Gill\x27s forte and with Circus of Horrors she has really surpassed herself. Having read a number of her earlier works, I expected something similar in this, her latest work, but...no! She totally surprised me with this tantalisingly terrible tale of the most gruesome group of circus performers you are likely to meet, though God forbid that you do! I really don\x27t want to give any of this wonderfully scary tale away, but will say that it had me feeling edgy and nervous throughout. Just when you reach a point where you think Fred and his old Dad are about to be shown as the heroes of this well crafted tale, you are faced with a revelation that is quite simply totally out of left-field and makes you re-think just how the story is going to end. Let me also say that the clowns are clowns, without a doubt, but unlike any clowns you\x27ve met or seen before, and the ensemble cast of surrounding characters are never quite what they seem. Congratulations, Carole Gill, Circus of Horrors truly had me mesmerized!

Great job and a must read!

product_title: Adult Onset
review_body:
\x5C\x22Whenever the past starting piling up behind Mary Rose, threatening to collapse, the family would move and presto, she would get another chance. She got good at being new. \x5C\x22

This time however, Mary Rose McKinnon, Mister as she has been called since her childhood, appears to be stuck. Taking a break from her successful writing career to look after household and her and her wife\x27s small children, she cannot \x5C\x22just move\x5C\x22 and start again when the many demands on her seem to overwhelm her. Running the household while her life partner, Hilary, is out of town for an important theatre production, is not Mister\x27s only challenge, however. She is worried about her aging parents and there is concern that her mother may be developing dementia.

In her new novel, Ann-Marie MacDonald creates an intimate portrait of a middle aged woman at a crisis point in her life. We are close observers as Mister struggles through one challenging week, one day at a time. Written in the voice of Mary Rose and as a kind of memoir, the reader follows the protagonist\x27s meandering reflections and recollections of present and past events. Like memory events are not recalled in linear fashion, one small irritation now triggers a circumstance in the past that suddenly grows in importance, raising more questions that need to be considered if not answered. It takes her (and us) a while to untangle the connections and the background to her current concerns. At times, Mister\x27s behaviour becomes quite erratic and even friends and Hilary wonder about her mental health.

As a young child Mary Rose suffered from a \x27bone cyst\x27 in her left arm and required several surgeries including a bone graft to heal her arm. Suddenly now, she feels pain in that arm, but, so the doctors had assured her a long time ago, that her arm was totally healed. What to make of phantom pain if that is what she feels? Can it be triggered by long forgotten emotional trauma? In particular, she recalls the time when she was Maggie\x27s age. But does she really remember what happened to her or does she piece stories together in her mind, stories that she heard from her older sister Maureen, of totally imagined scenes based on photographs she has seen later? Whatever the source, these memories are now coming back with a vengeance. Or so it seems to her. But why now? Does her behaviour towards Maggie mirror what she remembers of her mother\x27s treatment of her at that age? There are suggestions to that effect. But is she - and we - correct in our assumptions?

Ann-Marie MacDonald is a very engaging writer. She captures the pace with which Mister is being bombarded with the daily challenges and upheavals very effectively. Her backstory, clearly inspired by her personal story provides much food for thought as well as questions about how parents behave towards children which does not necessarily match how the grown-up children later perceive and understand that behaviour. Yet, this is not a novel that will appeal to every reader in the same way or to the same degree. It will depend on their own experiences in life. While I enjoy non linear stories, I found the narrative flow at times too interrupted, and not only by Mister\x27s childhood memories. Another deep-seated pain from her young adulthood takes over her mind and emotions. It has overshadowed her relationship to her parents ever since. Furthermore, the protagonist interleaves chapters from her successful YA novel. Each narrative thread is relevant for the whole, but it takes time to work out the connections for the week in question. Having heard the author read from the beginning of the novel, I discovered the funny side of her writing more directly than by reading it quietly to myself. [Friederike Knabe]age. product_title: The Gentle Man (Love Eternal Book 1)
review_body:
Anastasia Trent is a woman of a certain age, about to be downsized from her tech job, and getting by on her part-time bartending gig and her husband\x27s sporadic home sales commissions. One day, a mysterious, gentle man known only as Lord Domn comes into her life, seducing her to a life she never knew existed.

First, the good stuff. I am such a fan of a romance that has an older woman as a main character, exploring her needs and desires, which are often overlooked in our society that focuses on youth and, barring youth, Viagra. This book goes into the details of Ana\x27s rocky marriage, the twists and turns, and the things that satisfy and that, after 30 years, may not be enough. Those were the details that kept me reading through.

There were a few things that did not ring true. (Some spoilers ahead.) First, this book is categorized as paranormal romance. In the romance genre, a main character (male or female) who commits adultery cannot be seen as sympathetic, according to genre tropes. So readers coming to the books with the expectations that it will be a typical example of its genre will be disappointed. Also, Ana falls in love with Domn not because he\x27s really interesting or anything, but because he says he loves her, bites her and turns her into a vampire. In fact, he spends most of the book locked up in the psych ward - where she put him - and so he\x27s not even around when she realizes she loves him. I can buy the supernatural enhancement of her attraction, but to leave her husband and fall in love with someone who wasn\x27t even there, I just wanted more of Domn\x27s development. Then, at the end, her husband forgives her everything and they are right back together. That is one superhumanly forgiving spouse. (End spoilers.)

I enjoyed very much the author\x27s treatment of the vampire mythology, especially how she positions the real world around the transition. Even as the main character embraces her change, she has to face annual physicals, bar shifts, finding a job she can work at night, and an extended family who keeps calling her cell phone. All of these added up to an interesting read; and I found myself intrigued all the way to the end.

product_title: Twisted Tales: Four Short Stories from the author of \x22Gypsy Hunted\x22
review_body:
Quick, GREAT read. I loved this book from beginning to end. Andrea Drew is quickly becoming one of my favorite authors!
First, this book is a grouping of four very different short stories.
The first story was very interesting to me. I wasn\x27t sure where it was going, but quickly realized where I thought it was going to lead. Man, was I wrong! Jimmy walks into a bar- yeah, great image, right? He confesses to the bartender that he has had a horrible day, but seems to think it may get better. I choose to believe his side of the story that he was stunned to find things about his wife he was previously unaware and it is her fault things come to end the way they do. I, however, am worried his wife\xE2\x80\x99s story is more the truth of the situation. Either way, Jimmy is very crafty and probably has the final say in the situation!
The second story made me laugh out loud. All I can say is imagine a grave, hay, and fire\xE2\x80\xA6..
The third story is about a girl who has the (un)fortunate ability to talk with and see spirits. She grows up with her parents ignoring her or telling her she isn\x27t really seeing what she is claiming to her sisters using her when they think they may need her abilities, but don\xE2\x80\x99t listen to her advice. A couple of the characters introduced would be perfect for a longer version of the story or as a spin off for a new novel, especially the man in the corner.
The forth story is a short tale about crime. Crime doesn\x27t pay. It took me a second to realize what happens. Never leave the hot kettle on the porch.
There may be some coarse language in the stories, but they help to enhance the characters. Who would believe ladies like Lee and Janet wouldn\x27t be a little \xE2\x80\x9Cfreer\xE2\x80\x9D with the language while expressing themselves?

product_title: Hope Crossing: The Complete Ada\x27s House Trilogy, includes The Hope of Refuge, The Bridge of Peace, and The Harvest of Grace (An Ada\x27s House Novel)
review_body:
I loved Hope Crossing The complete Ada\xE2\x80\x99s House Trilogy by Cindy Woodsmall. This book includes 3 novels: The Hope of Refuge, The Bridge of Peace and The Harvest of Grace. I am not a huge fan of Amish fiction but every book I have read by Cindy Woodsmall has been wonderful and this one is no exception. Plan on spending time reading this one since it is three novels in one it is over 1000 pages. The good thing is they all keep your interest.
The Hope of Refuge introduces us to several characters Cara Moore isn\xE2\x80\x99t Amish but finds herself fleeing from a bad situation that lands her in Hope Crossing. There is a little mystery as to who she is and how she ends up here. The characters were fun to get to know and this book shows struggles among both the English community as well as the Amish community. At first I got frustrated at the way the Amish acts toward outsiders but Cindy does a good job at explaining why.
The Bridge of Peace continues the characters that were in the first book but focuses more on Lena and her struggles with the life she is dealt being marked with a birthmark on her face. Then she faces criticism from other members because of things that happen at the school where she teaches.
The Harvest of Grace introduces us to new characters as well as bringing forth the characters we have grown to love in the first two books. This book focuses on forgiveness.
If you like Amish novels you will definitely enjoy this one. If you are looking for something that will take you a while to read and take you away you will enjoy this one. If you want something that is quick for a weekend or vacation read pass on by. It is a larger book and somewhat cumbersome I prefer reading on an electronic reader in this case. These books have a little romance, mystery, conflict and resolution. I always enjoy Cindy Woodsmall\xE2\x80\x99s books and I\xE2\x80\x99m glad I chose this one. It is a good value since it is three in one.

I am very happy with my addition of this wonderful album to the rest of my Wagner Collection. A Million thanks to Mr. Dudamel and the Simon Bolivar Symphony Orchestra for giving us a perfectly detailed and energetic recording of some of Richard Wagner\x27s master pieces.

product_title: Karen Carpenter
review_body:
As a self proclaimed drummer first and singer second,Karen Carpenter always possessed just what it took to make it on her own without brother Richard. While he was in treatment for addictions to Quaalude\x27s,label owner Herb Alpert got Karen hooked up with producer Phil Ramone. This was the man who was helping Billy Joel to churn out hit after hit during the late 70\x27s and early 80\x27s. To bring in the new decade,Karen hoped to forged out an identity all her own with help of a very different team of musicians and songwriters,such as Peter Cetera and the iconic Rod Temperton,for what would\x27ve been her solo debut album.

"Lovelines" and "My Body Keeps Changing My Mind" are melodically strong disco friendly pop/soul numbers-the later with a hard grooving instrumental breakdown. "All Because Of You" is an acoustic guitar textured country-pop ballad while "If I Had You" begins as a slow pop love song but turns into phat jazz-funk on the refrains. "Making Love In The Afternoon" and "Still In Love With You" blend new wave and heartland style pop/rock with their melodic guitar power chords. "If We Try","Still In Love With You" and "Guess I Just Lost My Head" are all dyno\x27d Rhodes piano heavy mid tempo jazz-pop numbers. "Remember When Lovin\x27 Took All Night" is a more uptempo extention on the same vibe with the multi tracked sea of Karen harmony vocals taking huge significance.

Paul Simon\x27s "Still Crazy After All These Years" and the closer "Last One Singin\x27 The Blues" get the crunchy blues/rock treatment to close out the album. While opinions seem to vary in terms of how well the music here suited Karen Carpenter? I personally feel it\x27s her finest and most appropriate musical statement. Even if it sadly didn\x27t come out in her lifetime. With the Westlake studio crew of John Robinson,Louis Johnson and Greg Phillinganes being augment by Airto and Richard Tee? This album gives Karen\x27s trademark rangy,deep yet gentle vocal insinuation it\x27s best setting within a relatively stripped down set of mostly keyboard and rhythm heavy fusion/pop-funk and disco-pop numbers. The sexual energy and passion of the lyrics are also far removed from the usually coy and sweet nature of her music with Richard as well. Though I have a huge soft spot for the Carpenters classic music? This showcases Karen as more than having the ability to stand alone as a totally different (and surely very jazzy and funky) solo artist.s album gives Karen\x27s trademark rangy,deep yet gentle vocal insinuation it\x27s best setting within a relatively stripped down set of mostly keyboard and rhythm heavy fusion/pop-funk and disco-pop numbers. product_title: Videogame Classics for Piano Vol 1 inc. Final Fantasy, Nier Gestalt, Ico & Shadow of the Colossus
review_body:
There\x27s a piano album put out by a man who identifies himself as daigoro789. My guess is if I went searching around the youtubes or broader internet, I could have found a little more out about this before purchase, but at $7 for the album, its not a big risk to take, and as far as the music is concerned, its not a loss.

What I will say is that the guy can clearly play the piano. The strengths of the album really are that the work is compitent and some of what is being played here is difficult (if not impossible) to find published in any other location.

That said, the quality of the recordings and/or (more likely) the piano itself is not what you would typically expect in a piano recording. Much like the cover, you get the feeling that this may have been recorded on an upwrite piano in someone\x27s den. There is something just a little tinny and the fullness of the reverberation seems less than your typical professional recording. There are a few imperfections in the recording, as far as I can tell. I have downloaded, deleted, redownloaded, and listened via cloud as well, but they are still noticable.

Overall, my purchase was largely based on being able to hear a few renditions of ICO and Shadows of the Colossus music for piano. They\x27re pretty decent. Many of the other peices on this album, particularly the Final Fantasy work, are available elsewhere and are probably better recordings.

product_title: Alan Lomax In Asturias, November 1952
review_headline: The man who recorded the world.
review_body: I didn\xE2\x80\x99t know until recently that Alan Lomax had been doing fieldwork and research in my birthplace back in 1952. I knew Lomax from his previous and extensive work with American folk and blues music, but I didn\xE2\x80\x99t know he had been traveling around the world too, working for the USA Library of Congress. I got completely taken aback by this book and the quality of the field recordings, providing that they have been done with the portable equipment available at that time, far away from the top notch gear we have today. In the book \xE2\x80\x9CAlan Lomax. The man who recorded the world\xE2\x80\x9D, by John Swzed, Lomax speaks at length about his experience in Spain, not always very well, due to the political situation at that time, under Franco\xE2\x80\x99s dictatorship, and the difficulties he had to overcome, mostly with local authorities thinking of him as a secret agent from a foreign country.

product_title: Ella Fitzgerald: Encore!
review_headline: Mostly from Jazz At The Philharmonic performance - some real gems
review_body:
This album features Ella backed by smaller ensembles. I love the more intimate feel of each track versus the \x27corporate\x27 albums that feature her backed by stings and other ensembles. To my ears she was always best in trios and quartets. This album features her in those settings. Give the sound samples a run through to get a feel for the music, Each track swings like the title promises, but also captures Ella at what may have been her peak.

I used the Marty Robbins song as a starting point and found that a good may of the tracks on this album are from a Jazz at the Philharmonic performance at the Konserthuset in Stockholm, Sweden on April 28, 1957. She is backed by Oscap Peterson, Herb Ellis and Ray Brown on those tracks.

Unfortunately I could not account for all of the tracks on this album, but in the long run it does not matter as much as the music itself. The recording quality is very good and the selection of titles is delightful. If you are an Ella fan it\x27s possible that this collection may have eluded you given the obscurity of the source concert. However, you will not be disappointed.

product_title: Juggernaut: Alpha [Explicit]
review_body: Rather than reviewing both albums separately, I am reviewing both here under Alpha.    So here we have another offering from the immensely talented Periphery, a band which essentially consists of virtuosos on their respective instruments. They have continued to fine tune their sound since their debut back in 2010. Back then, all instrumentals were written by the band\x27s leader and founding guitarist, Misha Mansoor. Misha has a true talent for songwriting and production. The band has evolved in the past 5 years and the song writing process now consists of the band as a cohesive unit, in some ways for better and in others for worse.    This record is full of the usual \x5C\x22djenty\x5C\x22 riffing, but incorporates more elements of jazz in certain sections (take the end of MK Ultra, for example). There are, however, several songs on this record that I found to be pretty unmemorable, lacking some of the catchiness that was found on the first few albums. I can\x27t do a Periphery review without talking a little about Spencer\x27s vocals. Since Periphery began, fans and critics alike have formed love/hate opinions about his vocals. Let\x27s just say one thing - he is extremely talented. This record has some of his best range on display, from emo-like wailing to death growling. For any light moments, the band makes up for it with some other absolutely brutal songs (\x5C\x22Hell Below\x5C\x22 for instance, which almost overcompensates by being so heavy it is almost unlistenable). However, I must say this is a first Periphery album where I haven\x27t wanted to listen to every single song. The title track \x5C\x22Alpha\x5C\x22 is just a little too poppy for me. It sounds like it could be on daily rock radio. \x5C\x22The Event\x5C\x22 will probably bore most regular listeners as well. But putting my personal complaints aside, some of the tracks here are some of their best to date. I found \x5C\x22Psychosphere\x5C\x22, \x5C\x22Omega\x5C\x22, and \x5C\x22Stranger Things\x5C\x22 to be fantastic.    The musicianship here is top notch. But that is a constant for Periphery. Maybe I didn\x27tlike it as much as their second album, but who am I to judge? They are taking risks and progressing. Isn\x27t that what a progressive band is supposed to do? This is some of the most innovative music in metal today, and I can\x27t wait to see what the future has in store for them.

review_body: The lead single from \x27Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit\x27 is a high octane barrage of rock \x27n\x27 roll that was hinted at on Barnett\x27s \x27The Double EP: A Sea of Split Peas\x27 but never quite executed in a manner THIS punk rock.  It may be slightly alarming at first for those who took comfort in her mellower, melodic moments on Split Peas but listeners will quickly recognize the trademark characteristics: The literate, caustic, free-flowing stream-of-consciousness narrative is distinctively Barnett.  The guitars are on fire on this track.  They squeal and crunch and shimmer in all the right places.  The hooks are there. product_title: David Neil - The Wilderness Years [Explicit]
review_headline: Who is David Neil and Why Is Steve Kilbey Singing These Wonderful Songs About Him?
review_body: I will direct you to Wikipedia to answer that question.  All you really need to know however, is that this album is yet another gem in the rather obscure Steve Kilbey catalog. What you will find here is a collection of stunning numbers built around beautiful shiny electric (12 string and lap steel even I think) and strummy acoustic guitars and frequently, piano. Steve sounds positively terrific, maybe the best instrument on display on this record, which is really saying something because musically speaking this album is marvelously accomplished.  It is one thing to have a great voice but to really know how to sing is another thing altogether. Steve has the voice and he knows how to use it. Listen to this album through headphones and you will hear him doing a world more than just singing notes, song after song.  Instead he uses his voice like paintbrush and paint, tailoring technique and color to the contours of the canvas.  And it is not "arty", just really super pop music.  This is a great album, just one of the very very many that Steve Kilbey has brought into being either solo or through his many collaborations.  The man deserves huge recognition for his incredible talent and prodigious contribution to the arts.

product_title: Greatest Hits
review_headline: Has the biggest but could have been better
review_body: Although Rodney\x27s first greatest hits compilation has his biggest hits, including all of his #1 hits , this compilation could have dug deeper.  Missing are the hits "Honesty" (#4), "15 Minutes" (#20), "Sing Along" (#37), "My Old Man" (#36), and "Just Wanna Rock and Roll" (#31).  Instead we have the #41 single "Invisibly Shaken", and the album cut "About the South," both from the If You\x27re Going Through Hell album.  Which means 6 out of that albums 10 tracks appear here, making up half of this compilation CD.  Not that they are not good songs, but at the very least "Honesty" should have taken prescience over an album cut!  Since there is only one new song on here ("Eat Sleep Love You Repeat"), the more hardcore Rodney fan could simply download this song and make their own hits compilation.  The 3 star rating is no reflection of the great music, but for the lack of thought and effort Curb Records put into this compilation.

review_body: I first stumbled upon Hotel of the Laughing Tree on bandcamp a few years ago after the release of their first full-length record, \x5C\x22Terror and Everything After\x5C\x22. A sucker for bands with more of a \x27progressive\x27 slant (I was listening to a lot of Porcupine Tree and Dear Hunter at the time), I was really impressed by the creativity and depth of the album. It managed to tread a thin line between complexity and accessibility, something many bands fail to do successfully, combining genre-bending and unconventional song structures with catchy enough hooks to keep things interesting. And though it was a great album, the myriad influences and ambitious ideas on display had the side effect of what felt to me like a lack of consistency, and it gave the impression of a band that was still finding its voice.    In the years since, I\x27ve followed them closely, during which time they had a lineup change and released two great EPs that featured a more unified sound and hints of the direction the band\x27s music would take them. I couldn\x27t be happier with where they\x27ve arrived with \x27New World Sundown\x27- on it, we hear a band that knows what it\x27s best at and plays to its strengths, resulting in a tighter, more memorable collection of songs, and cements a sound that Hotel can call completely their own. Don\x27t misunderstand, many of the hallmarks of what made their debut album so unique are still here - transformative pieces that play fast and loose with the conventions of rhythm and tempo, the blending of jazz, rock, and blues elements to create songs that land somewhere in between, the multilayered tapestry of vocal harmonies and an interplay of guitars, horns, strings, and keys - but they are more reined in, more refined, and work together to create a whole that feels more cohesive and deliberate than anything they\x27ve done before. Toned down are the meanderings of their more adventurous experiments - you won\x27t find an analogue to \x5C\x22Terror\x5C\x22\x27s 8-minute title track here- but in their place aresongs that find the heart of that adventurous spirit and condense it into a more streamlined, purposeful experience. The album encompasses a wide range of not only styles, but also moods, from the theatrical (opener \x5C\x22Brussels\x5C\x22) to the uplifting (\x5C\x22Aging Archimedes\x5C\x22) to the melancholic (\x5C\x22The General\x27s Girl\x5C\x22) to the downright danceable (\x5C\x22Duo\x5C\x22). Later in the album, on \x5C\x22Hurricane Music\x5C\x22 and \x5C\x22Stray\x5C\x22, we hear a more emotional side of the band than we have previously, with the former being the closest they\x27ve ever come to a straight piano ballad. Through it all, every song feels fresh and interesting, and exhibits the same impressive level of polish that I\x27ve come to expect from them. The band is bursting at the seams with talent, and as many of the songs were written by the band as a group, each musician has ample opportunity to show off. It all comes together to form an album that is, in my opinion, the best work the band has produced by far. It\x27s some of the most interesting and inspiring music I\x27ve heard in a long time, and it makes me really excited to see what the future holds for them. While it saddens me to know that the answer probably isn\x27t \x27mainstream fame\x27, from what I can tell they\x27re the type of band that\x27s perfectly content to stay under the radar, making music because it\x27s what they like to do rather than to garner recognition. Regardless, I\x27m going to recommend this to everyone I know who\x27s interested in good music, because this is an album that deserves to be heard.    Speaking of which- hey you, listen to this album!

product_title: Chicago Fire Season 1 (Original Television Soundtrack)
review_headline: Great Melodic Score Not Usually Heard In Broadcast TV From Örvarsson
review_body:
Television scoring has taken leaps and bounds over the recent years with the boom of cable TV series. There is still a difference when you look at network television versus cable television when it comes to a dramatic series. A cable series usually has season long arcs with a shortened episode count (i.e. Game Of Thrones, Breaking Bad, The Knick). A network series will usually have a higher episode count and a narrative that is in itself more episodic, meaning the episodes are not as tightly contained (i.e. NCIS, Law & Order, Person Of Interest). Chicago Fire falls in that latter group. These types of shows make it really difficult for a composer to craft a traditional score. It\xE2\x80\x99s often joked that these are all scored by ominous tones. Thankfully one of the more melodically driven composers out there found himself in the TV market. Atli Örvarsson has surprisingly been able to inject emotionally driven and melodically engrossing music into his scores for not just Chicago Fire, but Chicago P.D. as well.

Chicago Fire: Season 1 definitely acts more as a sampling of Atli Örvarsson\xE2\x80\x99s thematic material for the series. Creating an album from a season of 24 episodes is never easy, especially when it\xE2\x80\x99s for a show like this. So what we have here is actually a pretty great collection of moments. You won\xE2\x80\x99t find an overall narrative arc of the show within the music presentation, but the score presented here is a great selection of emotional highlights. The Season 1 album focuses more on those heroic highs and lows. Taken on its own one may assume it\xE2\x80\x99s very melodramatic, but keep in mind we are being given a whole platter of the exciting moments as well as the deeper emotional currents. If you listen to the Season 2 album you will notice more focus was put on character moments in that album. Overall though, Atli delivers the goods and injects his melodic sensibilities into a genre of TV that is known simply for \xE2\x80\x9Cominous tones\xE2\x80\x9D.

Chicago Fire: Season 1 may be your typical network fluff, but Atli Örvarsson jumped into TV after already having established himself as a premiere film composer. He learned the ropes working on huge blockbusters, and then creating a sonic style of his own for his solo projects. He has now taken that school of learning and injected it into network television, and the result I must say is pretty refreshing. It\xE2\x80\x99s great to hear old-school thematic work like the stuff from the 90\xE2\x80\x99s infused with heroism and emotional undercurrents. product_title: Vivaldi Cello Concertos
review_headline: HAN-NA CHANG, THE LCO, AND VIVALDI\x27s CONCERTOs: A REMARKABLE MATCH
review_body:
Five REMARKABLE Stars!! A match made in baroque musical heaven! Award-winning cellist Han-Na Chang continues her remarkable cello ascendancy with another wonderful CD: this time playing the music of Antonio Vivaldi. A child prodigy, she astounded the musical world by studing at Julliard at age 10 and winning the Fifth Rostropovich International Cello Competition at age 11 against stiff competition, prompting Maestro Rostropovich to oversee and conduct her first recording. Since then the 26 year old, globe-trotting Ms Chang has steadily expanded her musical universe, this time taking on 7 cello concertos by the \x27Red Priest\x27 (none of which were performed during his lifetime): the early A Minor, RV 420 with its continuo solo exposition; C, RV 400; C Minor, RV 401; E-Flat Major, RV 408; B Minor, RV 424; D Major, RV 403; and A Minor, RV 418 concertos; many characterized by more than one brisk \x27Allegro\x27 or \x27Allegro" variation within a concerto and many tending towards the mid and lower cello registers. All pieces are wonderfully buoyed by Maestro Christopher Warren-Green, leader Rosemary Furniss, and the London Chamber Orchestra: continuo: cello, double bass, harpsichord & organ, theorbo (lute) & baroque guitar. (Ms Chang jokingly describes the continuo in a YouTube interview as "the rhythm section" and at times, it is.) She totally understands Vivaldi, his music, and influence: then and now.

The \x27best of the best\x27 begins with the urgent Allegro movement of the A Minor concerto: my favorite of the CD. Then there is the challenging bowing of the largo movement of the Concerto in C which Chang dispatches with much elegant ease and verve. The E-Flat Major dirge-like Largo and the super-charged Allegro non Molto are superb allowing Chang to express her lyricism and unleash her bowed fireworks. The kinetic Allegro movement of the D Major concerto is swirling beauty played very energetically. One minor note is that the harpsichord, while clearly evident in many instances, seems at times sonically farther back than necessary while playing a pivotal role in the continuo. This is a generous CD with lots of Vivaldi and in each concerto Ms Chang and the LCO create soaring, emotional, energetic music. Highly Recommended. Five ENJOYABLE Stars. product_title: My Longest Way Home
review_body:
I heard about A/G/D before this album came out and was pretty impressed with their EP. This album falls somewhat short of that impression.

I would describe this band\x27s music as angry, desperate, frustrated, determined, punitive, confrontational, ballistic, psychotic, and dynamic with a somewhat-evenly-distributed mix of screaming and melodic vocals.

While they definitely win points with me for passion/heaviness and to a decent extent also rhythmic complexity, I find much of Any Given Day\x27s work to be melodically uninventive. They like to tune so low that one can hardly tell the difference between one chord and the next in the rhythm section, and when the chords aren\x27t completely unintelligible, they\x27re often just humping on one extremely low chord for bars and bars at a time, relying on a few extra notes here and there to keep it interesting. This gets really, really monotonous before too long and doesn\x27t leave much room for replay value. Contrary to apparently popular belief, this is no substitute for a willingness to write with innovation and diversity, melodically and harmonically on the fretboard. Just because you come up with a complex, spitfire, blast-beat rhythm doesn\x27t make it interesting to hear the same chord again and again, especially not when that happens in several songs on the same album. At least they\x27re not guilty of recycling the same exact one-two-one-two-one-two-drumroll-one-two-one-two rhythm like a lot of their peers. For that, I\x27m extremely grateful.

I\x27m also not as big a fan of the album version of \x5C\x22The Beginning of the End.\x5C\x22 I notice that they \x27curb\x27 the rhythm guitar a lot, making it less visceral and also much more difficult to hear, especially in places that made the EP version of the song such a favorite of mine. That warping, dancing, dynamic bounce-around riff in the chorus can now barely be heard behind the much-more-present lead guitar. In my opinion, the latter was much better off lending some extra spirit and dimension to the brutality of the rhythm guitar from the background in that section than it is standing in the forefront and keeping pace with the volume of the vocals.

That being said, this album wasn\x27t totally a \x5C\x22miss\x5C\x22 with me. I highly recommend \x5C\x22Home is Where the Heart is\x5C\x22 (the album\x27s first single,) and to some extent also \x5C\x22Dead Forever,\x5C\x22 \x5C\x22If Tomorrow Never Shows,\x5C\x22 \x5C\x22Never Say Die\x5C\x22 and \x5C\x22Possession.\x5C\x22 If you want to hear this band do well with \x5C\x22The Beginning of the End,\x5C\x22 I recommend digging-up a copy of the EP version on YouTube. Finally, much to the contrary of my impressions of these other songs, I think the album version of \x5C\x22My Own Sweet Hell\x5C\x22 was actually much better-produced than its EP predecessor. However, Deihl (or whomever is writing their lyrics) loses respect from me over that \x5C\x22... the devil has taken my soul\x5C\x22 line. Ugh, rly? This band is talented enough not to need to fall-back on tired religious charicature-stereotypes in order to express and describe the \x5C\x22darker\x5C\x22 parts of their minds and spirits.

Overall three out of five stars, and I feel that\x27s pretty generous. I believe this band can do much better and hope to hear some more inventive sounds from them on future albums.

product_title: Josep Soler: Meditaci\xC3\xB3
review_body:
Josep Soler was born 40 years too late and in the wrong country. Despite his Catalan roots, there is nothing remotely Spanish about his music. Soler\x27s heart is in German expressionism and thus he sounds like a disciple of the Second Viennese school, particularly Berg. But that\x27s not all to his aesthetic. The ghost of late Scriabin hovers over these works, as Soler is obsessed with ultra chromaticism in both his harmonic language and melodic lines. Soler seems more comfortable in the middle-high registers of the piano. His tempo rarely exceeds largo and the dynamic level is mostly p or pp with occasional expressionist outbursts. There\x27s a static, desolate, and bleak atmosphere that pervades these works, so if you\x27re looking for buoyancy and energy, look elsewhere. It\x27s worth pointing out that Soler is a contemporary composer; most of these works date from the 90s and early 2000s.

\x5C\x22Meditacio\x5C\x22 sets the tone for the rest of the music on this recording: slow-moving highly concentrated chromatic lines punctuated by dissonant chords. Likewise, the two \x5C\x22Paisaje nocturnes\x5C\x22 are icy cold soundscapes with occasional spiky moments of harsh dissonance, both sounding like they were written in the 1920s. One has to listen very carefully to the \x5C\x22Escenes de Via Crucis\x5C\x22 (1995) to imagine what part of the crucifixion story Soler is conveying. There isn\x27t a clear-cut narrative as with Liszt\x27s Via Crucis, but it doesn\x27t matter. Soler\x27s music is severe and contemplative, but always through the prism of a dodecaphonic language. Although poorly translated into English, the liner notes offer some guidance to understanding the emotion behind each movement or \x5C\x22Station.\x5C\x22

\x5C\x22Sans soleil\x5C\x22 (2000-2006), an allusion to Mussorgsky\x27s Sunless song cycle, is world-weary and introspective, not much different in mood or style from the other pieces. Ponderous clouds of ambiguous harmony and delicate twisting chromaticism predominate. Sudden accelerandos and eruptions of violence are also prevalent in the more agitated pieces. The Piano Sonata No. 11 is the longest and most extroverted work on this recording. Of course, extroversion for Soler means he\x27s merely more impulsive with his loud dissonances and lets loose some unexpected thunderous chords in the bass. Overall, the style is uniform with the neighboring pieces: lethargic, austere, and dodecaphonic.

Miguel Alvarez-Argudo\x27s performances are passionate and nuanced. His pacing is appropriately slow and meditative, and his temperament is in tune with the otherworldly aspect of Soler\x27s music.

Bottom line: Soler is not a melodist. His aim is expressing a pained and troubled world via the atonal language of Schoenberg and Berg. These pieces are all cut from the same cloth and even blend into each other after repeated listenings. But as with Feldman, there is a hypnotic quality and haunting power to these works that will appeal to those who welcome music for the dark nights of the soul.he more agitated pieces. review_headline: ... believe I\x27m reading so many negative reviews on this great record! I am a Soulfly fanatic and I ...
review_body: I can\x27t believe I\x27m reading so many negative reviews on this great record! I am a Soulfly fanatic and I like Sepultura also, but this is neither those bands and if it is, it would be more like Soulfly only because it pretty much is Soulfly but with Max\xE2\x80\x99s brother on drums and not the complete groove oriented music style of Soulfly. As a matter of fact the song \xE2\x80\x9CLosing the Edge\xE2\x80\x9D sounds like something that should belong on one of the more recent Soulfly records, probably the album "enslaved\xE2\x80\x9D being that it is probably the heaviest Soulfly record. Having that arabian sounding riff Marco brings with his pedal board is just stellar man. Horns up to this album and especially that song. When I was over sea\x27s with my platoon a lot of what we listened to was Soulfly because of all of the lyrics and riffs that got us stoked. Whoever said this was going to be called by Max F" the Groove. Really I\x27ve never read anywhere or heard Max not talk about ALWAYS wanting to incorporate at least some form of groove in all of his music, and you definitely get some groove elements with this record, actually a lot but it does get over shadowed at times mostly from just straight thrash brutality. The song "Scum" towards getting close to the end of the song, when all you hear is a little quick interlude of guitar, we hear Max with a doom metal voice yell Go...and the rest is history with how awesome that riff and with marco\x27s solo coming in, and igor just pounding those drum beats, just epic. I know good music, and yea it is very different compared to say the first C.C. record but why is that a bad thing? Other than vocal approach I see similarities still from the previous two records. Anyway give this record a chance again. A few listens as some songs had to grow on me and after a few more listens also, but overall I\x27d say this whole record just about rules including the bonus songs. Keep rock\x27n my metal friends! \x5Cm/

product_title: Sid Meier\x27s Civilization: Beyond Earth (Original Soundtrack from the Video Game)
review_headline: A Huge Canvass Of Melodies And Ambience That Send The Listener On A Cosmic Journey
review_body:
Strategy games are a very interesting media canvass for music because of how unstructured the canvass is. The Civilization series has been a PC gaming staple since 1991 when the first game was released. There have been many entries in this saga, but Beyond Earth takes the turn-based strategy game to a sci-fi realm. The thing is, I don\xE2\x80\x99t connect to these games that much, but I love the scores they allow composers to cook up. Cris Velasco\xE2\x80\x99s Company Of Heroes 2 is an example of how great of a role music can play on this structure. I\xE2\x80\x99m happy to say that Beyond Earth is another fantastic example of music knowing no bounds, and resulting in sonic worlds worth getting lost in.

Since Beyond Earth is all about building civilizations on different planets, you can imagine the huge blank canvas this group of composers had to work with. While the game has a loose central storyline that defines the events in the game, it\xE2\x80\x99s mostly gameplay focused instead of narrative. So in this case, music\xE2\x80\x99s role is not to craft a narrative or tell a story, but instead to build sonic worlds. Each track is like visiting a different planet or different world. Some tracks are more melodic and structured than others, while some are pure ambient textural builds. The 4 composers divided work based on their stylistic strengths, and together they congeal to form a massively scoped score. With over 2hrs45min of music in this release, you can bet you will have plenty to get lost in. I like that there was a nice selection of epically scoped tracks mixed with tracks meant merely to build simple sonic textures. Overall it\xE2\x80\x99s an immersive listen that may test your limits of exhaustion if you try to dig through it all in one sitting. This music is meant to be spread across hours upon hours of gameplay. But as a standalone release, it offers some wonderful worlds to discover.

Beyond Earth is a giant entity of a score that some may find hard to tame. Don\xE2\x80\x99t attempt to take it all in with one sitting. I decided to discover each of the 4 composers separately by listening to their music lumped together. You get a better feel of their strengths and what they are offering to this massive game. That became a wonderfully immersive experience for me. The score is designed to fill the air of a strategy based interface, but on it\xE2\x80\x99s own becomes this sort of meditative look on the universe. The music truly does feel like it\xE2\x80\x99s taking you on a cosmic journey, some tracks melodic while other ambient. It may struggle to be continually engaging throughout, but if taken in steps proves to be a worthy experience.sitting. product_title: The Woman In Black 2: Angel Of Death (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
review_headline: Decent Continuation That Feels A Bit Watered Down Versus The First Score
review_body:
The first Woman In Black surprised me immensely, both the film and Beltrami\xE2\x80\x99s score. It was a wonderfully crafted horror tale that utilized atmosphere and production design to get your heart pumping instead of relying on jump scares and cheap editing. Beltrami delivered a score that focused on the characters instead of shadowing the edit, it was eerie and orchestrally lush which made everything feel uneasy and dangerous. While sequels are expected if a horror movie does well, they usually lose the luster of the first outing. The Woman In Black 2, unfortunately follows that trend. With Beltrami pretty much sitting this one out, it was on the shoulders of his additional writers Marcus Trumpp and Brandon Roberts to carry this one home. The result is a pretty fine-tuned lesson in horror scoring that showcases some talent from Beltrami\xE2\x80\x99s two young apprentices even though it\x27s rough around the edges.

The Woman In Black 2 is nothing terribly different from the first score. Beltrami made sure the music stayed on track and didn\xE2\x80\x99t derail into formulaic territory. So the music itself here is lush and foreboding. It doesn\xE2\x80\x99t quite have that personal character touch that made the first score notable, but the presence of character themes woven through the score makes it engrossing. Unfortunately, those character themes aren\xE2\x80\x99t the most memorable. Nothing thematic truly jumps out at you, and that can result in the music feeling a bit muddled. I usually compare horror scores to Hans Zimmer\xE2\x80\x99s The Ring because it\xE2\x80\x99s a notable example of a strong thematic score that focuses on characters yet still exudes danger through foreboding. Also The Ring 2 was taken over by two of Zimmer\xE2\x80\x99s collaborators very much in the same way as The Woman In Black 2 was taken over by Beltrami\xE2\x80\x99s collaborators. However, with The Woman In Black 2 the whole narrative feels like someone dipped their hands in paint and made swashes all across a blank canvass. You can feel patterns and structures, you can follow the path fine. However, it all comes across as muddled and has dull edges verses the sharp strokes you are looking for. The score is effective when it needs to be, but isn\x27t as engrossing emotionally as Beltrami\x27s solo score to the first film.

The Woman In Black 2 is an effective score done in the same spirit of Marco Beltrami\xE2\x80\x99s first outing. It lacks the more defined character shaping that the first score had, and the thematic work is nothing to write home about. It\xE2\x80\x99s still an engrossing score that serves its purpose. product_title: What A Terrible World, What A Beautiful World
review_headline: And so far this review could really be for any Decemberists album because they are so consistently amazing. What isn\x27t clear is
review_body:
The album gets 5 stars because the music absolutely calls for it. The tunes are complex and interesting and they\x27re even complex and interesting in different ways from song to song. The lyrics are thought provoking and very memorable. They are not just a vehicle for the singer\x27s voice; they carry the songs and are very nearly the 6th member of the group.

And so far this review could really be for any Decemberists album because they are so consistently amazing.

What isn\x27t clear is how this album stands on it\x27s own as compared to the other works by this group. In some ways this album almost seems like a sampler to me. There are elements from past albums all throughout this record with a smattering of a definite new sound coming through. I\x27m personally happy for all of it because I wasn\x27t sure we would see another album from these guys. I don\x27t think they need to apologize for The King is Dead or for making any other changes to their sound. Their sound has always changed and evolved from album to album and it is just continuing that trend.

Favorite tracks on this album for me are Lake Song, Til the Water\x27s All Long Gone, The Wrong Year, Make You Better, The Singer Addresses His Audience, Beginning Song and Mistral. Lake Song and Til the Water\x27s All Long Gone are beautiful and haunting and when I listen to them I immediately feel more peaceful.

The Singer Addresses His Audience is a solid piece of music but what it means is really more important here and somehow the song feels personal in a way that you wouldn\x27t think it could. The song allowed the band to gather all their fans into a huddle for a quick explanation, a gentle acknowledgement of the past and a look toward the future and I really love that they did that.

Make You Better is also solid and it\x27s catchy and that\x27s not always a bad thing. It\x27s extremely listenable. Mistral and Beginning Song feel like some of my favorite Decemberists songs and they always make me feel a tiny bit like a felt when I heard my very first Decemberists track off The Crane Wife and was totally hooked.

So I love this album. I love it for the music itself and I love it for what it means for the band and for me as an avid listener. I only covered a few songs off the album but there isn\x27t really a band track on it.

product_title: The Phosphorescent Blues
review_headline: An Outstanding Synthesis of all Previous Work into one Album
review_body:
The Punch Brothers soar beyond their previous works and amaze and dazzle once again. It\x27s not the easy listening of Who\x27s Feeling Young Now, nor is it the at times totally wacko Anti-Fogmatic, and yes I know their previous albums, but those are my references for this review.

It is a perfect synthesis of the two previous albums. There\x27s nothing more I could ask for out of this band. Wonderfully, genre-bending, postmodern music that makes you work for true love of it. It is said of some great books such as Infinite Jest, Gravity\x27s Rainbow, Ulysses, etc. that they "are not beach reading." To myself, this is the perfect phrasing for this album. It is not beach listening. But if you\x27re someone who loves a band that bends the laws of music, taps into impossible timing, and does things with acoustic instruments that would make many old men despise such a thing, claiming it unnatural, then this is an album for you. This is a band for you. Just go ahead an download everything they\x27ve ever done.

product_title: Chicago Fire Season 2 (Original Television Soundtrack)
review_headline: Season 2\x27s Soundtrack Adds More Character And Is A Great Companion To The Season 1 Soundtrack
review_body:
Television scoring has taken leaps and bounds over the recent years with the boom of cable TV series. There is still a difference when you look at network television versus cable television when it comes to a dramatic series. A cable series usually has season long arcs with a shortened episode count (i.e. Game Of Thrones, Breaking Bad, The Knick). A network series will usually have a higher episode count and a narrative that is in itself more episodic, meaning the episodes are not as tightly contained (i.e. NCIS, Law & Order, Person Of Interest). Chicago Fire falls in that latter group. These types of shows make it really difficult for a composer to craft a traditional score. It\xE2\x80\x99s often joked that these are all scored by ominous tones. Thankfully one of the more melodically driven composers out there found himself in the TV market. Atli Örvarsson has surprisingly been able to inject emotionally driven and melodically engrossing music into his scores for not just Chicago Fire, but Chicago P.D. as well.

Season 2 acts as a great companion album to Season 1. Both albums aren\xE2\x80\x99t really structured to provide a narrative flow, but Season 2 is more along the lines of that if that\xE2\x80\x99s what you were missing. So in short, Season 1 album = melodic action / Season 2 album = character development. This album provides some great builds and textures that fit into the soundscape of the show. product_title: The Scorpion King 4: Quest for Power (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
review_headline: Zanelli Delivers Fun Adventure In The Style Of Pirates Of The Caribbean For This B-Movie
review_body:
If there is a will, there is a way. I guess that would be the motto of Universal\xE2\x80\x99s The Scorpion King spin-off franchise. Believe it or not, we are at #4. The films offer up some stupid fun at the cost of good filmmaking, but luckily some of action\xE2\x80\x99s best composers have found themselves on these films. Starting with John Debney, we then saw Klaus Badelt take on #2, Trevor Morris take #3 and now Geoff Zanelli takes a crack at #4. Geoff puts on his best B-movie hat and just has a blast with this score. The music feels born of Pirates Of The Caribbean (which Geoff worked on all 4 films), and plays out like any great adventure score should.

Quest For Power will go through the motions of your standard action/adventure movie. Geoff never treats the movie as a joke though, even though he plays off the cheesy nature of it from time to time. He starts off with a great theme and goes from there. He builds off his main theme throughout most of the score, and it results in some great musical set pieces. The tracks are beefy and long, meaning you get to hear Geoff flex his action builds. The score is very easy to compare to Pirates Of The Caribbean, because like that franchise there is an edge of comedy and fun to it while still having an adventurous scope. So we have a waltzy bounce to the music, which helps add some different dimensions from the robust action cues. Surprisingly, Geoff managed to find a way to inject a sense of awe and wonder as well. You wouldn\xE2\x80\x99t expect that from a score that suddenly breaks out into an electric guitar solo. The second half of the narrative is much weaker musically than the first, but it doesn\xE2\x80\x99t kill the experience. We lose a bit of that thematic momentum entering the third act, but still finish on a strong note.

The Scorpion King 4: Quest For Power won\xE2\x80\x99t be winning any awards and won\xE2\x80\x99t be credited for advancing the art of filmmaking in any direction, but it doesn\xE2\x80\x99t mean you can\xE2\x80\x99t enjoy it. The movie may be unwatchable, but the score is not unlistenable. This is top-notch Zanelli here. In fact I\xE2\x80\x99m just a little bummed that Geoff\xE2\x80\x99s musical efforts will be tied down to a direct to video movie. He demonstrates some amazing thematic gravitas here that would be worthy of a swashbuckling adventure with a $200million budget behind it. product_title: Words and Pictures (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
review_headline: Nice To Listen To, But Uninspired
review_body:
Australian director Fred Schepisi has only worked with 3 composers over his notable career. He started with fellow Australian Bruce Smeaton who scored films like Plenty, Roxanne and A Cry In The Dark for the director. Schepisi then built a notable collaboration with Jerry Goldsmith which resulted in films like The Russia House, Six Degrees Of Seperation and I.Q. After Goldsmith\xE2\x80\x99s death, Schepisi found and stuck with Paul Grabowsky who has scored his past five films including Words And Pictures. For this film we are given a very simple and a very short score. There is an admirable shine and bounce in the music, however due to its limited range it can\xE2\x80\x99t offer much in terms of narrative pull.

The story follows Clive Owen and Juliette Binoche, they play an English teacher and an art teacher respectively. They form sort of a competition as to which form of artistic expression is more valuable, words or pictures. The film follows typical romantic drama structures, and the score is really there only to add that shine on certain moments. It\xE2\x80\x99s a 28-minute score with 26 tracks, so we have lots of tiny cues. When films implement this kind of scoring it always results in an interrupted musical flow. The music here is from a small orchestra with heavy focus on piano and strings. So with that being the case, the score sounds like tons of other romantic dramas that have come before it. There\xE2\x80\x99s some quirkiness, there\xE2\x80\x99s a lightness, some serious moments, and things get romantic when they fall in love. By the time we\xE2\x80\x99ve gone through the motions of the tired plot, we aren\xE2\x80\x99t left with anything truly memorable in terms of style or approach. If I had a romance film about an English teacher and an art teacher, I probably would push my composer to create two themes for these two characters to contrast their differences. Then allow the themes to mesh and blend into a new love theme as the relationship develops. In the end it pretty much ends how it starts.

While the score is nice, it isn\xE2\x80\x99t really memorable or really that unique. You can feel the composer\xE2\x80\x99s hand behind the music, but the approach and structure leave it feeling familiar and disconnected. I feel like there was a missed potential to do something different, and the safe path was what was settled on. Grabowsky\xE2\x80\x99s melodies are pleasant and the score doesn\xE2\x80\x99t offend, it\xE2\x80\x99s fine for the purpose it serves. product_title: Sonny Rollins and The Big Brass Trio & Quintet
review_headline: A FIERY, INVENTIVE SONNY ROLLINS BIG BAND & TRIO GEM
review_body:
Five BIG Stars!! This outstanding but under-appreciated classic jazz CD captures Sonny Rollins, the \x5C\x22Tenor Sax Colossus\x5C\x22, at the height of his powers before he left the music scene for his famous \x27hiatus\x27 and his legendary night-time solo practice sessions on New York\x27s Williamsburg Bridge, preparing for the next phase of his career. In a rare big band setting for half the songs and a hot trio setting for the other half (with great support from bassist Henry Grimes and drummer Charles Wright), Mr Rollins improvises with speed, fire, and swagger, giving a virtual seminar on the art of \x5C\x22thematic improvisation\x5C\x22. This CD shows how awesome and mind-boggling Rollins already was BEFORE his career pause (check out the heralded CD \x5C\x22[[ASIN:B000EGDAI4 Saxophone Colossus]]\x5C\x22 (20 Bit Mastering), and his emergence to record the landmark recording \x5C\x22[[ASIN:B00004ZD5S Bridge]]\x5C\x22 with guitarist Jim Hall.

Tightly and imaginatively-charted by the great arranger Ernie Wilkins, this big band set kicks off with the high-voltage \x5C\x22Grand Street\x5C\x22 with Rollins soaring and swinging, creating a mood that flows through the entire set, featuring fiery solos from cornetist Nat Adderley and guitarist Rene Thomas (the last-note coda has been edited out). \x5C\x22Who Cares?\x5C\x22, \x5C\x22Far Out East\x5C\x22( an allusion to Rollins\x27 famous \x5C\x22Way Out West\x5C\x22), and \x5C\x22Love Is A Simple Thing\x5C\x22 are hard-swinging affairs with Rollins deftly surfing and swooping over the band with declarative thematic phrases. The trio set begins with the Broadway song \x5C\x22What\x27s My Name?\x5C\x22 with Rollins ripping through this song that alternates between 4/4 swing and a latin beat (which went straight to my iPod). The uptempo \x5C\x22If You Were The Only Girl In The World\x5C\x22 (which continues the Rollins trend of selecting unusual songs to bend to his musical will) has free-blowing \x5C\x22thematic improvisation\x5C\x22 thrills and shows the fact that Rollins may be one of the all-time champs at \x5C\x22trading four bars\x5C\x22 with a drummer. The beautiful standard ballad \x5C\x22Manhattan\x5C\x22 is taken at a leisurely pace with lots of room for exploration. Perhaps best of all is Sonny Rollins playing all alone for an entire song on \x5C\x22Body and Soul\x5C\x22 in a superb performance as he turns this classic song inside out at the core. This cult classic is some of the best Sonny Rollins on record and finally in MP3 format with 3 bonus tracks, including \x5C\x22Sonnymoon for Two\x5C\x22. My Highest Recommendation. This is a no brainer win-win to me. Excellent product and I will continue to use it each year for my taxes.

review_body: I purchased this because of the reviews saying that even though it\x27s not as "fancy" as TurboTax, it\x27s easy to follow and some said it was easier. This program showed we were owed back almost $1500 less than the previous 7 years. product_title: Cloverfield
review_headline: Oh, the Horror...the Horror...but not here!
review_body: Ouch...this movie redefined terrible.  When it originally came out, we bailed around mid-point.  J.J. Abram\x27s decision to employ the latest state-of-the-art \x5C\x22Shaky Cam\x5C\x22 left my wife with a migraine and me nauseous.  So, I tried it again on DVD.  Like tuna fish, Cloverfield does not improve with age. The concept is solid, but in almost every other aspect the film falls flat on its face.  We are introduced to a group of self-absorbed twenty-something, cartoon characters who, quite frankly, grew more annoying as the movie progressed.  From the opening bon voyage party for a friend relocating to Japan, to the climax in Central Park I never cared a wit for any of them.  Amazingly, the entire movie is filmed by Hud (T.J. Miller), a self-professed newbie with a video camera, who somehow manages, within the span of less than half an hour, to single-handedly becomes the greatest combat photographer since Robert Capa or Matthew Brady.    While the monster is original and the CGI effects excellent, it isn\x27t enough to rescue the film from the endlessly idiotic decision the main characters make or the wretched visual quality.  For the life of me I cannot understand the military in this film.  It was obvious that this-would-look-cool overruled this-would-be-accurate.  I can\x27t believe Abrams couldn\x27t hire a military adviser for a couple of hours.  Really?  Small arms fire against a creature the size of a 20 story building?  A B2 Stealth bomber? Why? Does the monster have X-Band radar?  Jeez, the monster has been ripping apart Manhattan for hours so collateral damage can\x27t be that much of a concern.  Deploy a squadron of A-10 Thunderbolts.  Their 30mm. depleted uranium shells chew up tank armor like construction paper.  Then when the creature is down, have a C-130 fly over and drop a MOAB (Massive Ordnance Air Blast) the most powerful non-nuclear weapon in the USAF arsenal.  The confinement of the blast within the canyon-like streets of New York would have reduced the monster to jelly.  I could go on but what\x27s the point.    Save yourself a headache and an upset stomach, fire up some popcorn and just watch The Beast From 20,000 Fathoms.

product_title: Alien Storm - Trailer
review_headline: A Good Punishment For Watching Too Much Television
review_body:
Forget the trailer. I just got done suffering through the entire movie! This is unquestionably one of the worst movies ever made. The plot? Ridiculous. The acting? Beyond horrible. The casting? Highly questionable. The script? Craptastic. The special effects? They seemed to rely entirely upon the use of one\x27s own imagination.

This is one of those rare movies that is so ridiculously bad that it isn\x27t even good to make fun of. It just takes bad cinema to a whole new level. How any of these \x5C\x22actors\x5C\x22 made it through 10 continuous seconds of dialogue without busting into laughter or wanting to kill themselves for taking part in such an insult to human intelligence, is beyond me.

The part of the film that caused to to lose all hope of this movie having any redeeming qualities whatsoever was a scene in which the Sheriff is gasping in horror at how aliens had supposedly destroyed this entire city. Cut to the city. Well, it looked painfully normal. As in, no damage. Nothing out of the ordinary. It was as if the people making the film had simply forgotten to add special effects. There seemed to be a light mist hovering over the town, but that was about it. When even a Sci-Fi production is too lazy to add crappy CGI, you get the impression that they had planned all along on making the movie so bad that no one was ever intended to have watched it up to this point.

The only thing I can see this movie as being good for is perhaps as a punishment to your kids for watching too much TV. If this doesn\x27t get them to turn off the television, nothing will.

review_body:
This review is an excerpt from my book \xE2\x80\x9CKiller B\xE2\x80\x99s: The 237 Best Movies On Video You\xE2\x80\x99ve (Probably) Never Seen,\xE2\x80\x9D which is available as an ebook on Amazon. If you enjoy this review, there are 236 more like it in the book (plus a whole lot more). Check it out!

WHITE HUNTER, BLACK HEART: In the early 1950s, director John Wilson (Eastwood) packs up his cast and crew and heads for the shores of Lake Victoria to shoot an African adventure film. He develops a slightly different agenda, however, when he arrives; as he explains to his friend and script doctor Pete Verrill (Fahey), \xE2\x80\x9CWe\xE2\x80\x99ll shoot the film after we\xE2\x80\x99ve shot our elephants.\xE2\x80\x9D Bagging the big game becomes his obsession, and he alienates everyone who opposes him, risking the film, his career and even his life to satisfy his twisted desire.

Discussion: \xE2\x80\x9COf all the wild animals in Africa,\xE2\x80\x9D his producer exclaims, \xE2\x80\x9CJohn Wilson is the wildest!\xE2\x80\x9D This thinly veiled account of filming \xE2\x80\x9CThe African Queen\xE2\x80\x9D under the capricious leadership of John Huston, based on Viertel\xE2\x80\x99s 1953 memoir-cum-novel, attempts to provide some insight into why. Discussions of Huston always use the same phrases: legendary, larger than life, full of Hemingway-style virtues like courage, nobility, honesty. And they are honor-bound to mention the other side of the Huston coin, too; i.e., his reputation as an abrasive, grandiose, bull-headed, egotistical [expletive deleted]. Eastwood manages to portray every one of these character traits in this character study, while performing a low-key impersonation of the man himself, particularly in the measured cadence and singsong drawl of his speech.

The intelligent dialog and Eastwood\xE2\x80\x99s excellent performance paint a vivid portrait of a man ruled by a passion for life and haunted by complex personal demons while remaining oddly committed to simplicity in story and deed. In addition, we attain some insight into the conflicts an artist suffers\xE2\x80\x94and how these conflicts don\xE2\x80\x99t always result in art. The film is fascinating both as a bit of cinema history and as a character study of a rapidly vanishing breed: not the elephant, but men like Huston, driven to drill deeply into the dark continents of their own psyches, sometimes striking oil\xE2\x80\x94but sometimes striking tar.

review_body:
Cannibalistic witches, deadbeat dads, idiotic sidekicks, angry spouses, and incompetent cops collide in the Spanish flick entitled "Witching and Bitching."

All Jose wants is some quality time with his son. His ex-wife berates him, and he has no money. So he hatches a plan to steal some gold. And he includes his son in the plot. It\x27s not a wise idea. But neither is his sidekick Tony, who realizes that involving your son in an armed robbery isn\x27t good parenting, but that\x27s where the extent of his insight ends.

As Jose and Tony try to escape town, they hijack and occupied taxi and find themselves in a town full of cannibalistic witches.

Loopy and campy and, at times, laugh-out-loud funny, "Witching" subscribes to the theory that women are far too hard and demanding on men, and that they (women) need to take their power back from the men who would attempt to subjugate them. It\x27s an interesting message in a tale where the men are dumb and the women are evil. But message aside, for those who like camp, the movie is pretty damn funny.
