product_title: The Man In the High Castle - Season 1
review_headline: Not sure if characters will fight Nazi evil or explore sci-fi
review_body: I was profoundly moved by this concept. It made me realize how much we take for granted that our grandparents were able to defeat fascism. The setting put me into the same moral conflict and DEMANDED that I ask myself how I would respond if we\x27d been raised under Nazi rule. It challenges how we live today: do I do enough to protect freedom of religion and the rights of minorities? How do I protect the rights of the disabled?    I picked up from the film reels that the characters will be trying to explore some sci-fi alternative realities along the way and I think this will be an epic and monumental distraction.    I\x27d much prefer so see tension around the failures of Nazi philosophy. Imagine the last 70 years without the contributions of the Jewish people and all the others the Nazis excluded from their vision. Imagine those years without basic human rights on a worldwide scale.     Will these characters be allowed to learn freely? Travel internationally? How would they do business based on merit rather than inherited genes? Would they have the internet to freely express their thoughts? Would they have any technology invented outside of Germany? Would they marry who they love? How would they worship God as they wish?    This premise is interesting and valuable to explore on its own. Just as the colonies cast off British colonial rule and eventually all of the European colonial powers, the Nazi philosophies would fail over time and be replaced by a more sustainable and inclusive system.

product_title: Behaving Badly
review_body: Enthusiastic but not particularly funny sex comedy about an unlikable dweeb named Rick Stevens (Nat Wolff doing a very poor job of trying to channel Ferris Beuller era Matthew Broderick) who has the hots for goody two shoes classmate Nina Pennington (Selena Gomez) and makes an ill-advised thousand dollar bet with a classmate/mobster\x27s son that he can get into her pants within two weeks.  Rick is a virgin with no game and Nina is an unapproachable no sex before marriage type so the bet literally makes no sense on any possible level.  Rick\x27s mother (Mary Louise-Parker) is an alcoholic who is always passed out or slurring her words.  His best friend\x27s randy mom (Elisabeth Shue) starts having sex with him (well at least the virgin part of Rick\x27s problems is taken care of) which is a bad idea for an assortment of reasons, not the least of which is the fact that her husband owns a gun store and is the jealous type.  To pad out things there are an assortment of supporting characters--Rick\x27s sister Kristen is a stripper who is trying to get into Stanford although at no point does the movie ever allow her to be smart; Rick does odd jobs for her sleazy boss, strip club owner Jimmy Leach (Dylan McDermott--not a natural comedy performer but he definitely makes the effort); there\x27s also something strange about the priest (Jason Lee, underutilized) who hit his parked car at a funeral and doesn\x27t want the police involved.  To add a bit more bad behavior to the mix Rick happens across his dad and his best friend\x27s dad in a hotel room with an underage hooker and takes pictures for blackmail purposes and also finds photographs that indicate the principal is spying on underage high school girls in the locker room--plus there are some Lithuanian gangsters.  While everything is played very broadly with the tone of farce virtually nothing is funny and the various plot strands and outrageous characters never come together in a way that is clever or satisfying.  Mary-Louise Parker and Elisabeth Shue are both wildly over qualified for this material but they deserve credit for their willingness to sacrifice their dignity so completely in pursuit of elusive laughs.  Selena Gomez is adorable but not funny, although she does get to play pretty much the only character who gets out of this thing with her dignity completely intact.  Heather Graham turns up for a couple scenes as a lawyer and is actually amusing, which is pretty shocking under the circumstances.  The Gary Busey outtakes over the end credits are much funnier than anything in the movie.  Behaving Badly\x27s soundtrack is filled with 1980\x27s songs by groups like The Cure, New Order and INXS even though the movie doesn\x27t take place in the 1980\x27s--I\x27m not sure of the reason for that but at least the soundtrack doesn\x27t suck.

product_title: Alien Outpost
review_headline: but all around this was a good movie to see at least once
review_body: It felt campy at parts, but all around this was a good movie to see at least once. The actors did a great job in their roles, the setting was very reminiscent of Restrepo, and the action/CGI scenes weren\x27t too bad at all. The story itself focuses more around the men of Outpost 37 making this feel and act more like a documentary than a science fiction action movie. Probably one of my only griefs with the film is that the technology employed by the humans seemed more modern than you would expect in a world now filled with remains of alien technology to exploit. Of course, this can always be offset by possible answers, such as that the alien technology is too advanced to backwards engineer, or that humanity is still desperately just trying to rebuild from the devastation unleashed upon its world. All around, though, this film is worth at least a one-time see for those that enjoy this type of indie project, scifi-setting environment.

product_title: Day of the Falcon
review_headline: One of my favorite movies. Acting and cinematography is outstanding Antonio Banderas ...
review_body: One of my favorite movies.  Acting and cinematography is outstanding Antonio Banderas has aged quite a bit since The 13th Warrior (another favorite) and is again, a pleasure to watch.  The story line is portrays two, Islamic, Arab leader, who clash over their interpretation the Koran.  Both want what is best for their people, however one tenaciously, inflexibly adheres to rigid ultra conservative interpretation  while the other seeks a more liberal interpretation that will allow drilling for oil so as to bring wealth and a better quality of life for his people.  It is a sensitively sculpted movie that thoughfully exposes the conflicts of  old  vs modern;  literal vs interpretive,  women\x27s value & rights;  young vs old, father vs son;  father;  nomadic existence vs a city based society; and a great number of other yin & yang coupled  topics that provoke thoughtful reflection of the morals & messages this movie conveys and it\x27s relevance and applicability to the  Arab & Islamic world today.  The music is superb. May favorite piece, Father & Son.  I highly recommend this movie.

product_title: Fury
review_body:
I really really enjoyed this film, I actually watched it twice through in two days and enjoyed it just as much as the first time. What I like so much about this movie is that it does not glamorize war, nor does it paint the characters as overt heroes. What it does do as present war as what it really is, horrific. Without in the same time not going over the top. Its motif and approach is very subtle. I have read several reviews where this movie has been labeled similar to a Horror genre War story. And I am inclined to agree.
This movie is absolutely intense from start to finish, and the acting by all the actors is top notch. Especially the 5 main characters, where all the actors in my opinion should get an Oscar nod for because they all did a wonderful job.
As a synopsis of the story without giving away too much, we are given a small snap shot of 4 tankers we find at the tail end of the war pushing through Germany. There assistant driver and front gunner has just been killed and the replacement they get is a fresh recruit 8 weeks into the army that wasn\x27t even trained as a tanker. We then follow the characters through a number of battles, where the focus of the story is very much on the Newbie, Norman.
Near the end of the film after we have watched Norman be presented with the unnaturalness of the horrors of war, and be dubbed "Machine" as his war name.
I very much feel that this an allusion to that man, by his nature, must force himself to not feel, to turn off his emotions and be a cold machine to kill and commit the atrocities which war requires of them. I feel this is summed up in one line said by Pitt\xE2\x80\x99s characters to Norman. After pointing out an entire city on fire in the distance. He says "Many have died in this war and many more will have to die before it is over."
The movie is very much a study of men doing what they can to hold on to their humanity by having to do something which by its extremity, killing scores of other men, who are trying to do the same in a matter of moments over and over again.
The battle scenes are intense, and the ending battle fits the title of the movie so well, as we see through these men\xE2\x80\x99s actions the absolute "fury" which they must embrace to force themselves to face their fears and continue to fight. As the Webster\xE2\x80\x99s dictionary definition states of the meaning of the word fury, "unrestrained or violent anger, rage, passion, or the like."
Overall, there is so much that could be said, and read into about this film, and I honestly feel that that was the point.
This movie in my opinion is showing us for once a non cynical side of humanity, that rather than showing us that all men are monsters by nature, that we are violent, uncaring killing machines, which we certainly can be, but points out that by our natures, we have to force ourselves in many ways to be that way. That really brotherhood of man can and does happen, but points out that for us to kill one another, so brutally, forces us to have to in a way forsake our humanity, and then in some way still be able to keep it. I think this notion of war is certainly what humanity needs to keep in mind as we move into the future. That even though what these men did in the end of the film was "heroic" per say, what was still done was also horrific, as we watch Norman pulling away from the scene in the end of the film, he is told he is a hero as he is placed in a medic truck. And we can see on his face such a shock of mixed emotions... It really leaves the viewer speechless, at the depth of what can be taken from his situation and what he has done...
This is certainly a movie I will watch again, and ponder over for years to come I am sure. product_title: The Lodger
review_headline: Camera and character, rather than plot, drive this late silent film and early Hitchcock classic
review_body:
Near the end of the silent era, Alfred Hitchcock marshaled the format\x27s strengths to create his first masterpiece. 1927\x27s "The Lodger," a dark adapted tale concerning a London serial murderer, employs the kinds of creative camera angles and major plot twists that would later become hallmarks of Hitchcock\x27s work. Consider, for example, the ways Hitchcock signifies vertical space in the lodging house where most of the action takes place. The titular lodger, a pale, staring, partially-obscured figure who could have been imported from a German expressionist horror film of the early part of the decade, lives upstairs. The landlady and her husband, great sources of physical comedy as they clutch each other or trade off yawns, live downstairs. Their beautiful daughter and her detective suitor spend most of their time on the middle floor. When the lodger is the subject of other characters\x27 thoughts or conversation, the camera cuts or pans or pulls back from them to reveal a light fixture that sways almost imperceptibly due to his movements above. A glass floor is also employed to look up at the lodger\x27s feet as he paces the floor. When the lodger or another character climbs or descends the stairs, the camera may look down the middle of the stairwell from directly above. This technique is used in one of the movie\x27s most dramatic sequences, when the lodger appears to leave the house to commit a murder. The landlady listens in terror to every footfall and shutting door, then climbs the stairs to snoop around. A hand on the railing winding up each flight is seen from a nice, symmetrical, overhead viewpoint that a real person in the house could not attain. The effect of seeing feet and hands from dramatic and unnatural angles is exciting, dizzying, and eerie. It helps to create the awe and tension that Hitchcock loves to instill in an audience. He toys with extreme close-ups as well, having the participants in a kiss practically kiss the camera lens. Though not the first director to use intense emotionality or surreal, dreamlike imagery, Hitchcock used them unabashedly to make his first thriller a memorable one.

Every role in "The Lodger" is strongly conveyed without too much reliance on dialogue cards. An early action by the antagonist feels spot-on for a serial killer: in his rented room, he turns around every portrait of a woman so that it faces the wall. The heroine\x27s bathtub scene, in which she undresses behind a veil of steam and wiggles her toes in the water, is typical of a pre-code film, but it doesn\x27t add much to the plot. Like so much else in a Hitchcock film, its primary purpose is to keep the audience entertained. Yet there is a lot of clever character work done with her and the detective protagonist, who tries hamfistedly and mostly without success to endear himself to her. She seems to be in a bind regardless of the story\x27s outcome: either she will be murdered by the villain (when he kisses her, we see rapture in her eyes), or she will settle for a goofball husband (when he kisses her, we see boredom and resignation there). The major twist near the end, while impossible to predict in exact detail, is disappointingly arbitrary, but it paves the way for a resolution of the triangular character drama.

The final shot is a bit unsettling and ambiguous. As the happy couple kisses in the foreground, the killer\x27s catalyst, a marquee sign advertising "Golden Curls," blinks on and off in the foggy distance. Whether this is meant to be darkly funny, or ominous, or whether it merely seems ominous because of the atmosphere that Hitchcock successfully creates for the film, I do not know.director to use intense emotionality or surreal, dreamlike imagery, Hitchcock used them unabashedly to make his first thriller a memorable one.

review_body: I think that the author of the review entitled \x5C\x22Should rename this Farbs R Us\x5C\x22 hits it on the head.    I do have a few philosophical concerns to address:    If the producers/writers/directors truly desired to make a series which would do justice to this historic American era (one of which most children in our public schools are woefully deficient in understanding), they would have done well first of all to utilize proper accouterments. Secondarily, the bawdy and lewd  behavior of those living at Honor Point Plantation (particularly the youngest daughter) is quite immersion breaking, in my estimation, having read extensively the letters, personal memoirs, and literature of that time period, and having detecting nothing of similar impropriety.    Furthermore, if this was altered, it would in no way do damage to the message of the series thus far. As it stands, this series appears to be an over the top anti-slavery gesture against the Southern States. By over the top I mean they are willing to sacrifice historical accuracy by envisioning the Northern states as a virtuous entity against and corrupt Southern entity. Perhaps they are attempting to demonstrate the evil of slavery by presenting this lewdness of the main characters at the plantation. However, part of the insidious nature of the Southern Slave states (note that slaves were not freed in the North until a full two years after the start of the Civil War, by the Emancipation Proclamation), is that they were a self proclaimed society committed to a Christian ethic. I do not mean by this to do any violence to the general abolitionist movement which gained greater momentum in the North. No doubt the abolitionist movement gained more power there due to the industrialized power center of the North not needing slave labor as they possessed a similar resource in the abuse of immigrant labor from Ireland and other places, whereas in the Southern states, those with political power were often those who benefited greatly from the labor of slaves. The point here is that both North and South were corrupt in various senses. The war in question, just like virtually every war in history, was fought over money and power.    The point I wish to stress regarding this miss-characterization of Southern Ladies and Gentlemen (in the literal sense), is that the very propriety and presumed morality of the Southern, church-going, bible-memorizing, liberal-arts-educated elites, is the very thing which makes the practice of slavery so hypocritical and insidious to their society. Therefore, the insertion of 21st century sexual mores into 19th century upper class Southern society does even less to impugn their cause than if it had been presented accurately. In other words, if we see a society practicing slavery which is full of liars and adulterers (cheaters), then we think \x5C\x22Ah, yes that makes sense. They are a bunch rascals after all!\x5C\x22 However, the more poignant message is what history actually bears out; the South was in many ways an ethically and morally fastidious society, so when we see that they practice slavery, it makes their evil all the more odious by virtue of their hypocrisy.    To relate this to popular cinema, consider the Hunger Games. We are not surprised by the extravagant, Bacchanalian indulgence of the Capital after seeing the grisly conditions under which the slave nations are persecuted, particularly in the games. However, if we were to see the oppression we find in the Hunger Games, and find that the culprits are the Hobbits of the Shire, we are all the more shocked.    Yet, I cannot give this series one star because it does have at least a few virtues:  1. Fair acting  2. Beautiful Sets  3. Interesting costuming (withstanding the anachronistic and misappropriated dress of certain ladies mentioned in other reviews)  4. Fairly intense battle sequences that point to the brutality and inherent evil of war  5. A sense of foreboding by some who realize the true cost of war balanced by the joy of the foolhardy who rejoice at the chance to fight    If they could capture the mood and tenor of something like Glory, or God\x27s and Generals, I think they would find a much more impressed audience, and might potentially produce a series worthy of an Emmy with this story.

product_title: Defense Of The Realm
review_body:
Quite a stunning film. Very surprising quality of the script, the acting, and the feel of the film. Top drawer thriller and if it were made today, it would be full of high tech devices and CG work, which is appropriate in many stories to effectively relay the plot and feel of the film, but in this case, DoR can stand alone as one which needs no high tech wizardry to give you a great experience.

In my opinion, this film is a treasure. It is a dark, cold, and eerily filmed story with intrigue and callousness from the bad guys.

By all means, if you wish to see how a great, suspenseful British mystery can unfold, you must see this film.

Kudos to everyone involved in the production.

product_title: Venice/Venice
review_body:
This review is an excerpt from my book \xE2\x80\x9CKiller B\xE2\x80\x99s: The 237 Best Movies On Video You\xE2\x80\x99ve (Probably) Never Seen,\xE2\x80\x9D which is available as an ebook on Amazon. If you enjoy this review, there are 236 more like it in the book (plus a whole lot more). Check it out!

VENICE/VENICE: Dean (Jaglom) is an independent filmmaker attending a film festival in Venice, Italy. One of his numerous interviewers is Jeanne (Alard), a Parisian journalist smitten with his films and their sensitive insights. His wheeling, dealing and schmoozing at the festival, however, shatters her romantic illusions about his screen persona, and she leaves, disenchanted and disappointed. Cut to Venice, California, some time later. Jeanne shows up unexpectedly at Dean\xE2\x80\x99s home to pursue their initial attraction. Problem is, Dean\xE2\x80\x99s already living with someone. Whose true love will overcome all obstacles?

Discussion: \xE2\x80\x9CIt\xE2\x80\x99s really hard to think that real life exists independent of the movies,\xE2\x80\x9D Jaglom-as-Dean admits. He might as well have entitled this film \xE2\x80\x9CReal/Reel,\xE2\x80\x9D as his experiments in cinema faux verit\xC3\xA9 reach new heights of integration here. Or is that new depths of self-indulgence? The film ponders that question too, as well as more important questions, like: How do movies affect our life, especially in terms of self-concept and romantic expectation? And: Are movies\xE2\x80\x94even \xE2\x80\x9Crealistic\xE2\x80\x9D movies\xE2\x80\x94an accurate reflection of life? Illustration is punctuated by discussion in a brave attempt to blur the border between life and film.

Admittedly, the film has its flaws, which are magnified by its audacious experimental nature. It\xE2\x80\x99s occasionally frustrating to watch Jaglom grapple with a subject he can\xE2\x80\x99t quite seem to bring into sharp focus, for instance, and despite his defense and denial of self-indulgence, he occasionally flirts with narcissism. He must have [expletive deleted] big enough to fill a blimp hanger, for example, to expect to pull off a \xE2\x80\x9Crealistic\xE2\x80\x9D scene in which his past, present and future lovers all share a heart-to-heart, and all end up liking, understanding and respecting one another. Now there\xE2\x80\x99s a self-indulgent fantasy!\xE2\x80\x94particularly when he plays \xE2\x80\x9CDean\xE2\x80\x9D as a cranky, obnoxious, abrasive and sometimes downright nasty little egotist.

Yet despite its flaws, this is the film Jaglom has been trying to make most of his life\xE2\x80\x94and it\xE2\x80\x99s as unique and thoughtful an attempt to fuse film and fact as has ever been committed to celluloid.

product_title: Die Hard
review_headline: Heart and the ability to surprise make \x22Die Hard\x22 a gem among action movies
review_body:
The very best action movies are the ones in which the heroes are like us. As fun as a good James Bond movie can be, his been-there, done- that demeanor can\x27t help but put a low ceiling on the stakes. But when the star is more or less an average person swept into a crisis unwilling and unprepared, there is a sense, however artificial, that anything might happen. There is also the possibility that the character will exhibit real emotional range. Deep into "Die Hard," after Bruce Willis\x27s John McClane has wasted over half a dozen terrorists and proved himself a master of gunplay, explosives, and witty repartee many times over, his voice still cracks with fear and heartache. That humanity, buried only shallowly below the swagger and the caked blood (lots of blood), is no small part of the movie\x27s successful formula.

Another is its ability to create surprises between the inevitable moments that define the genre. The fact that bad guys waste their advantage over McClane by toying with him instead of shooting him outright, and that he uses each such reprieve to regain the upper hand, is a given. But there are several situations that seem entirely fresh. Alan Rickman\x27s criminal mastermind, a man of ambiguous motivations, mercurial identity, and palpable confidence, finds himself unexpectedly in McClane\x27s hands. Because the movie has been so carefully plotted and has kept McClane largely isolated from friends and foes alike, this is the first time the two stars have come face to face. We know the bad guy recognizes McClane, but we do not know what McClane knows. The movie seems to move in slow motion for several moments as this inventive situation plays out.

The supporting cast is a veritable parade of cynical expectations and pleasant subversions thereof. Two seemingly expendable black characters, a chauffeur and a cop, show up early in the movie. The cop, Al (Reginald VelJohnson), even mentions a pregnant wife. We\x27ve heard this kind of thing before; in a more typical movie, one or both of them would bite the bullet as a way to create quick pathos. But just when they seem to be on the cusp of ignoble sacrifice or of missing the chance to call for backup, leaving McClane alone and outnumbered for maximum heroism, things get interesting instead. The chauffeur hunkers down in the garage for a long while before coming back into play in a modest way, but Al dodges certain death to become McClane\x27s partner-at-large. "Die Hard" is not normally remembered as a buddy cop movie, but in large measure it is. The dynamic that "Lethal Weapon" defined plays out almost to a tee as the Al and McClane bond over their wives and their careers. The homoerotic dimension of the genre is present, too; McClane and Al\x27s hug at the end is even more emotionally charged than McClane and his wife\x27s. After that, the trope of the bad guy coming back for one last shot happens exactly as it does in Mel Gibson and Danny Glover\x27s earlier film, which like "Die Hard" takes place during Christmas. But "Die Hard," not to be outdone, finds yet a third emotional beat to finish on. McClane\x27s wife Holly (Bonnie Bedelia) is a strong and central figure throughout the movie, which makes a socially-conscious statement about women in the workplace and never places her in sexualized peril. Appropriately but still surprisingly, it is Holly who gets the final word. Also appropriately, she delivers it with her fist.

Not everything about the film is as brilliantly-conceived as McClane\x27s explosive romp through the Nakatomi Plaza or his vulnerable, equitable relationships with his wife and his colleague. The movie continues an action movie legacy of paranoia established at least as long ago as "Dirty Harry." The press and law enforcement bureaucracy are cast as self-interested bumblers, as dangerous in their way as the murderous criminals. It\x27s not an unreasonable position to take, but it\x27s unreasonable to think that a hostage negotiator would be as distracted and preening as Paul Gleason\x27s character, or that an FBI big-shot would be as evidently unstable as Robert Davi\x27s. The casting is right, and these skilled actors\x27 shifty faces could have spoken for themselves without so much on-the-nose dialogue.

This, though, is a quibble. Too much about the movie works, too much is surprising, too many characters are likable and reasonably real, to conclude that "Die Hard" is anything less than one of the best action films ever made. product_title: Guinea Pig\x27s Life
review_body:
I\x27d agree that the film won\x27t do much for people who aren\x27t already GP fans or keep kids entertained (my 4-year-old grand-daughter requires Batman among other superheroes). But as a guinea pig fan, I enjoyed this little film for the following reasons:

1. It focuses primarily on a single guinea pig, exploding the myth that a single GP is necessarily an unhappy if not an abused animal. Attend to its needs and give it minimal but regular attention, and piggie will welcome your handling.

2. The film captures the pig in numerous poses, other than its familiar \x5C\x22fight or flight crouch.\x5C\x22 Instead, we see how a secure guinea pig will lie on its side with legs to the side, balance frequently on its hind legs, and (one of my favorites) occasionally yawn (though it\x27s rare to see, let alone film, the animal with eyes closed.

The minuses (or missed opportunities):

1. The music track completely covers up any sound from the animal. Perhaps the star of this film is too spoiled to be reduced to \x5C\x22wheeking\x5C\x22 for its dinner. Nevertheless, that sound is one of the most distinctive features of the animal (closer to a bird\x27s than a mammal\x27s sound).

2. The film portrays guinea pigs as little more that \x5C\x22perpetual eating machines,\x5C\x22 especially grateful to owners who release them in actual vegetable gardens or in a grassy field untreated by chemicals. Probably true, but it doesn\x27t make for the most gripping drama (kids will tune out in a couple of minutes). There isn\x27t enough attention to piggy\x27s sporadic little happy dances (\x5C\x22pop-corning\x5C\x22), one of their most endearing qualities.

3. It wouldn\x27t hurt to show the day in the life of the owner. Kids are a major nemesis to these fragile animals, frequently stressing them out or dropping them to the floor, resulting in serious damage to their spindly, breakable little legs. And they\x27re not completely harmless. Its teeth never stop growing, and a guinea pig who is really hungry, afraid, mad can easily drive one of those sharp spikes through human skin.

Given the title of this film, a viewer can\x27t help but wonder whether or not the uncharacteristically docile and lifeless guinea pig we see in the last minute is on its \x5C\x22death bed.\x5C\x22 GPs are \x5C\x22prey\x5C\x22 animals, and it\x27s rare to see one looking so defenseless, lying still while passively and resignedly accepting the petting and prodding of a human.arp spikes through human skin. product_title: Why Do We Cover the Mirrors?
review_body:
It took me a while to get past the subject matter and give this series a try, because on the face of it this was not something I\x27m particularly interested in, to be honest.

When I did finally decide to watch the first episode, after reading complimentary critical reviews of the series and thinking that it was worth checking out, I found myself interested. As the series progressed I enjoyed it greatly and was very impressed.

I think that Jeffrey Tambor has done a superb job in a very challenging role, and his personality turns out to be a great fit for the main character. The supporting cast is also a good one, although I think that the subject matter is more heavily oriented towards the various sexual indiscretions of the family members than necessary. I\x27m sure that there are one or two \x27normal\x27 people in the family, although I\x27d have to think for a second to figure out who they might be, and so on reflection maybe that is the point of the show - that \x27normal\x27 is not what we\x27ve always felt it was, or should be.

It could be that this is simply the next evolution of our society, now for the most part welcoming and accepting LGBT peoples (and that very acronym - LGBT - is in itself a relatively new development and one that is more encompassing than we\x27ve had in the past).

What kept me watching Transgender was the characters and how they are portrayed, with sensitivity and compassion. Well done. Give it a try; even if the subject matter doesn\x27t appeal to you immediately, you might find yourself drawn in, as I did.

product_title: There\x27s Something Wrong with Aunt Diane
review_headline: Teach your kids as young as possible
review_body: I think this was well filmed.  It allowed the people who were willing to speak their minds be heard.  The parents of the three sisters killed, because of the hurt, or because they didn\x27t want to make more pain for their relatives, stayed quiet understandably.  They could have added valuable insight I think.  How well do you need to know someone before you let them drive your kids around is a good question.  I\x27ve allowed at least one friend to drive my child when I was in a pinch that I admit I didn\x27t know super well.  If they are a relative, do you automatically give them more trust?  It is easy to trust more than we should when we care about someone and they share some good qualities like Diane did.  Accidents do happen and we can\x27t easily prevent them all, but this was not just an accident.  I drink sometimes as much as two to three margaritas or glasses of wine, but it\x27s when my son is asleep or being babysat by my non drinking mom.  Many of you readers may disagree, but I would not bring vodka on a camping trip with children, especially as young as two and five years old that could  drown in a lake.  I haven\x27t used pot, but using it around children?  Sure there are nice people that use pot and people in pain, but those are not the people I\x27m going to knowing trust my kid with.  I learned something else from watching this video.  Watch out for the extreme perfectionist that won\x27t seek help in time.  Super moms don\x27t exist.  Was she an alcoholic, I don\x27t know enough about her or alcoholism to know.  I think her friends and family likely knew she used even around kids, but thought she was in control.  Killing the pain of a tooth, maybe she was.  I can\x27t tell you how many people I\x27ve met that think they can drink without waiting the necessary amount of time for it to wear off.  The eight year old tried her best to get help.  We must teach our kids as soon as they can understand it to never get into a car with someone they have seen drinking or smoking pot.  Maybe, when they are eleven or twelve they might be to the point that they can learn to read a blood alcohol chart like the dmv sends out and parents can rightly convince them that they ate and waited the appropriate amount of time before driving.  Teach kids at a young age to even recognize the different types of alcohol and the smell of pot.  And all of you "were just partying a bit" parents that do this when you should be babysitting, please wake up.  You "may" be in control with your colada to relax, but getting your kids used to this atmosphere is dangerous.  Okay, I\x27m on my high horse, and like I said I do enjoy a little buzz like many do, but I was tought never, even with a tooth ache to drink ANY alcohol in a car.  I was told very young about drunk people driving on the wrong side of the freeway.  Don\x27t keep your kids innocent about this.  Start young, you may save a life.  My condolences to all.

product_title: Nights With Theodore (English Subtitled)
review_headline: SOMEWHAT EXPERIMENTAL FRENCH CINEMA WITH A UNIQUE ROMANCE AT ITS CENTER THAT CAN STILL BE ACCESSIBLE
review_body:
LOVE STORY WITH AN ODE TO PARIS\x27 BUTTES CHAUMONT PARK THROWN IN (some analysis taken from directors comments)

I confess, I had to seek out comments from the director to understand some of the more artistic elements of the film. I do enjoy French cinema a great deal and I found the relationship at the center of this tale intriguing and the history of the gorgeous park engaging. However, the movie as a whole really didn\x27t deliver much beyond that for me. The movie begins with a true history of the park with old film footage mixed in. The fact the location was used as a gallows from the 13th century and the revitalization by Napoleon III are touched, as well as many of it\x27s geographical points of interest. The movie then steps one notch from its informal documentary feel into a closer tone and heavier musical backdrop to discuss more mysterious points of it\x27s history. The movie then takes the final larger step from reality into the fictional portion of the story as the two central characters are seen meeting at a party in Paris. These steps from history into fiction are the more experimental part of the film, but the relationship at its center can be accessible for those who are into it. As a whole, I just felt it lacked the soul and feeling I expected, though I would still call the film a success.

THE PLOT (No spoilers): Anna and Théodore meet at a party in Paris and find an immediate attraction. On a whim, they run out and climb a fence to enter the gorgeous Buttes Chaumont Park at night though it is not allowed. As they explore, talk, and touch, their attraction draws closer and they decide to spend the night. Following the encounter, they are still drawn to each other and the mysterious park. They begin an odd relationship meeting over and over each night, but just in the park. The movie describes the park as being a somewhat powerful place and there are people in the story who meet there and believe the park gives them energy. As the relationship progresses, some people around Anna express concern over her withdrawal and the relationship. Meanwhile, Théodore seems to have some sort of condition that we don\x27t understand.

OTHER THOUGHTS: The movie is well acted and the park is beautiful to be sure. The odd premise of the romance is intriguing from a fantasy perspective and I did wonder what was happening and how it would resolve itself. In my opinion, the viewer can explore or savor the relationship itself even without pondering the artistic side. Ultimately though, I just couldn\x27t completely engage in the film. I suspect that most U.S. audiences will not be attracted to this film unless they are really into unique or experimental cinema, or the park itself. As I said, the discussion on the artistic elements and the ode to the park were taken from director\x27s comments. So, I am not making this up just to pretend I understood the film. I purchased this for my daughter through Amazon Instant Video. I had no trouble with my purchase, no picture problems or play issues. I was expecting the picture to be dull, considering the age of the movie, but it is not. In fact I\x27d say the picture is more vibrant than I remember it. product_title: Mugshots: Beth Carpenter
review_headline: Murder, Sure, but the Ol\x27 \x22Hair Flip\x22 Thing?
review_body: (2015-02-08:  changed my score from a 3 to a 2.  After thinking about it, this episode lacks objectivity to such a high degree that I cannot recommend it.)    While watching, you will most likely groan, \x5C\x22OK.  I can understand Beth Carpenter wanting this guy dead.  I get it.  But a hair flip?  Really?\x5C\x22    Naturally, I\x27m being a little facetious, and it might be the case that the actual woman doing the ol\x27 \x5C\x22hair flip\x5C\x22 in this documentary is really just an actor.  (Whatever happened to the word \x5C\x22actress\x5C\x22 by the way?  Another casualty of Political Correctness?). But if I were up on murder charges, even if I were a gal, ESPECIALLY if I were a gal, I might get that ol\x27 mane cut and avoid the whole \x5C\x22hair flip\x5C\x22 thing while being flown back to America, or dragged into court.  It just isn\x27t very becoming.    Even though I\x27m a \x5C\x22fan\x5C\x22 of true crime -- the genre, not the crimes themselves, for those who like parsing sentences -- I\x27ve complained ad nauseum that our judicial system seems to always want to give females a free ride when it comes to crime.  I just watched and reviewed \x5C\x22There\x27s Something Wrong with Aunt Diane,\x5C\x22 and this theme seems to follow suit here.  But with \x5C\x22Mugshots,\x5C\x22 at least with this episode, it seems as if the documentary wants to paint a rosy picture of Ms. Carpenter, at least until just before the end, and put the blame on all of the males in her life.  She did bail to Ireland -- which at least implies that she knew she might be indicted -- after all, and while the show tries to say that she flew there because that country doesn\x27t extradite criminals in death penalty cases, I think it was for another reason:  she has red hair.  So she\x27d fit in.  And she could do the ol\x27 \x5C\x22hair flip\x5C\x22 thing with that red hair.  Makes sense, right?    Well, for you people out there thinking about committing murder, I would think long and hard about it first.  But ultimately, I would recommend that you take a pass; it\x27s only a matter of time before you go to jail.  But if you can\x27t follow that advice, don\x27t let other people know about the murder at least, or even worse than that, don\x27t hire someone to do your bidding.  You\x27ll only get ratted out in the end, and end up with at least a ratty hairdo.    And more importantly, if you\x27re up on murder charges, there is one thing you should never do:  the ol\x27 \x5C\x22hair flip\x5C\x22 thing.  It just makes you look more guilty.

product_title: The Man In the High Castle - Season 1
review_headline: High Quality Cinema from Amazon and Ridley Scott
review_body: I must admit to being a long-time classic SF reader and PKD fan of many years standing.  So I was thrilled to see this story out as a dedicated TV production. The pilot is true to the spirit of the book (to the end of the first episode).  The overall ambiance of an alternate future in which a dismembered USA has adapted to defeat in war 20 years before by Germany and Japan is both chilling and believable.  The details are which convince a viewer here.  There is a casual scene involving a helpful patrolman (himself a US Army veteran) interacting with a male lead character where a fall of ash on Tuesday afternoon from a local hospital is explained and accepted without surprise.  This vignette indicates how far the country has evolved (?) toward NAZI values.    The female lead is striking and compelling in character. Her portrayal of a person born after the defeat and raised in Japanese-America is fascinating in its detail.  She avoids eye contact only with Japanese men in positions of petty authority while maintaining her sense of self in these situations.  She is equal to the men in her Ikido (spelling?) class in every respect.  She is decisive as the plot sends her toward an uncertain destination.    The direction, cinematography, special effects, musical score, costumes and sets evoke an alternate history of the early 1960s that is close to but not quite the same as the one that many of us lived.  A key feature between the Eastern and European cultures about which the book turns was introduced early in the pilot episode (twice I believe) but in a mater-of-fact way.  If the remaining episodes are as excellent as the pilot, this series will stand with other PKD inspired material such as \x5C\x22Blade Runner\x5C\x22 as among the very best hard SF ever brought to the screen.

product_title: The New World
review_body:

Even the way things unfold, such as the \x27Gestapo\x27 show up to raid the factory and find the truck was so poorly executed.

Terrible acting, directing and incongruous design. Iron Railway style Mono-Rail systems that weren\x27t in use at the time; American weapons being used that weren\x27t even produced yet; French Citroen 2CV cars that would not have been used (why are most of the cars in this pilot French?); Aikido movement and etiquette that is false and incorrect. Such a terrible job. What a shame.

product_title: Tusk
review_headline: Very Good for a Movie That Patronizes Its Audience
review_body:
I wavered between 3 and 4 stars, but finally decided to be generous. Honestly, I would give it 3.5 stars. As many others have said, this is Kevin Smith\x27s version of The Human Centipede. However, The Human Centipede is simply sick for sickness\x27s sake. Tom Six got the idea from a combination of Josef Mengele, and an inside joke about pedophiles being punished by having their mouths, "stapled to a fat truck driver\x27s ***." Tusk, on the other hand, has more of a point to make, whereas The Human Centipede was really just about being as horrible as possible simply for shock value.

That said, I think Kevin Smith hammers the point home a bit too hard. We\x27re not stupid. We get that that Wallace had become an insufferably insensitive excuse for a human being, and it was only upon being mutilated into an animal that he truly begins to recognize his humanity. This point would have been clear enough without constant, unrelenting references about the differences between man and human ("who on earth would want to be human, anyway"), and what it means to be human ("it\x27s good to cry; it means you\x27re human").

Yeah, we get it. We\x27re not stupid. Good movie; I just felt it underestimated the intelligence of its audience. People who are watching films like this are smart enough to understand themes without having them shoved in our faces. If we were that dumb, we\x27d be watching Thor or Predator vs. Alien.

Honestly, I\x27ve not felt so patronized to since Don\x27t Blink (another good movie that ruins itself by assuming its audience is too stupid to pick up on themes).

product_title: We\x27ll Never Have Paris - Trailer
review_headline: GET WHAT OUT OF YOUR SYSTEM?
review_body:
Quinn (Simon Helberg, writer, director) is almost dysfunctional from his phobias and not as funny as Bill Murray in "What About Bob?" He wants to propose to Devon (Melanie Lynskey) a college professor and girlfriend of 10 years. They go back to High School. However, whenever the moment is upon them, she must leave. Quinn works in a flower shop and confides his plan to Kelsy (Maggie Grace) his hot long time friend. At this point she informs Quinn of her love for him and desire to do the nasty. This sets off a downward and ruinous spiral as Quinn attempts to win back the love of his pathetic life, not knowing when to speak or when to shut up.

Quinn, our protagonist was basically unlikeable. He is a man with flaws on top of his flaws. It is as if someone explained to Simon Helberg what a Woody Allen movie was like and he attempted to create one without ever seeing one and on half the intellect. This is a different type of romantic comedy that doesn\x27t feel like a romantic comedy but more like a tragedy. It will certainly attract some die hard indie fans, but I am not one of them.

product_title: The Man In the High Castle - Season 1
review_body:
Philip K Dick is one of my top 10 favorite authors, but I hadn\x27t yet read this book. When I saw that Amazon was making a TV series based on it, I immediately added the book to my queue in front of everything else and forced myself to wait until I was halfway through the book to watch the show.

I think this show holds up really well to the book. You can\x27t just get mad at a show because it isn\x27t exactly like the book, there are some things that just don\x27t translate to the screen. So there are some variances. Quite a few, really. But they stay true to the meaning of the book and the characters. Some things are cut, some are added, all to try to get the powerful punch that Philip K Dick delivers in his books into the TV. I think it works.

And that\x27s a pretty freaking solid review from an avid reader who usually hates TV and movie adaptations of books.

product_title: Strange Magic (Plus Bonus Features)
review_body:
I have seen many musicals, and this is a musical times ten. There is literally a song every minute. It feels like the story is just setting up for the next song, not the other way around. So, something will happen for about one minute, and then there is a song for about three minutes, and then something else happens for about one minute, and then there is another song, and over and over, and that is the whole movie.

There are no original songs. All of the songs have been on the radio a million times, and many of the songs are very old. Many of the songs did not fit the situation, so it felt like the story was just an excuse to set up for another song.

The entire movie is about "love." Falling in love, being in love, wanting to be in love, and heartbreak. And everything has a song.

There is so much more that could have been done with this movie. The animation is good, but it could have been better. For example, the fairies could have been dressed in beautiful dresses or gowns, but they were not. The fairies had plain solid purple wings, when they could have had beautifully colored wings like butterflies. Some of the characters were really ugly and horrible to look at. The scenery, such as the trees and flowers, could have been more beautiful. I was looking for more beauty and fantasy. At one point, there was a kaleidoscope which was very beautiful and colorful, but that scene was very short.

There was a riddle in the movie, which I guessed immediately. The ending was predictable. It wasn\x27t funny. It wasn\x27t drama. It was just a weak and predictable story with a song every single minute.

product_title: The Bridge On The River Kwai
review_headline: A powerful statement on the madness of war
review_body:
Why I waste my time watching all of the newest films that come out (of course, not all of them are bad) when there are plenty of tried-and-true classics waiting to be discovered is something I\x27ll never completely understand. It\x27s not even like I have the excuse that I don\x27t know about them, or even don\x27t have the time (because I do). Still, I do like the feeling of seeing something for the first time and THE BRIDGE ON THE RIVER KWAI delivered everything I expected and more. The story is set during WWII and is about a group of British POWs who arrive at a Japanese labor camp in the Burmese jungle (modern-day Myanmar). They are tasked with building a bridge over the Kwai River, but initially have difficulty because the camp\x27s commander Colonel Saito (Sessue Hayakawa) has a clash of wills with their own commander, Colonel Nicholson (Alec Guiness). There is also an American POW, Shears (William Holden) who manages to escape but is \x5C\x22recruited\x5C\x22 to lead a team back to the jungle to blow up the bridge.

If there\x27s one thing that David Lean knows how to do, it\x27s craft an epic film and that\x27s exactly what he did here. It did drag a little bit for me in the first hour, but it was an engrossing watch after that point. It almost goes without saying that this film is perfect from a technical standpoint, and some truly great images were captured. The acting was also just as good, especially from the three key players: Alec Guiness, Sessue Hayakawa, and William Holden. Each of them brought their A-game and turned in probably the best performances of their entire careers. One aspect of the story I really liked was the psychological battle of wills that occurs between Saito and Nicholson. Both of them were equal in rank, but also similar in their approach to their own specific situations. One might say that they were cut from the same cloth. William Holden rounds out this trio of characters by portraying a man who is drafted for a difficult task in spite of his desire to just keep on surviving, and in a cruel turn of irony, puts him at cross-purposes with Nicholson who feels like he is doing good work by building the bridge.

Although the film plays it rather close to the vest in terms of message-making, only really making its statement in the final minutes, I thought that it handled the subject of war in a rather balanced and mature way despite taking a stand against it. Nobody is turned into a villain, instead having each major character be an unwitting foil to the other in a way that suggests what is later explicitly stated (by the medic) as madness. It\x27s not perhaps the most original of anti-war statements, but it was portrayed to extremely good effect. Also, the last 20 minutes or so is as riveting and tense as anything that has come out since. Granted, it\x27s not perfect as there is a rather superfluous romance between Shears and his nurse but, studio-mandated love interest aside, this film stands as not only one of the best anti-war films ever made, but one of the best films period.ust keep on surviving, and in a cruel turn of irony, puts him at cross-purposes with Nicholson who feels like he is doing good work by building the bridge.

product_title: The Frame
review_headline: If you were looking for another INK, this isn\x27t it.
review_body: One gets the feeling that Jamin Winans got a laundry list of criticisms from his previous film INK and tried to make a more mass audience friendly picture with THE FRAME.  I loved INK.  For me, that film has a very special personal/spiritual resonance to it, and despite any awkwardness of style, it had such a strong emotional message about redemption that I feel it is one of, if not the best indie fantasy films ever made.  I covered it lovingly on my youtube review channel.  I\x27d been looking forward to the Frame for the past few years but when I finally sat down to watch it, I was blown away by the superficial level it took with it\x27s storytelling, implying a link between worlds that makes the plight of each central character meaningless by comparison. Breaking the fourth wall for 2 hours without a satisfying punchline. Don\x27t get me wrong, this film is expertly done for a small budget, it\x27s exciting and tense, but there are no arcs for the characters and no resolution to the problem. What I get from the FRAME is that Jamin Winans wants to work in television, and I think the Frame could have easily been cut to be an hour length pilot, or a 20 minute short.  Definitely rent it first.

review_body:
This review is an excerpt from my book \xE2\x80\x9CKiller B\xE2\x80\x99s: The 237 Best Movies On Video You\xE2\x80\x99ve (Probably) Never Seen,\xE2\x80\x9D which is available as an ebook on Amazon. LEVIATHAN: Three miles beneath the Atlantic, deep-sea miners extract precious metals from the ocean floor during an \xE2\x80\x9Cextremely hazardous\xE2\x80\x9D 90-day shift. When they find a sunken Russian ship, Sixpack (Stern) confiscates the safe, which is filled with the personal effects of numerous crewmembers who died from some mysterious malady. He also filches a bottle of vodka, which makes him deathly ill\xE2\x80\x94then kills him. The Doc\xE2\x80\x99s (Crenna) best guess is a virus causing genetic alteration. Good call: It transforms Sixpack into a slimy, gut-crunching monster, half human, half deep-sea creature. When the thing goes on a rampage looking for new meat and tearing up the station in the process, can any of the others escape? And why is The Company dragging its feet in sending in a rescue?

Discussion: Call it \xE2\x80\x9CAlien from the Abyss\xE2\x80\x9D; when first released, the comparisons were inevitable (and fair). And how could it measure up to either? As a pastiche, however, it\xE2\x80\x99s entertaining enough for those who enjoyed the originals. So the script\xE2\x80\x99s not original. So what? It\xE2\x80\x99s still a solid thriller, and the flick\xE2\x80\x99s main draw lies not in its oft-told story of sacrificed miners versus an alien killing machine and a corrupt corporation, but in its suitably detailed sets, its atmospheric photography, and its cast of second bananas with appeal. And it\xE2\x80\x99s not as though the writers were trying to put one over on us; the fact that it\xE2\x80\x99s a conscious homage to \xE2\x80\x9CAlien\xE2\x80\x9D is made perfectly clear with the inclusion of a slyly clever shot panning across a big bowl of popcorn just prior to the chest-chomping monster\xE2\x80\x99s first appearance. Enjoy it for what it is: a mutant B-remake of two superior thrillers.

product_title: A Clockwork Orange
review_headline: \x22The Greatest Director of the Latter Half of The 20th Century\x22
review_body: "A Clockwork Orange" (1971) and "Paths of Glory" (1957) are my 2 favorite Stanley Kubrick films.  Malcolm McDowell gives an absolutely brilliant performance, and Kubrick (as always) is stunning in his direction of this film. Many people don\x27t realize what a low budget film (for him) this was. I have all of his films; even the ones he took out of circulation. The blu-ray disc ofd "Clockwork" (2007) has hours of wonderful interviews, commentary, etc. I believe Kubrick is the greatest director of the latter half of the 20th century, bar none. All of his films are timeless. Whether you loved him or hated him, you had to respect him. He was a director\x27s director. He never repeated himself; all of his films are of a different genre. As Martin Scorcese said in one of the interviews, it is almost impossible to stop watching a Kubrick film, once you have started; whether it is the beginning, middle or near the end. I loved him dearly, and he is missed by so many. Get your hands on a copy of "Stanley Kubrick; a Life in Pictures".  You will understand what I am writing about.

review_body:
This review is an excerpt from my book \xE2\x80\x9CKiller B\xE2\x80\x99s: The 237 Best Movies On Video You\xE2\x80\x99ve (Probably) Never Seen,\xE2\x80\x9D which is available as an ebook on Amazon. If you enjoy this review, there are 236 more like it in the book (plus a whole lot more). Check it out!

PAPERHOUSE: 11-year-old Anna (Burke) is experiencing nightmares and odd fainting spells. Even more curious, whenever she\xE2\x80\x99s unconscious she finds herself in the same landscape: an open field in which the only structure is the strangely shaped house she\xE2\x80\x99s been sketching in her notepad. As she falls more ill, her dreams continue\xE2\x80\x94and evolve. Eventually she enters the house and meets its sole inhabitant, Marc (Spiers), a boy about 12, crippled from the waist down.

Only when Anna\xE2\x80\x99s doctor mentions she\xE2\x80\x99s treating a boy named Marc for paralysis does Anna realize her drawings are a door into an inner world where she and Marc are bonded emotionally\xE2\x80\x94and that whatever she draws comes true. Too bad, because she\xE2\x80\x99s recently added a dark stalker to her drawing\xE2\x80\x94and then lost the drawing. In her fever dreams, she and Marc are able to fight off this evil figure long enough for Anna to regain her health. Marc, however, is not so lucky, and a distraught Anna must decide whether to forget him...or to follow him into a world beyond drawings, beyond dreams\xE2\x80\x94and beyond death.

Discussion: How thin is the membrane between fantasy and reality? Is it permeable by osmosis in both directions? One of the nicest things about this film is that we never doubt the actuality of the psychic connection between the kids; it\xE2\x80\x99s proven real, and its mystery is never cheapened by any pseudo-scientific explanations. The manner in which Anna\xE2\x80\x99s inner and waking worlds overlap, and the correspondences between them, are logical, consistent and clever: The two worlds are, we realize, not separated by fact, but only by one\xE2\x80\x99s state of mind. Although the film gets off to a slow start, it\xE2\x80\x99s worth thewait: It\xE2\x80\x99s filled with beautiful, honey-hued photography as well as startling and haunting imagery. The plight of the abject adolescent, dealing with grief far too deep for her tender age, is effectively poignant, and the bittersweet ending strangely satisfying.

product_title: Transformers: Age of Extinction
review_headline: The \x22best\x22 Transformers yet.  Great visuals and effects, better cast and acting than in the previous films - no Shia LaBeouf!!
review_body:
I find it a bit funny that those who do not enjoy these kind of movies in general would go ahead and watch it and then complain that the story wasn\x27t great, the characters were one dimensional, that its all mindless action, or that they wasted their time. I don\x27t watch an action movie expecting an intricate story, complex & developed characters, or interesting dialogue. Its only the fourth Transformer movie by the same director so you really should know by now what to expect. Its like watching an Expendables movie and making similar complaints.

The Good: I found the cast and acting in general to be much stronger than in the previous installments. Wahlberg was a much better lead character than Shia Labeouf(can\x27t stand him), Tucci was pretty good, and Kelsey Grammar playing a villain was probably the best part of the film. Of course I can\x27t complain about seeing the beautiful Li BingBing in a movie either. The visuals/effects are great, and I\x27m really glad the final confrontation wasn\x27t anti-climatic like in the 2nd and 3rd films where after a tough struggle, Optimus suddenly tears his opponent apart very easily in a matter of seconds. The character designs and action sequences were more streamlined and less jumbled. The main villain was actually a bit menacing like Megatron was in the first film.

The Bad: The biggest problem for me is that there is no tension, suspense, or surprise in any of the films in the series. And of course there are a TON of things that don\x27t make sense in the action scenes, such as Lockdown & Cemetary Wind simply letting Optimus drive off during their first encounter, the countless missiles that miss the Autobots, Optimus\x27 arms having less power than a tow truck, and the calm residents inside the apartment who didn\x27t seem to notice all the gunfire and explosions happening right outside and on the roof. Lame, corny stuff like the samurai Transformer having a Japanese accent, another having a beard and smokinga cigar(?), and Optimus riding a dinosaur while holding a sword really took away from the film. The female lead was annoyingly useless and the boyfriend character was a bit weak as well.

I didn\x27t mind the problems so much since I went in expecting it. I just wanted to relax, watch some cool action sequences, and have some good escapist fun, which the film delivered.

product_title: Lowlife
review_headline: This is why independent movies matter - an unforgettable film made with $5,000 and a lot of passion
review_body: ***** 5 Stars ***** If David Lynch had made this movie (think \x5C\x22Eraserhead\x5C\x22) it would have been a big deal.  But he didn\x27t - it was made on a less-than-shoestring budget, with borrowed equipment, friends working for free, and a guerilla film attitude - by amazingly talented people who had never made a film before.  And it is the best film about drug addiction and obsession I have ever seen (even if there are no needles).  It is as surreal as \x5C\x22The Naked Lunch\x5C\x22 but more disturbing.  Much of the film is in black and white, and masterfully done - many shots are every bit as good as early Lynch or early Polanski (\x5C\x22Knife in the Water\x5C\x22 or even \x5C\x22Repulsion\x5C\x22), but my favorites are the shots that feature Nova Scotia\x27s landscapes - they are like Ansel Adams photos come to life (although this is Nova Scotia, not a sunny and more forgiving California).  The music score is unique and just right, much like GYBE (if you recognize this acronym, just stop here and watch the film).  And like GYBE, the creators are a Canadian team composed of musicians and other talented artists.  Based in Nova Scotia, Seth Smith - the film\x27s writer / director - is the frontman of the band Dog Day, and also a very talented graphics artist.  But Smith\x27s vision could not have worked without the extraordinary acting of Kate Hartigan (Elle) and Chik White (Asa). Check out dogdaymusic dot com and sethsmith dot info, and also indiegogo dot com (search \x27lowlife\x27) to learn more about the film, the music, and this very talented crew.  I DO NOT KNOW THESE FOLKS - I live in Northern California and have never been to Nova Scotia ... I was simply blown away by the film and I want you to watch it, too.  Thanks for reading!

product_title: Pariah
review_headline: coming out/coming of age story with a great cast
review_body: 4.4 stars    Wow!  What a hidden gem among all the lez-themed films out there.  The casting/acting is superb, the story is very realistic, and you don\x27t have to be a particular race to relate to this one.  I\x27m not a teenaged black girl, but plenty of the characters from this film are familiar and were part of my own coming out story as a full-fledged lesbian (the bisexuals, conservative parents, obnoxious sister, awesome best pal, etc).  I\x27m not surprised a number of reviewers said they watched it for a class or that it\x27s honest and well-developed enough to promote a good deal of discussion.    Alike (pronounced A-lee-kay) is a 17 yr old middle class black lesbian living in Brooklyn and struggling with both her sexuality and the expectations of her overly conservative parents.  Her mother (Kim Wayans) is traditional, religious, and very controlling.  She doesn\x27t approve of her daughter\x27s tomboy nature or her masculine best friend Laura (a stud), so she\x27s doing her best to ensure her daughter doesn\x27t morph into a man.  She buys her feminine clothes she\x27s forced to wear and sets her up with a \x5C\x22normal\x5C\x22 friend she\x27s forced to spend time with.  Alike\x27s father (Charles Parnell) isn\x27t much more helpful.  He\x27s a stern looking cop with a conservative exterior... but mostly absent on a number of levels and preoccupied with his philandering deeds.    As a result, Alike (Adepero Oduye) has a few secrets.  She changes her clothes on the way to school into her preferred dyke-wear.  She explores the local girl club with her bud Laura (Pernell Walker).  And she admires girls from afar. She\x27s also an in-betweener... not the stud her best friend is, though she kind of emulates her... and she\x27ll never be the femme her mom wants her to be.  Finding your way through this spectrum is always an interesting journey to me, lol.  Alike is also an aspiring writer/poet and spends a lot of time writing down her perceptions on life... which are far more limited at the start of the film as she isa closet case virgin who is afraid to act or act up.    Once Alike takes that first step in exploring other women... things get more intense at home.  But she learns.  She learns some hard lessons... about women, about family, about best friends.  I appreciated this honesty, and I\x27m sure this helped her to grow as an artist, but it also made the story more than a little angsty and sad.  Even though the conclusion leaves us at the threshold of her adulthood with plenty of implied hope... I really wanted a better ending for Alike.  Don\x27t get me wrong... there are some definite highs in the movie... it\x27s not all angst.  But, well, I just wanted to see Alike matched beyond the elusive bisexual and the flakey bi-curious... and to find an emotionally available woman who will give her the love she deserves.    Yeah... I like my happy HAPPY endings, what can I say.    Well worth watching... but a sharp taste of real life here.  A full cast of likable talent here... don\x27t know why I\x27m not seeing them in more mainstream movies.      There is kissing and implied sex here. And no lesbians die in the end...  :)

product_title: Wings of Desire
review_body:
This review is an excerpt from my book \xE2\x80\x9CKiller B\xE2\x80\x99s: The 237 Best Movies On Video You\xE2\x80\x99ve (Probably) Never Seen,\xE2\x80\x9D which is available as an ebook on Amazon. If you enjoy this review, there are 236 more like it in the book (plus a whole lot more). Check it out!

WINGS OF DESIRE: Angels walk among us. Innocent children sometimes see them. The angels listen in on our whispered inner monologs, often offering a comforting touch. One among them, Damiel (Ganz), is tired being a disembodied spirit, envying us our ability to touch, to feel, to love. When he becomes enamored of lonely French trapeze artist Marion (Dommartin), he decides to trade an eternity of observation for a few short mortal years of living experience. But first he must locate the missing Marion. Will destiny\xE2\x80\x94or a guardian angel\xE2\x80\x94allow their paths to cross again?

Discussion: Would you trade eternity for love? Renounce immortality for a transient, yet sensory, life? Evidently many angels do, as the lightness of their ethereal existence contrasts with the weight of their burden of separation. They speak, appropriately enough, in a kind of Rilkean poetry, and seeing the world through their eyes, as they pass through a library or a train car, allows us a glimpse of the ineffable sadness and longing that is our condition and their perception.

With his world-weary face and deep, soul-filled eyes, Ganz makes a perfect angel, and a fine human, too, responding with childlike delight to the mundane\xE2\x80\x94colors, coffee, cold\xE2\x80\x94and leaving us with one final question: Is it possible that a mortal life lived in love and wonder can transcend even an angelic existence? A lovely, somber dirge, filled with vivid imagery and a deep appreciation of the fleeting.

product_title: The Exorcist 2: The Heretic (1977)
review_body:
This review is an excerpt from my book \xE2\x80\x9CKiller B\xE2\x80\x99s: The 237 Best Movies On Video You\xE2\x80\x99ve (Probably) Never Seen,\xE2\x80\x9D which is available as an ebook on Amazon. If you enjoy this review, there are 236 more like it in the book (plus a whole lot more). Check it out!

EXORCIST II: THE HERETIC: It\xE2\x80\x99s been four years since Father Merrin (von Sydow) exorcised a demon from Regan (Blair), now a typical teen with a gift for healing troubled youth. But Merrin\xE2\x80\x99s protégé, Father Lamont (Burton) has been assigned to investigate his death, which risks opening up old wounds\xE2\x80\x94and summoning up old demons. Regan\xE2\x80\x99s psychiatrist, Dr. Tuskin (Fletcher), is wary, but allows Lamont and Regan to use an advanced biofeedback device to hypnotize themselves into a \xE2\x80\x9Csynchronized altered state of consciousness,\xE2\x80\x9D where they inhabit a shared virtual reality of memory.
The machine proves scientifically that the demon is real\xE2\x80\x94and still locked up inside Regan. Further \xE2\x80\x9Ctrips\xE2\x80\x9D convince Lamont that a tribal healer in Africa, also once possessed by this demon, holds the key to triumph over the \xE2\x80\x9CKing of the Evil Spirits of the Air.\xE2\x80\x9D Risking his life to find the grown boy is the easy part. But he\xE2\x80\x99ll risk his faith, and Regan\xE2\x80\x99s life, in a final confrontation\xE2\x80\x94and their minds will become the battleground for this ancient evil.

Discussion: It\xE2\x80\x99s decades old and the most reviled sequel in cinema history. So why the five star rating? Well, I think I know why audiences hated it\xE2\x80\x94and why it should be given a second chance. People went to this sequel expecting more of the same: more turnstile heads; more pea soup puke. What they got was a philosophical treatise on science and religion working in harmony; a psychological study of a good man suffering a crisis in faith, and the trials he must endure to renew that faith; a conflict between our primal fear of ancient mysteries and our rational aspirations for human evolution; and a visionary trip through the mythological stratum of the psyche. Who wants that [expletive deleted]? Bring on the barf!

If the movie has a weak point, it\xE2\x80\x99s not the script but the acting: Burton is aggressively hammy in his agony; Fletcher is a lethargic cardboard cutout; Blair, pudgy and vapid.

Points in its favor, however, begin with the direction. Boorman suffuses the film with symbolism, from the obvious to the subtle\xE2\x80\x94Lamont under the spell of the locust-demon, for instance, \xE2\x80\x9Cbrushing wings\xE2\x80\x9D with the crowds on the street and in the train station.

There is also an entire symbolic language in the use of color and light at play here\xE2\x80\x94not just in every scene, but in virtually every shot. Black, red and white battle for dominance throughout the film, and even the colors of the characters\xE2\x80\x99 clothing changes to reflect their psychological states. Notice the regular appearances of flashing lights\xE2\x80\x94emergency vehicles, stage lights, the sun, marquee signs\xE2\x80\x94indicating subliminal repetitions of the \xE2\x80\x9Csynchronizer\xE2\x80\x9D device, unconsciously cueing us that these characters are walking between two worlds: the waking world of the conscious mind and the archetype-inhabited realm of the unconscious. Watch the lights; watch the reflections; watch the way images overlap to indicate the overlapping levels consciousness. This remarkable achievement in direction gives the film a hypnotic, almost hallucinatory, tone, mirroring the interpenetration of worlds that Lamont is experiencing. (Boorman discussed this aspect of the film in his 2004 autobiography, \xE2\x80\x9CAdventures of a Suburban Boy\xE2\x80\x9D: \xE2\x80\x9CMy aesthetic theories and colour codes seemed like indulgent whims to the crew of hardened cynical technicians.\xE2\x80\x9D)

Lamont\xE2\x80\x99s task is to enter this internal realm, face his\xE2\x80\x94and Regan\xE2\x80\x99s\xE2\x80\x94demons, and have faith that he can find his way back to rationality. Once exposed to the light of consciousness, the monsters of the unconscious cannot survive. The ending isa brilliant integration of the main elements, where the action is simultaneously literal and symbolic. Are there \xE2\x80\x9Creally\xE2\x80\x9D two Regans? Of course not. Is there \xE2\x80\x9Creally\xE2\x80\x9D a plague of locusts? No: It\xE2\x80\x99s clear that these events are not taking place on the material plane. And the symbol system makes it very clear when they do re-enter \xE2\x80\x9Creality.\xE2\x80\x9D

\xE2\x80\x9CI understand now,\xE2\x80\x9D Tuskin tells Lamont near the end of the film. \xE2\x80\x9CThe world won\xE2\x80\x99t. Not yet.\xE2\x80\x9D Maybe Boorman understood his own experiment too well. Maybe the world of 1977\xE2\x80\x94the year of \xE2\x80\x9CAnnie Hall\xE2\x80\x9D and \xE2\x80\x9CStar Wars\xE2\x80\x9D\xE2\x80\x94wasn\xE2\x80\x99t ready for a film of this mystical nature. Maybe in today\xE2\x80\x99s action blockbuster market, it\xE2\x80\x99s still not. But, if you\xE2\x80\x99ve read any Jung or Joseph Campbell, maybe you are ready to appreciate this mythological movie, and to appreciate it as a thought-provoking spiritual horror story: Not a bomb, but a time bomb.integration of the main elements, where the action is simultaneously literal and symbolic. product_title: Joe
review_headline: Pleasantly surprised. Great movie! Deeply stirring and disturbing. Do not watch if you are just looking for easy entertainment.
review_body:
I read some of the one star reviews only because I could not understand how someone could give this movie one star. I am not a huge Nicolas Cage fan, but now and then he turns up in a movie and truly entertains. Personally, I think that this is one of the best roles he has ever played, and I applaud him for taking it on. Many of the one star reviews talked about how dark this movie was, that there was no happy ending, and that the movie did not have a point.

Well, this movie is dripping with messages, but you need to possess a little human empathy and understanding of the world that is out there beyond the pretty. The point(s) is not spoon fed to you off of a silver platter. People live like this. Children are raised in environments like this. I found nothing in this movie shocking, though it is depressing. If you are looking for a good time, do not bother. This movie is meant to make you look at the darker side of humanity, and I do not mean a peek - I mean stare it right down. It is gritty, hard, and very well acted, which I think is why it makes people so uncomfortable. No one likes to look at portrayals of this side of humanity because it strips away our feel good sense that all is right in world.

Spoiler: Do not read, if you do not want to know the end. There is a happy ending to this movie. The kid prevails. He lives through it all. He maintains his own integrity, his work ethic, his good heart... This is not a Cinderella story, it is something far closer to reality, which is subtle, harsh, and sometimes ugly. Nicholas Cage plays Joe who is an imperfect hero, as, in reality, most are. This is about the triumph of good in the human spirit. There is no metal. There is no standing ovation. There is no dramatic battle scene with the monster\x27s being blown to dust. There is just a kid who survives sinking into darkness and comes out in tact. At the end, Tye Sheridan makes you feel the human potential within the character.

We turn away from these atrocities every day because they make us uncomfortable. We leave kids struggling in impossible situations because we would rather not look, some of us cannot even stomach a movie about these topics - let alone the reality of them. Bravo, Nicolas and Tye. They did an incredible job of acting difficult roles with a challenging story.

product_title: What\x27s Eating Gilbert Grape
review_body:
This review is an excerpt from my book \xE2\x80\x9CKiller B\xE2\x80\x99s: The 237 Best Movies On Video You\xE2\x80\x99ve (Probably) Never Seen,\xE2\x80\x9D which is available as an ebook on Amazon. If you enjoy this review, there are 236 more like it in the book (plus a whole lot more). Check it out!

WHAT\xE2\x80\x99S EATING GILBERT GRAPE: Meet the Grape family! There\xE2\x80\x99s dad, who\xE2\x80\x99s dead; Momma (Cates), who weighs 500 pounds and hasn\xE2\x80\x99t left the house in seven years; accident-prone daughter Amy; teenage Ellen; and retarded Arnie, a 17-year-old who loves to climb trees (and the town water tower). Holding them all together in some semblance of sanity is 20-ish Gilbert (Depp)\xE2\x80\x94and he\xE2\x80\x99s overburdened with responsibility.

Good-hearted Gilbert has his hands full, stoically dealing with his megadysfunctional family\xE2\x80\x94he\xE2\x80\x99s practically St. Gilbert of Grape. But even a saint can make mistakes\xE2\x80\x94and even a saint can snap if pushed past his limit. Gilbert\xE2\x80\x99s limit arrives in the form of young Becky (Lewis), who\xE2\x80\x99s just passing through town. Her understanding and affection are the first things Gilbert\xE2\x80\x99s ever encountered that he wants purely for himself. But who\xE2\x80\x99ll hold the Grape bunch together if he chooses selfish love over his selfless duty to the family?

Discussion: \xE2\x80\x9CNothing much ever happens\xE2\x80\x9D in rural Eudora, Iowa, Gilbert explains, \xE2\x80\x9Cand nothing much ever will.\xE2\x80\x9D He couldn\xE2\x80\x99t be more wrong\xE2\x80\x94Eudora is overflowing with small-town drama; it\xE2\x80\x99s just all on a very humble, human scale. The plot is episodic, but it\xE2\x80\x99s the performances that are central\xE2\x80\x94and uniformly excellent. Depp radiates melancholy, and an innocent and wistful wisdom; Cates (in her film debut) hits just the right tone in a physically and emotionally demanding role; Lewis, as the wise waif, is particularly sweet and understated. Best of all is DiCaprio\xE2\x80\x99s sympathetic and uncannily accurate portrayal of retarded Arnie. (I worked with retarded kids for a year and can attest that his performance is gesture-perfect.) Add in some stunning photography and compassionate humor, and you\xE2\x80\x99ve got a movie that will make you laugh out loud\xE2\x80\x94and cry out loud.
