product_title: Twelve Preludes & Fugues for Piano
review_headline: ... a Scottish composer whose Gaelic background comes across most beautifully in this 24 piece suite for the piano solo
review_body:
David Charles Johnson (27 October 1942 in Edinburgh \xE2\x80\x93 30 March 2009 in Edinburgh) was a Scottish composer whose Gaelic background comes across most beautifully in this 24 piece suite for the piano solo.

Ian Hobson of the Sinfonia da Camera in Chicago plays these rarely heard, hard to find beautiful pieces in a clear and most enjoyable manner that does a great honor to the composer\x27 music.

Johnson details the methods by which he threads all 24 pieces together in a short discourse in the notes that accompany the CD (a four-note motif representing the Scots Gaelic word beatha, meaning life, welcome, livelihood, food - [positive].. These pieces were so interesting to me that I purchased the sheet music.

I highly recommend this CD to those who enjoy wonderful modern piano that is neither intrusive nor overwhelming but stimulating and exemplifies the beauty that a modern composer has created in his far too short a lifetime.

Enjoy!

product_title: Only To Rise
review_headline: Modern hard rock with plenty of groove and swagger
review_body: Michael Sweet is busier now than he\x27s ever been. After Stryper released \x27No More Hell to Pay\x27 in November 2013, arguably their best album, he released a long-awaited solo album last year, and now this collaboration with George Lynch. Stryper have also reportedly started working on their follow up to NMHTP. Like I said, busy.    Sweet doesn\x27t sing as high as he used to -- not because he can\x27t do it (he can), but to make those high notes stand out when he *does* hit them -- and I actually prefer his vocal style now to his 80s heyday with Stryper. While his range hasn\x27t decreased by any measurable amount, his voice sounds fuller and more muscular, and those high notes -- when he hits them -- sound more incredible.    I was never a huge Dokken fan, but I could appreciate Lynch\x27s guitar mastery, and he hasn\x27t lost anything, either. Every song has some special flourish, and the riffs and solos are just -- well, \x5C\x22tasty\x5C\x22 is the word that comes to mind. I\x27ve listened to it several times now, and I hear something new each time.    The rhythm section of Brian Tichy (drums) and James Lomenzo (bass) is solid. They don\x27t do anything flashy, and that\x27s just fine. This isn\x27t a progressive rock album where everyone is out to show just how proficient they are on their instrument of choice (not that there\x27s anything wrong with that....). This is a down \x27n dirty, guitar-driven, hard rock album, with plenty of groove and swagger. Topped off by Sweet\x27s amazing vocals.    Lyrically, this is a positive album, but there are no blatantly Christian Stryper-esque songs. This doesn\x27t bother me one way or the other, but your mileage may vary. If you are fan of any of the players involved, though, I don\x27t think you\x27ll find anything to complain about.    Roll down your windows, crank it up, and hit the road.

product_title: Rescue & Restore
review_headline: Very good, but just how good really depends on what kind of metal fan you are
review_body:
August Burns Red is much more than just talented a metalcore band. They are passionate, and their energy infects their songs. ABR albums are fast-paced, aggressive, and exciting. Rescue & Restore can stand up to their previous outing, the excellent Leveler. They tried to experiment this time around, bringing in several unfamiliar instrumentals to spice up their sound. The result is hit or miss, but always curious and interesting.

Songs I particularly enjoyed were probably a bit more of the straightforward sort. Sincerity, Animals, and Provision gave me more of the tight, clean metal that ABR is known for. There is no doubt that ABR is going for a versatile, artistic theme on this album with all the variety and experimentation. As a metal album, Rescue & Restore is lesser than Leveler. As an album, it may be better, depending on what kind of music you appreciate.

product_title: Music From Big Pink
review_headline: Important, Influential, but not where you should start
review_body:
Looking back through the lens of history, now 47 years back, today\x27s listeners may scratch their heads and think, "I\x27ve heard this all before." A wide range of genres from alt country, roots rock, and the latest neo folk movement owe a huge debt to The Band and specifically Music From Big Pink. Today one might wonder why this album is revered. At the time, nothing sounded like it.

It\x27s the summer of 1968, the period between the Summer of Love and Woodstock, when the hippie ethos was in full swing, the Vietnam War was at its peak, and college campuses were in turmoil. Dylan had already announced his disconnection from it all with the release of John Wesley Harding in December of \x2767. Ignoring the psychedelic hippie music that was popular, and after spending time with The Band recording The Basement Tapes, Dylan headed to Nashville to record a roots album. The Band followed with this, also inspired by The Basement Tapes.

The importance of Music From Big Pink must be weighed against its tremendous influence through the years, and even immediately. It (along with John Wesley Harding) had a profound effect on The Rolling Stones who had fumbled psychedelia and returned to a rootsier sound on Beggar\x27s Banquet. The Beatles had fared better during \x2767, but also abandoned psychedelia in favor of the stripped down sound on The White Album.

Every folk, country, and roots artist since has regarded Music From Big Pink as a a Rosetta Stone. I personally know many people, some are even my age and lived this, who admit they still don\x27t get this album. It\x27s more of an idea or a direction, yet it is stylistically cohesive. It\x27s a group of talented musicians testing new ground, yet relying heavily on the past. Except for The Weight, Tears of Rage, and I Shall Be Released, much of it doesn\x27t sound very much like The Band that we are most familiar with. But however you look at it. Music From Big Pink is an important touchstone in the history of American music.

The Band\x27s followup, titled simply The Band, feels more like a "first album" and is probably the one you should seek out first. Then listen to The Basement Tapes, and Dylan\x27s John Wesley Harding, before diving into this one. Then you\x27ll understand the grand exercise that is Music From Big Pink.erican music.

product_title: Overture Solennelle
review_body:
Batten down the hatches and keep an eye on the pets: this one is demonstration-quality for sure. This "1812", originally recorded in experimental quadraphonic sound by Philips in 1975, makes its reappearance as a Pentatone surround SACD. Davis conducts a "kitchen sink" performance, with chorus and the Symphony Hall organ in addition to the full Boston Symphony and the usual cannons and bells--even some New England muskets show up during the concluding bars. It all makes a glorious racket, and the DSD engineering creates a wide and deep sound stage, along with great depth for the front-to-back sound effects. I have other versions of this showpiece (Gerhardt, Kunzel, and Maazel to name three) but none come close to the realism and impact of this performance. If you want to break a lease or bother the neighbors, this one\x27s for you. But as always with Sir Colin at the helm, everything remains musical, colorful and well-proportioned.

The Sibelius suites and tone poems are more than fillers and are well worth your time. Indeed, the "Karelia" suite places you in a realistic orchestra seat perspective in Symphony Hall where you can feel as well as hear the full range of the BSO...this may be hard to find new, but well worth seeking out nonetheless.

product_title: Original Album Series
review_body: Texas-based southern rock/blues trio ZZ Top has become a respected force in the modern music scene, and deservedly so.  This collection is a relatively well-selected choice of 5 of their best-remembered albums, spanning a career that gradually lifted them to commercial success.  They have a good musical sense and feel for the blues.  They can be serious and also have a sense of humor, flaunting a party-animal side that you have to love......for instance, it\x27s no secret that the band took their name from their 2 favorite brands of cigarette rolling papers (even though they didn\x27t claim to be rolling tobacco).  Songs of drinking and hookers etc. blend well with their more serious side.  Guitarist Billy Gibbons is a talented frontman, while bassist Dusty Hill and drummer Frank Beard add admirably to the mix.  This collection begins with their second album from the early \x2770s, Rio Grande Mud, which brought them radio play with Just Got Paid, a great example of the bluesy tone of this disc.....although that tune probably got more popular after their third album, Tres Hombres gave us the big hit La Grange (about a Texas cathouse), blues medley \x5C\x22Waiting for the Bus/Jesus Just Left Chicago and the rockin\x27 Beer Drinkers & Hell Raisers.  Their fourth album Fandango was not nearly as impressive overall, but it brought us the huge hit, Tush.  One live side combined with a side of short, quick tunes made the album seem rushed and uninspired, but it did have great moments, such as Blue Jean Blues.  Then this collection skips to their sixth album, Deguello because it gave us the huge hit Cheap Sunglasses, the popular I\x27m Bad, I\x27m Nationwide and their cover of the old Motown hit, I Thank You, which was co-written by The Temptations\x27 Dave Porter and Isaac Hayes (who is best remembered for writing the music score for the \x2770s movie Shaft, and is more recently known as the voice of Chef on the animated series South Park).  Deguello is a great improvement over their fourth album.  Thenfor the last disc of this collection, they jump one or two albums ahead to Eliminator, which is the \x2780s album that brought us the hits, Sharp Dressed Man, Legs and Gimme All Your Lovin\x27.  Although the album is a bit over-produced in a typically \x2780s fashion (this was obviously done to increase the chances of making this work sell better), it is a little spotty, but predominantly a good album. (note how their album titles often playfully boast their Texas origin)  I\x27ve seen reviews on this site claiming this collection was poorly remixed and remastered.  It\x27s difficult for me to argue.  I\x27m not the world\x27s biggest audiophile.  Admittedly, these discs are not all remastered to an optimum volume and quality.....and they don\x27t even match each other in quality.  But they sound good on a decent stereo.  And for me, this is a pleasant collection of well-selected albums that go well together and is a fine showcase of an impressive career that gradually brought this powerful group to the level of popularity they deserve.  Audiophiles may be right to complain, but I find this a real fun collection that I\x27m going to thoroughly enjoy!!

product_title: The Heart of Everything
review_body: 2014 was a banner year for Within Temptation not unlike 2007, which saw the release of their breakthrough The Heart of Everything and subsequent live tour and Black Symphony DVD/Blu-ray. In light of recent successes I was \x5C\x22tempted\x5C\x22 (possibly compelled) to go back and revisit this amazing recording. There was a balance of more commercial rock with the gothic/symphonic style of earlier works that was and remains very satisfying. Certainly \x5C\x22Our Solemn Hour\x5C\x22 - one of the greatest songs ever - retains that gothic vibe, and Sharon does soar vocally in the operatic style on a number of the tunes (\x5C\x22The Cross\x5C\x22 and the epic \x5C\x22The Truth Beneath The Rose\x5C\x22). The Keith Caputo duet \x5C\x22What Have You Done\x5C\x22 hints at what the band would take on a much larger scale with Hydra. And then the more balladic \x5C\x22Frozen\x5C\x22 and \x5C\x22Forgiven\x5C\x22 stand out to this day as amazing outpourings of emotion and passion, with the tender, cello-accompanied \x5C\x22All I Need\x5C\x22 not far behind. \x5C\x22Final Destination\x5C\x22 and \x5C\x22The Howling\x5C\x22 delivered the heavier riffs and epic and bombastic feel of great symphonic metal. And of course the fan favorite anthem \x5C\x22Stand My Ground\x5C\x22 made a re appearance here as well. In retrospect, this album is every bit as good as it was 7 years ago and the music was obviously well-suited for the amazing production (replete with full choir/symphony) that would follow with Black Symphony. For me, this release represents everything great about symphonic rock/metal in general and Within Temptation specifically. Classic.

product_title: Casualties of Cool
review_headline: This is my favorite recording from 2014
review_body: This is my favorite recording from 2014, easily.  Whenever I hear any of my cranky older friends (my category!) complain no good music is being made today I\x27ll just throw this right in their face.  Of course, there is always great music being pumped out in the world, it just always seems to bubble under.  And here is my admission.  I\x27ve never heard of Devin before CoC.  I\x27m not a metal fan... not really even a fan of progressive rock for the most part.  But this stuff is undeniable, creative, full of talent all over the place.  I agree that there is a Pink Floyd airy vibe here, along with some Dire Straits in a few spots.  A review below mentions the Plant/Krauss pairing and there is some of that as well.  "The Bridge" goes from quietly beautiful into something Swans would be proud of.  I could name checking this pup, but it doesn\x27t matter.  It\x27s still original sounding even with these touchstones.  I\x27m super happy this album is available and hope there will be more!

With Roland Grapow (ex-Helloween, Masterplan, Level 10) on guitars and Thomen Stauch (ex-Blind Guardian, ex-Iron Savior) on drums, it shouldn\x27t be any surprise that Serious Black play power metal. They\x27re not a one-trick pony, though, so take that description with a grain of salt. That\x27s just the foundation. Yes, there\x27s plenty of double bass on display, but they add plenty of variation and melody. This is really just modern melodic metal, with plenty of power and speed.

The vocals are provided by Urban Breed (Project Arcadia, Trail of Murder, ex-Bloodbound, ex-Tad Morose), who has recently become one of my favorite vocalists. After hearing him for the first time last year in Project Arcadia, I tracked down everything else he\x27s recorded. Everything I heard only raised the level of anticipation for this release, and he does not disappoint. He has a great range, can sing smoothly or with a rasp, and has excellent vocal control. He also comes up with some great melodies. One thing he doesn\x27t do, though, is show off. He does what is needed for the song instead of making it all about him. Granted, in this style of music, that sometimes *requires* a little showing off, but he does it tastefully. :-)

The other players were new to me: Dominik Sebastian on guitar, Mario Lochert on bass, and Jan Vacik on keys. After this album, though, I imagine I\x27ll be seeking out their other projects as well. The keyboards, in particular, stand out. They provide just the right amount of atmosphere on the rockers and some beautiful piano on the ballads.

I won\x27t go through all of the individual songs. I\x27ll just say there\x27s a lot of variety, with an excellent rockers to ballads ratio (more of the former, less of the latter). The special edition comes with three bonus tracks: two originals and a cover of the Genesis song, "No Son of Mine." All of these are worth the extra price, but the cover, especially, is incredible. I was not familiar with the original, so I didn\x27t realize it was a cover at first. I just thought it was a pitch-perfect homage to Genesis. They wisely don\x27t try to "metal it up." They play it straight, if a little beefier, and do it beautifully. Urban Breed shows that he could sing pop music if he wanted to (although I hope he sticks with metal), and his voice packs an emotional wallop during the chorus.

This was my first 2015 release, and it started the year out right. I\x27m definitely hoping to hear more from Serious Black.

product_title: Chapter 10
review_body: Just three months after the better-than-expected Allen/Lande album, \x27The Great Divide,\x27 Russell Allen is back with a new super group. The names above the band name are Allen\x27s and bassist Mat Sinner (Primal Fear, Sinner, Silent Force, Voodoo Circle, and a host of other projects), but the other members are worth mentioning: guitarist Roland Grapow (Serious Black, Masterplan, ex-Helloween), guitarist Alexander Beyrodt (Primal Fear, Silent Force, Sinner, Voodoo Circle), drummer Randy Black (ex-Primal Fear), and keyboardist Alessandro Del Vecchio (Silent Force and a host of other projects). These guys bring the expectation of some serious chops, and they do not disappoint.    The opener, \x5C\x22Cry No More,\x5C\x22 is a blistering sonic assault that sets the stage for the entire album. It starts off with just the riffs from a twin guitar attack by Grapow and Beyrodt before being joined by the rhythm section of Sinner and Black. Black\x27s drums make sure you know there will be no slowing down after the intro. At the 30-second mark, Allen\x27s larger-than-life voice comes at you full force. Del Vecchio\x27s keys join in on the first chorus, and then it\x27s time for the first guitar solo. Later, Grapow and Beyrodt trade off for a face-melting axe duel.    I won\x27t go through the rest of the songs. I\x27ll just say that the rest of the songs vary in speed but not in intensity. There isn\x27t a single stinker on this album. The 12 tracks are muscular, testosterone-fueled modern metal that seamlessly meld aggression and melody, retaining the best aspects of classic hard rock and metal with none of the cheese. This is music to blast while driving at high speeds. Bust out your air guitar and air drums. Attempt (hopelessly, in my case) to sing along with Allen, if you dare. His voice is on full display here: smooth, gruff, growling, soaring, crooning. Whatever fits the song, he nails it. This is a dynamic performance, and he and the rest of the band sound pumped and energized.    I\x27m not sure if this is supposed to be a one-off or what, but I certainly hope there will be more.

product_title: Complete Sonatas for Piano & Violin
review_headline: A Glorious Issue Excellently Performed with Spectacular SACD Audio
review_body:
I am so spoiled in the Beethoven Violin Sonatas, with top drawer virtuosity among so many recent recordings. My favorite has been the collection by Augustin Dumay & Maria-Jo\xC3\xA3o Pires, with fiery and spirited playing matched to superlative sound engineering. But I listen just as often to Renaud Capu\xC3\xA7on & Frank Braley or Isabelle Faust & Alexander Melnikov\xE2\x80\x99s sets. All are excellent, different accents and qualities justify them. (When I went on disability and had to dispose of about one-third of my 2,000 recording collection while awaiting benefits, it is telling that all of these were retained).

And yet now comes this thrilling set by Isabelle van Keulen & Hannes Minnaar. I cannot believe that Minnaar, a relative youngster, can hold his own in competition with a seasoned pianist, a favorite like Pires. Golly, I had to keep comparing excerpts to prove it to myself, but in all my favorite passages, such as that rollicking scherzo of #10 / Op. 96 he most certainly does. What a great test of faith to bring him into this project, because van Keulen herself, such a consistently distinguished violinist / violist, usually is partnered with Ronald Brautigam. I had wished to hear her in Beethoven, and I could not be more delighted.

Indeed, it seems churlish to pick one favorite in a situation like this, but Challenge Classics provides a great asset in the best balanced engineering, and in issuing this on SACD. If you have a high quality system, this new set will bring extra delight. I continually went \xE2\x80\x9Cwow\xE2\x80\x9D.

Which makes me wonder if Challenge Classics might have issued van Keulen\xE2\x80\x99s somewhat overlooked Prokofiev on SACD (or might do so). That Prokofiev, in which she was accompanied by Brautigam is also excellent, and every bit as deserving as the recently feted issue with Alina Ibragimova & Steven Osborne.

product_title: Dvorak, Janacek & Suk: Works for Violin & Piano
review_body:
I don\x27t know whether it\x27s the Matteo Goffriller violin (1708), the Chandos engineering, or Jennifer Pike\x27s playing -- or some combination of all three -- but this is an outstandingly beautiful recording, and expressively amazing (to me at least) from a violinist in her 24th year. Pike is totally in tune with the distinctive Eastern European melancholy that finds expression through different musical means in the works of Janacek, Suk, and Dvorak recorded here, and her pianist, Tom Poster, also beautifully recorded, is equally impressive. The Janacek sonata for violin and piano (1914, rev. 1922) is the single most substantial piece on the disc. It\x27s tempting to describe the writing as \x5C\x22spiky,\x5C\x22 as it moves forward in quite brief note clusters or motifs that never cohere to form a melody and which yet attain the expressive power of melody. The character is elegiac and troubled, with the motifs being passed between the instruments in such a way that one always seems to be making counter-suggestions to the other, though never creating an inconsistency in the mood being expressed. The character of the musical means (as opposed to what\x27s expressed) is totally unlike anything I\x27ve ever heard. The heart of the piece is, for me, the third movement, which achieves a sense of bleakness or emptiness that seems to\x5C\x22explain\x5C\x22 the overall elegiac character of the whole. That third movement is a kind of dumka, functioning as a sinister and troubling scherzo that represents a vision of a world emptied of beauty and serenity, and that reminds me of Mahler, without sounding anything like Mahler. (Of the shorter Janacek pieces, the \x5C\x22Allegro\x5C\x22 is the rejected fourth movement of the sonata, and one hears in its opening an attempt to be assertive that is out of character with the first three movements in a way that Janacek\x27s final version is not.) Two other short pieces, a Dumka and a Romance, both from around 1880. are less spiky but no less melancholy, with the Romance coming closest to something melodic, perhaps even a folk melody.

The alternation of grave and gay, in music that seems based on dances, characterizes the Dumka, and Suk\x27s Four Pieces (op.17) from 1900 represent a dumka spirit, with the soberly beautiful odd-numbered movements contrasting with the high spirits of the even-numbered ones. The even-numbered ones require a lot of dexterity from both players, and it is in these movements that Pike\x27s virtuosity can be appreciated almost for its own sake, even as one registers the expressive power of the playing. The short Dvorak pieces that complete the disc are re-workings for violin and piano (by the composer himself, as far as I know) of other chamber pieces. The longest, the Nocturne of 1883, is the only one that threatens to outstay its welcome, but a surprising development in the final minute rescues it. The four Romantic Pieces of 1887 (originally for a string trio) take us back to something like a Brahmsian sound-world, and they give both musicians a chance to display the lyrical potential of their instruments. If you wondered earlier whether or not Pike could bring out her violin\x27s capacity for long-breathed melody, the Dvorak pieces give you the answer. There are a lot of similarities to Stryper, for obvious reasons, as well as a lot of Lynch\x27s projects, but a surprise to me was similarities the Lynch/Pilson.

Lynch is one of my all-time favorites and I\x27ve purchased everything he\x27s done since Dokken, but I\x27ve found that (other than Dokken and early Lynch Mob) when he\x27s not the primary driving force and the one that is, is as competent as someone like Sweet, the end result is usually better. At least when it comes to mainstream stuff. Kind of as if Lynch just needs to be corralled a little. My personal opinion, at least.

All that said, I absolutely recommend this to anyone that loves Lynch or Sweet\x27s various projects. REALLY glad this was released and I\x27m hoping there are more in the future.

product_title: The Queen Symphony
review_headline: It sounds like a good pop album, which essentially it is
review_body:
I admit it: I have always liked the music of British rock band Queen. For instance, I still think their 1975 album A Night at the Opera (a gratifying reference to one of my favorite Marx brothers films) is brilliant. Nor have I any objection to people reorchestrating pop tunes and playing them via full-scale symphony orchestras. So back in 2002 when conductor and composer Tolga Kashif orchestrated an EMI disc of tunes by Queen and played by the Royal Philharmonic, I merely shrugged and thought, "Why not?" Then I listened to the album, in which Kashif arranged some of Queen\x27s songs into what he called a symphony, and it all seemed more than a bit exaggerated to me. Still, what do I know: The disc garnered "Album of the Year" honors in some circles, attracted a host of devoted followers, and became a best-seller.

Kashif\x27s symphonic creation, which is close to an hour long, contains bits and pieces of songwriter and lead singer Freddie Mercury\x27s work for Queen divided into six movements. The trouble is, I found little continuity among the movements, little cohesion, just fragments of this and that held together through the brute force of the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra and Kashif\x27s fancy orchestration. Because I found much of the production a little tedious, about the only thing it made me want to do more than anything else was to listen to an actual Queen album and hear what the music originally sounded like.

You\x27ll find a Queen song such as "Love of My Life" coming up best due to its inherent lyricism, and the whole symphony certainly starts out well, everything lushly orchestrated. But then you\x27ll also find Kashif providing tempo markings within the movements like Allegro Scherzando and Moderato Cantabile, which seem overly pretentious to me. This self-reverential tone appears especially evident when Kashif, who not only arranged the music but conducts it as well, insists that this is a genuine symphony and not just a new arrangement of older music. I dunno; maybe Kashif meant the whole thing humorously, like some of Queen\x27s own music. Despite Kashif\x27s claim that it\x27s a serious symphony, however, the music just sounds to my ears like an inflated collection of disparate pop harmonies, with little musical focus other than what Kashif\x27s score attempts to segue into next.

Anyway, you\x27ll hear snatches of "Bohemian Rhapsody," "We Will Rock You," "We Are the Champions," and "Who Wants to Live Forever" tenuously woven into a single movement with little rhyme or reason. I admit it\x27s pleasant enough from time to time, especially if you\x27re already a Queen fan, but as a whole it fails to hang together any more than a multitude of ordinary theme albums do.

Moreover, the sound doesn\x27t help much, either. To my ears EMI recorded the orchestra too close up and in too many multi-miked segments, with a constricted frequency response, a slightly muted high end, a soft midrange, a weak deep bass, and a nonexistent depth of image. In other words, it sounds exactly like a lot of pop recordings, which, given that EMI made it at least partly in Abbey Road\x27s famous Studio 1, means it bears little resemblance to the kind of classical recording it would seem striving to emulate. So, in short, it sounds like a good pop album, which essentially it is. There\x27s nothing wrong with that as long as we\x27re not pretending it\x27s something more.

John J. Puccio

product_title: In the Hot Seat
review_headline: Not very good.  Bad songs and bad voice.
review_body:
My version came a bonus track of Pictures at an Exhibition, recorded in 5.1 surround sound. This track could not be played on standard CD players, but it plays in my new car stereo. It is 14 minutes. It is labeled as track 11 in the liner notes, but it is actually broken up into 6 separate tracks. I think it is pointless and tedious. I don\x27t see any reason for yet another truncated version of this piece.

The main album has 10 songs and is about 42 minutes long. The sound quality has that digital booming quality that was popular in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

This is a collection of songs that are not very good for the most part. And the musical accompaniment is not very interesting. There is a Bob Dylan tune, but I don\x27t like the way they play it. I think this album is worse than Black Moon and Love Beach.

The one song that is moderately good is Thin Line. There are two other songs that I didn\x27t totally hate: Change and Street War.
But, none of these songs are close to being as good as anything on the group\x27s first 6 albums.

Daddy is a really depressing song about a man\x27s daughter being kidnapped and murdered. It has a nice melody if you listen to it in the background, but you really don\x27t want to listen to the words.

product_title: Ghost Thief
review_body:
Living Sacrifice is up there with August Burns Red and Demon Hunter for one of the biggest names in Christian metalcore. Here they come out with possibly their best album yet, Ghost Thief. The album boasts aggressive vocals and some pretty intricate guitar work invoking a few hints of thrash. I could levy the claim that the vocalist, Bruce Fitzhugh sounds the exact same as he did for each and every album before. That isn\x27t bad, but it helps this album kind of blur together with the previous ones some. Bringing in Ryan Clark for a guest spot certainly spices up the record though.

The best tracks include Screwtape, which features Clark giving an inspired and versatile performance. Even better is the song Before, which can only be described as epic. Your War and The Reaping are up there as well.

Pick this album up if you like Demon Hunter or any other Solid State band. These guys are possibly the best of the bunch.

product_title: Paid In Full [ECOPAK]
review_headline: Rakim Tells The Hip-Hop World MC Means Move The Crowd!
review_body:
Basic structure in terms of hip-hop was still being heavily refined during the mid 80\x27s 1986 and 1987 were particularly important years in terms of innovation of the still often experimental genre as a full blown art form. The Furious Five,Afrika Bambaataa,LL Cool J and Run DMC had already made enormous strides in moving the music forward during before this. Yet the rapping techniques used on all of these generally still derived from earlier pioneers such as King Tim III and Kurtis Blow. That is hard,stripped down beats and a forceful vocal delivery. Looked as if two young men from Long Island were going to be the ones to change that.

"It Ain\x27t No Joke" features a fast,percussive and extremely funkified percussive number built upon Eric B\x27s scratch accents to the horn melody of the JB\x27s "Pass The Peas". "Eric B Is On The Cut" is one of two largely instrumental numbers here-this one built around Eric\x27s rhythmically precise scratching. "Chinese Arithmetic" has the synthesizer based melodies of earlier electro funk along with the stripped down beats and scratching-one generation of hip-hop translating onto another. "Move The Crowd" features a slow grinding go-go type jam created primarily from layers of bluesy synthesized bass lines while "My Melody" finds an reverbed Rakim harmonizing with himself. "I Know You Got Soul" is built on a JB style guitar line.

"As The Rhyme Goes On" has a slow funk rhythm and keyboard accent similar to Barry White\x27s "Never Never Gonna Give You Up". "Eric B Is President" loops the shuffling groove and wah wah of James Brown\x27s "Funky President" while "Extended Beat" concludes the album with an instrumental loop of "Move The Crowd" while the title songs tale of hip-hop overcoming a life of crime is set the bass line of Dennis Edwards "Don\x27t Look Any Further". "As The Rhyme Goes On" is presented as a bonus track here in it\x27s single edit. Cold Cut remixed this with more samples in a modern context for a bonus track.

Much seems to have been written about how this album altered the vocabulary of hip-hop with Rakim\x27s thick,internal rhyming and highly poetic storytelling technique. The sound the Bomb Squad/Public Enemy would achieve in a year or so came out of this album basically-as well as it\x27s heavy influence (and actual musical usage) of James Brown. Honestly though? I do feel that the relaxed,more intimate rapping style Rakin expressed here came off far better with both Chuck D and Q-Tip. My favorite aspect of this album is musical. It established that hip-hip,with it\x27s turntables and beats,could be a straight up instrumental genre without required association with rapping. While a very important album in terms of innovation? It provided more of a guidebook for other hip-hoppers to follow than an end unto itself.a bonus track here in it\x27s single edit. review_body: At the very least, a highly ambitious, polarizing album. This can not be said for basically anything else that came out in 2013. The dude that said it\x27s great for workouts is right. The beats; that dozens of creative minds worked on it is astounding. This record might be one of a kind in that it was DESIGNED. The raps are just as wild; absurd, hilarious, disgusting, thought provoking. Kanye wastes no words in New Slaves verse 2, even in repetition. The first verse on I Am A God is stellar in all its obsessive, paranoid glory. After he\x27s told you how he\x27s Michael Jackson status or whatever (so you\x27d better hurry up with the menage and the croissants), a scream pierces through and stops the beat. Soon, another scream. Hyperventilating. You\x27re not meant to hear this: the weight, the stress, the pain of being a cultural arbiter. A God, if you will. Of course the Porsche, the massage, the french-ass restaurant, the wife, all come at a cost. Few people did - and ever will - understand Yeezus. I could go on with all these tracks...they\x27re like aural expressionist paintings. I\x27m just saying there\x27s something to be taken from these \x27songs,\x27 even when he\x27s talking about himself.  I think a couple tracks could have been thrown out (Bound 2) with no detriment, but tracks 3, 4, 6, 7, and 9 alone merit 5 gold bright shining blinking stars. The rest are still pretty good.  Also, that\x27s probably the greatest album cover of all time.

product_title: Sorcerer 2014
review_body:
Very simply, the first disc of this two CD set is the best thing that Edgar Froese\x27s Tangerine Dream has released in quite some time. TD has been at this for a long time. That, of course, is an understatement. And since TD has been around so long, and has had so many lineup changes (the only constant being Herr Froese) that most are going to like some eras more than others and so I will state my bias as liking the first ten years the most. But that doesn\x27t mean I don\x27t like other eras or lineups, and frankly, if we could somehow erase the new age Miramar/Private Music years, I wouldn\x27t mind listening to any of their albums. And one should think of the artist,too. Has TD run out of ideas? The "remixing" and re-recording of TD\x27s and Edgar\x27s solo albums with varying results (mostly poor) says yes.

So here we have a their re-recording of the classics 1977 score for the mediocre film Sorcerer. Not TD\x27s best, but filled with classic (there\x27s that word again) analog synths, and a very very very original, an incomparable type of music of their own invention, sort of a Krautrock super-synthesizer onslaught. Gone was the washing machine melting minimalism of the million selling Phaedra and Rubycon and in its place a more simplistic creepiness. I loved it. And it\x27s limitations were imposed not only by the technology but their lack of proficiency on the keyboard. A trio of Rick Wakeman\x27s they were not. But that was then and this is now. So their musicianship is improved 100 fold, and the abilities of their instruments is pretty much limitless. Yet they are bound by the original compositions of the original Sorcerer. And this time Edgar didn\x27t mess it up! I really like it, I really like it. Other than an occasional tasty lick guitar solo (NOT by Edgar, but a ringer) I think the eeriness of the original is definitely intact. And they did not go overboard with rewriting of the original, nor is a speck of the original tape used. CD 2 is a more modern take on the score, and although "nice", unnecessary.

Edgar Froese, may he rest in peace, has gone out with a sequenced modulated VCO random sampled filter swept bang.e score, and although "nice", unnecessary.

product_title: Franck: Symphony in D Minor / Stravinsky: Petrouchka
review_headline: Definitive performances from an authoritative source
review_body:
My first classical concert was hearing Pierre Monteux conduct the San Francisco Symphony, and I have collected most of his recordings over the years. This pairs two of his best performances: the Franck from 1961 with Reiner\x27s Chicago Symphony at the top of its game. along with his stereo "Petrushka" from Boston. His Franck has always been at the top of the lists of recommended recordings because of his firm control of rhythm and pulse, not to mention his mastery of the idiom. The Chicago band is with him all the way, and the various woodwind and horn solos are all beautifully executed. The finale packs enormous propulsion without ever losing sight of the long melodic line. Having owned the earlier RCA "Papillon" CD, I can appreciate the greater clarity of the hybrid 3-channel SACD remastering; most, if not all, of the blasting and congestion of the earlier versions have given way to a more open and airy sound stage.

The association between Monteux and Stravinsky dates back to the Diaghilev ballet and "Petrushka\x27s" premiere in 1911, and note that this version sticks to the original full-orchestra score, not the reduced forces from the 1947 revision. Suffice it to say this is an authoritative reading, seasoned by nearly 50 years of performances around the world (indeed, I also own a mono Monteux "Petrushka" from Decca/London, featuring the Paris Conservatoire Orchestra, the group the maestro led at the Paris premiere). There\x27s no sign of a run-through here...Monteux inspires the Boston Symphony to a high level of execution (unlike the Paris ensemble), and the remastered 3-channel recording captures every note and nuance. From the piano to the bassoon and percussion, every choir registers with clarity and impact. It\x27s hard to believe that this reading dates back to the maestro\x27s 1959 visits to Boston. No need to look further for either repertory staple: it\x27s all here at a good "Living Stereo" reissue price.

product_title: Saint-George: Six String Quartets Opus 14
review_headline: Lyric String Quartets from St. George
review_body:
During the 1770\x27s in Paris, a French style of string quartet composition emerged, advanced by Gossec, Vachon, Cambini, and Joseph Boulogne, Chevalier de St. George (1739-1799). Known as concertante quartets, they developed a `conversation in music\x27 among the 4 voices, and these 6 quartets of St. George\x27s Op.14 are exquisite examples. For a brief biography of this colorful composer, see my review of [[ASIN:B000OCYGV8 Saint-George: 4 Concertos for Violin]].

Like his 2 previous sets of string quartets, all 6 are in 2 movements, with none of the 1st sections given tempo markings. This recording begins with No.4, written in G Major. After the initial theme is presented by the 1st violin, trading it back and forth with the 2nd violin before a rousing unison section sets the stage for the viola. Another appearance of the unison theme introduces the cello. While the solo voice takes the spotlight, the other three instruments usually provide a simple accompaniment, often repeated staccato notes. Little interplay or extended dialogue is offered, although the solo passages demand considerable technique. St. George was an acknowledged as a virtuoso violinist.

The brisk `Minetto\x27 that follows barely has enough time to allow anyone besides the 1st violin to shine before the trio shifts to G Minor. After the preceding sunny opening, this brings a dark counterpoint to the work before coming to a rapid conclusion.

Also in G Minor, Quartet No.6 starts with a delightfully charming melody that is presented by the 1st violin. Each voice then has the chance develop it, using a series of jaunty triplets running up and down the scales. Despite the minor key, this is cheerful, appealing music, bursting with lyric energy.

Late in the 1st movement of Quartet No.1 in D Major, the cello has a wonderful passage, full of vitality and skipping staccato notes deep in the lower register. The `Aria con variazioni\x27 that follows is the only movement on the entire disc that approaches an adagio. Leisurely, meditative, the work allows each instrument extended time to develop the melancholy theme initiated by the 1st violin.

Most quartets of this style are bright and sunny, written in major keys. That St. George composed 2 in minor keys is unusual, and No. 3in F Minor forms the emotional core of the set. Sweetly sorrowful, full of pathos, the 1st movement reveals a poignancy that is deeply moving. The sparkling `Vivace\x27 that follows offers a dynamic contrast.

Sharply syncopated rhythms characterize the opening movement of the final quartet, No.3 composed in E Flat. After a series of brisk unison passages, the cello introduces the second motif, written in B Flat. The concluding `Minetto\x27 begins with a fugal sequence before shifting into B Flat Minor, and a touching solo from the cello. This brief fugal section returns before softly fading away at the final bars.

This is elegant, graceful music, brought to life by the excellent recording by Avenira, and the Apollon Quartet. A long established ensemble from Poland, they give a polished reading to these 6 quartets from St. George. Particularly noteworthy are the 1st violin of Pavel Kudelasek, and the cello of Pavel Verner.

If you like the early string quartets of Mozart, these quartets by his Parisian contemporary should delight you.gio. A long established ensemble from Poland, they give a polished reading to these 6 quartets from St. George. Particularly noteworthy are the 1st violin of Pavel Kudelasek, and the cello of Pavel Verner. If you like the early string quartets of Mozart, these quartets by his Parisian contemporary should delight you.

product_title: Restless And Wild
review_body:
Origins of thrash, death, power, and neo-classical metal can all be heard on Accept\x27s breakthrough album.

It\x27s an album that\x27s simultaneously diverse, yet uniform in its rugged, pure spirit. That\x27s the beauty of it. The AC/DCesq rock love song, "Don\x27t Go Stealing My Soul Away" fits right in with the proto-death/black metal track "Demon\x27s Night," a song that Cannibal Corpse would later cover. Udo\x27s shrieking vocal\x27s and Hoffmann\x27s jagged, yet sophisticated lead playing tie the disparate tracks together.

"Fast as a Shark," is one of the heaviest songs ever recorded. The extreme metal template of rapid double-bass, chugging riffs, and violent lyrics are all there. Nine months later, Metallica\x27s Kill \x27em All set the heavy bar much higher, but the legacy of the song lives on.

"Neon Nights" is a semi-ballad with a solo borrowed from a classical piece that I can\x27t remember. Closing the album, "Princess of the Dawn," lays the groundwork for power metal with it\x27s epic feel, fantasy lyrics, and mandolin outro that is actually a manipulated guitar.

Yet Restless and Wild is not just seeds of what was to come. It\x27s a powerful, heavy, and catchy album in its own right. It\x27s an essential of the metalhead catalog.

**There is no official reissue for this album that I know of. There\x27s two different covers available, but there\x27s not much difference in the products, so in terms of the physical entity, Restless doesn\x27t give much to a album collection.

product_title: The Hoople
review_body: I figured the Hoople would be a natural continuation in style from Mott, but it\x27s actually quite different.  At least half of it is.  It feels like the band was more concerned with distancing themselves from straight ahead rock music and guitar riffs and wanted to give us something more pretentious and suitable for the music theater.  I honestly think it would be wise to not take my review as permanent because I need more time to absorb this album.  I\x27m not getting what I expected- this isn\x27t what I thought Mott the Hoople was like at all so I\x27m confused a bit.  I need time to warm up to this.    \x5C\x22Marionette\x5C\x22 is notable for the glamorous stage show-like verse melody and the briefly played upbeat piano, but when the song changes gears (rather quickly and shockingly) it feels more like a misguided circus act of some kind and loses focus a bit.  Actually it feels really messy.  The whole thing feels like a big put-on and even gets ugly during the \x5C\x22Marionette, teachers pet\x5C\x22 part which is really awful in my opinion.  Still a decent enough song if we ignore that part.  But then comes \x5C\x22Alice\x5C\x22 which marks a bigger improvement thankfully.  This time I really dig Ian Hunter\x27s lyrics, the vocal melody and the chugging pace of the piano work.  The bombastic elements have been lowered to a more tolerable extent while the storytelling lyrics take center stage.  Can\x27t quite say I know what the lyrics are supposed to be about though.    \x5C\x22Through the Looking Glass\x5C\x22 sounds like a dramatic conclusion to a Hollywood western stage show performance with Ian Hunter providing Jeff Lynne of Electric Light Orchestra vocal similarities and other ELO-resembling arrangements.  Not *quite* sounding like ELO\x27s \x5C\x22Wild West Hero\x5C\x22 from their Out of the Blue album but basically the same idea.  \x5C\x22Pearl \x27N\x27 Roy\x5C\x22 is an unimpressive mid-tempo rocker with sloppy singing from Ian Hunter.  Not really glam or rock- but something else.  Not sure what this is to be honest!  I admit it grows on me the more I playit though.  The rhythm is memorable, groovy and adequate enough to leave me satisfied, and the sloppiness of the vocals is charming in some unusual kind of way.    \x5C\x22Trudi\x27s Song\x5C\x22 begins on an interesting note with the \x5C\x22whoa oh oh\x5C\x22 repetitious part which is appealing.  The vocals are clearly imitating Bob Dylan\x27s softer moments.  This song represents the thing I was mostly concerned about while listening to Mott last night- Ian\x27s style of sincere balladry just feels too simplistic to make much of an impression.  The type of ballad where you\x27re supposed to focus on Ian\x27s tender voice while ignoring the rather bland lyrics and melody.  I don\x27t think I can ignore these flaws to be honest.  I understand there\x27s all kinds of Ian Hunter fans out there, and I\x27m totally not trying to disrespect any of them by any means by criticizing what I consider an artist with noticeable faults.    Now let\x27s talk about why I\x27m giving this album 4 stars instead of 3.  4 songs in particular miraculously elevate this album much higher.  Those would be \x5C\x22Born Late \x2758\x5C\x22 with its really good 50\x27s style rock and roll energy and catchy guitar riff.  Maybe the only moment on the album with a memorable guitar riff (or at least, a riff worthy of being placed in the same category as the stuff from Mott).  The vocals are wonderful as well.  Electric Light Orchestra wrote several songs just like this one throughout their 70\x27s career.  Maybe ELO were inspired by this band and realized simple rock can be a winning formula?  I doubt it but who knows.  \x5C\x22The Golden Age of Rock \x27N\x27 Roll\x5C\x22 begins with a tragic introduction very similar to mid 70\x27s T.Rex.  It\x27s glam perfection- the whole song.  Instantly likeable too.  \x5C\x22Crash Street Kidds\x5C\x22 is more of an aggressive rocker.  Mott the Hoople is simply a terrific band when they\x27re rocking out like this.  \x5C\x22Crash street kidds are comin\x27 to get ya!\x5C\x22 is a memorable part of the song despite how repetitive it gets near the end.    However let\x27s ignore the entire album for a moment and focus on how AWESOME \x5C\x22Roll Away the Stone?\x5C\x22 is!  If you\x27d have told me this song was actually Slade I would\x27ve believed you.  This song is incredibly sad and I especially feel like crying during the chorus.  I may have my issues with Ian Hunter\x27s singing style, but trust me I have absolutely *no* issues with \x5C\x22Roll Away the Stone\x5C\x22.  This song is pop perfection, right up there with the Raspberries \x5C\x22Go All the Way\x5C\x22 and several Travelling Wilbury songs.  \x5C\x22Won\x27t you roll away the sto-o-o-o-o-one\x5C\x22 (that\x27s me trying to emotionally sing the chorus in words... and failing hard, lol).  Seriously though, brilliant song.    Overall the theater aspects are quite dominant on this one, moving significantly further away from the rock and roll of Mott and into self-indulgent territory.  With that said though, I\x27m perfectly aware the theatrical portions of the album have NOT grown on me yet, so I\x27m admittedly writing from an inexperienced perspective for the time being.  Mott the Hoople is still a band I don\x27t quite understand yet.  If and when the album shows signs of improving I\x27ll go back and edit this review.

Big Big Train slapped together "English Electric Part 1" (september 2012) and "English Electric Part 2" (march 2013) with four more songs and sold the package as "English Electric: Full Steam" (september 2013). At moments (many moments actually) the music resembles amazingly closely the \xC2\xABclassic\xC2\xBB Genesis quintet\x27s style (Gabriel-Banks-Collins-Hackett-Rutherford), but the best episodes sport the peculiar Big Big Train style, like in "East Coast Racer", a personal favourite of mine, written by Greg Spawton, whose songs I generally prefer on those composed by David Longdon, by the way.

One thing I don\x27t like is the choice of "Make Some Noise" as the incipit of the album: it\x27s like offering first a beer can and then, a glass of fine wine (the second track is the vastly superior "The First Rebreather") -- or better a long row of these.

product_title: Mussorgsky: Pictures at an Exhibition No 1-10; Night on the Bare Mountain; Khovanshchina - Prelude / Rimsky-Korsakov: Russian Easter Festival Overture
review_body:
Charles Dutoit\x27s Montreal Symphony recording of "Pictures at an exhibition" has a very beautiful, "French" sound, but without the saxophone like wobble of French horns as in many French orchestras, i.e. "Orchestre de Paris" or "Paris Conservatory Orchestra."

Dutoit has been criticized for not having the appropriate heaviness for Russian music, but here the sound is excellent, playing by Montreal absolutely top notch. Dutoit characterizes each movement of Mussorgsky\x27s great war horse individually, and the end result is very satisfying.

Dutoit\x27s "Pictures", and the other tracks on this disc held my attention for the duration. I highly recommend it.

product_title: Prince of Pagodas Suite / Tabuh-Tabuhan
review_headline: Rare Britten ballet music with exotic scoring in superb sound
review_body:
As part of the commemoration of Britten\x27s birth during 2013, I was drawn to this disc to fill a hole in my collection. To my pleasure, both the music and engineering turned out to be first-rate. The exotic oriental instruments and colorful melodies are enticing, while Slatkin\x27s direction doesn\x27t force the music or call attention to itself. I checked out the complete ballet on EMI and decided this set of excerpts fills the bill nicely. Moreover, the Chandos SACD engineering opens up a realistic soundstage that lets everything show through with great clarity and transparency.

Some of the Britten completists might also enjoy his brief piano performance, while others may enjoy another helping of the unusual instruments via the McPhee filler. But I\x27ll take the Britten ballet excerpts in superb sound and declare victory at this point.

product_title: Creation/Destruction
review_headline: Fit For A King has come to play
review_body:
Fit For A King\x27s Solid State debut definitely retains the metalcore sound the label is well-regarded for, but they spice it up a bit, delivering a project that has hints of a harsher sound, almost a little bit thrash. The heavier sound is complemented by some really outstanding clean vocals, including a clean-only ballad, the excellent Skin & Bones, sung with a sweetness tat Ryan Clark or Bjorn Strid can appreciate. Along with the satisfactory levels of aggression, energy, and clean vocals, the album has plenty of melodic aspects to it, making it a much more versatile release than your average metalcore CD. Transitions are well done too, so the overall record never feels tired from throwing one aspect in your face repeatedly.

My favorite songs include the aforementioned Skin & Bones, Warpath, The Resistance, and Destruction, a nasty heavy track that closes the album out in satisfactory fashion.

Creation/Destruction is a great metal album, and the band from Texas is a very promising one. This album deserves a 4.5, and your undivided attention.

product_title: Power And Passion
review_body:
I recently picked up the vinyl edition of this Mama\x27s Boys LP from a local record store. My LP cover is actually an enlarged version of the picture on the back of this release - the three brothers posing with the flying V guitar. Not sure what the significance of the cover differences are, maybe the one sold at Amazon with the Girl cover is a re-issue...? Anyway, the track listing is the same.

Growing up with 80\x27s hard rock and heavy metal this was one band that I never had in my collection. I was always interested in getting some of their music ever since these guys did not show up to the Ratt / Twisted Sister / Mama\x27s Boys concert at the Dallas Texas Bronco Bowl (July 24, 1984). They just plain didn\x27t show up! Maybe they were stuck in Ireland or something.

Every song on this release is really good straight ahead rock \x27n\x27 roll with great melodies. Some of the choruses will easily have you humming or singing along. I really like the violin element as part of their music and the way they integrated the violin sound is done very well - not too overdone at all, yet just enough to add some uniqueness to their songs. The production seems very good for the era as well. I used my USB Turntable to convert the songs from my Vinyl copy to MP3 so I can listen to them anywhere and they sound great. Every song rocks on this release. I am on the hunt for some of Mama\x27s Boys other LP\x27s.

My favorite songs are "Straight Forward, No Looking Back", "Needle In The Groove", and "Don\x27t Tell Mama"
My least favorite songs are the last two "The Professor II" and "Let\x27s Get High".

I regularly mix songs from this release in my 80\x27s rock \x27n\x27 roll play list.

I recommend this release to any 80\x27s rock \x27n\x27 roll fan or anyone who likes music from bands such as Dokken, Ratt, Heavy Pettin, and Tokyo Blade.

product_title: Goliath
review_body: This album means even more than it is to those of us who grew up in the 80s and 90s and wanted to think brashly alongside our Christian music.  Steve Taylor was option #1, and there wasn\x27t a close second.  When he stepped back from making his own music, CCM lost something; when he stepped away from writing for others, something died.  He had swagger and mischief; he had an unending fount of cleverness; he was serious about his faith, and mine.  Mischief, cleverness, wisdom: that combination doesn\x27t come around often.  Hearing "Shortstop" some years later, a one-song performance well after his solo career had faded, felt like encountering a ghost--a real encounter, but one that made me feel absence even more than fleeting presence.  This album is the real thing, back not from the dead but from a long journey.  Jimmy A, John Mark Painter, and Peter Furler--all successful musicians within the CCM umbrella but who\x27ve found their way to its margins--gathered round Steve Taylor like the disaffected musicians who formed Chagall Guevara more than twenty years ago.  And each is very good on this album. What they do just with rhythm is enough to keep my ear interested.  Like them, Taylor\x27s lyrics are very good.  There isn\x27t quite as much of the showy wit of "Breakfast" or "Coffee Can."  He\x27ll go long stretches without a pun.  The lyrics are more mature in that regard, not youthfully testing how far they can go, not having anything to prove, not long-lined as if he felt the need to load a song with as many words and tricks as possible.  A lot of short lines, actually.  But the lyrics are solid, chewy, meant not so much to dominate a band as to take their place within it.  These four men work very well together.  They seem deferential to each other\x27s performances, restrained but not suppressed, justifiably comfortable and confident in each of their roles.  That three of them have been producers shows up in the little quirks and touches of music that makealmost no corner of the music monotonous.  I could maybe wish for a little more wisdom, more positive insight to go alongside the mischievous ("Moonshot") and angry ("In Layers") satire.  But it\x27s there with varying degrees of sophistication and emphasis in "A Life Preserved," "Rubberneck," "Double Negative," "In Layers," "Comedian."  And the album has been my much-welcome, much-needed soundtrack companion to a recent and difficult time.  The CD\x27s been playing in my car pretty much non-stop for about a month.  It bears repeated, repeated, repeated listening.

product_title: Load
review_headline: When Metallica Took an 80 Minute Load on Us
review_body:
If the music wasn\x27t bad enough, Metallica had to give us some urine and semen on the cover.

I don\x27t dislike Load because it\x27s a sell out. I don\x27t dislike it because Metallica was douchey about it. I don\x27t dislike it because it\x27s not heavy. I dislike it because it sucks.

I understand the desire to make an alternative rock album in the 90\x27s. Anthrax and some other bands pulled it off. If Load and Reload were condensed into one fifty minute album, Metallica would have pulled it off as well. But they had to make song after song, and bunch of them are really long and go nowhere.

They got diversity here. Alt rock with some country, blues, a bit of hard rock, and a tad bit of metal. But despite the genre blending, the songs are repetitive. It\x27s when Lars Ulrich gave up on trying to be a better drummer and actually started getting worse. And James Hetfield took his affair with the word "yeah" to a whole new level.

"King Nothing" is probably the best song from both loads. "Until It Sleeps" is an enjoyable Smashing Pumpkins song. In "Mama Said," Hetfield deals with his mommy issues with an acoustic guitar and cowboy hat.

I find the first two tracks intolerable. "Poor Twisted Me" is a real loser. "Bleeding Me" and "The Outlaw Torn" have moments but that doesn\x27t make up for their prodigious length.

There\x27s about half an hour of good material here, leaving fifty minutes of droll, not all of which can be divided by the skip button.

review_body: Naaman was the lead alto saxophonist in the Israeli Air Force Band when he came to the U.S. in 2004 to study jazz at the Berklee College of Music, Purchase College, and the New England Conservatory.  He has performed with artists such as Terri Lynne Carrington, Joanne Brackeen, Dave Samuels, and Winard Harper. His stylistic flexibility is evident also, ranging from fetching mainstream renditions of the standards "The Very Thought of You" and "Polka Dots and Moonbeams," to the hard bop or post bop of his originals.  Also heard is an appealing adaptation of a Yemenite Jewish song, "Eshal Elohai."  The musicians providing spirited support to Naaman on this flawless CD include trumpeter Marcus Printup, pianists George Cables and Roy Assaf, bassist Dezron Douglas, and drummers Gregory Hutchinson and Ulysses Owens Jr.  Naaman is already a mature and significant talent, and will hopefully have many future opportunities to record and broaden his exposure.

product_title: Jericho
review_headline: Minus Robertson but just as good
review_body:
This is one of my favorite albums by The Band. They seem to be having fun again, albeit without Robbie Robertson (maybe that\x27s why?). Of course, without their principal songwriter, the band relies on covering other songs - and what songs they are! Their version of Bob Dylan\x27s Blind Willie McTell is devastatingly good! The Band has always been Dylan\x27s best interpreters. If that isn\x27t good enough for you, they take Bruce Springsteen\x27s stark ballad Atlantic City from the Nebraska album and arrange it like only The Band can do, and hit another one out of the park. Just those two songs are worth the price of admission.

But you get more! Levon Helm\x27s vocal turn on The Stuff You Gotta Watch is a preview of his solo work. (In fact he re-recorded the song for Electric Dirt.) Helm provides the amazing Amazon (River of Dreams) and also co-writes The Caves of Jericho and Move To Japan.

The only thing missing is Robertson\x27s guitar. Jim Weider does a nice enough job but he\x27s not Robertson. But once you feel the spirit and energy coming through your speakers, you won\x27t really miss it. If you like The Band, this is one you have to hear.

product_title: Damnation of Faust / Harold En Italie
review_headline: the finest recording of this work ever committed to disc
review_body:
Faust -- This is it, the pick of the litter, the finest recording of this work ever committed to disc, originally as a 2-LP set. There are at least 2 small cuts in the music (an orchestral passage after Faust\x27s first aria, and the first verse of the Easter chorus, have not identified any others). Someone has speculated that the cuts were made to fit the performance onto 4 lp sides, but, I also have a live concert version of this which Markevitch made several months later, and the cuts are there, too. One high point in many -- in his tavern song, Brander really sounds drunk! Early stereo from May, 1959, but still very listenable. If you are into "La Damnation de Faust", this recording is essential (so is Munch/BSO, if you can find it now). Much better sound and almost as great an execution is to be had from that conducted by Dutoit on Decca. Sonically about the best is Chung on DG, but I fail to understand why other reviewers find that performance to be so good (it\x27s OK, but I prefer even the older Ozawa/BSO, also on DG, among others).

Harold -- This early version is nothing short of excellent.

product_title: Tchaikovsky: Symphonies Nos. 4, 5 & 6
review_headline: The best of Karajan in a favourite composer
review_body:
I\x27m not quite sure why Karajan felt such an affinity with these later Tchaikovsky symphonies, to the extent that he made half a dozen studio recordings of them over his long career but he certainly had a way with Russian music, as evinced by his Mussorgsky "Boris Godunov" and "Pictures", the live Shostakovich Tenth Symphony that he took to Moscow and his "Sheherezade". Perhaps Tchaikovsky\x27s orchestration and overt emotionalism allowed him to exploit both the virtuosity of his orchestras and the showman side of his personality; certainly you could not hear better playing than that of the greatest orchestra in the world in 1971 in the most grateful acoustics provided by the recording location of the Jesus-Christus-Kirche; the BPO purr like tigers before applying serious reserves of power in the big moments.

The 2007 remastering has polished what was already superb analogue sound, preferable to any other set for its depth and warmth. There is a glorious sweep to Karajan\x27s way with these works: in the opening movement of the Fourth we waltz blithely into oblivion before being consumed by the manic, screaming power of the last minute. The silky smoothness of the horn solo in the opening of the Fifth is emulated nowhere else but it is the performance of the Sixth which is the real marvel: how anyone could accuse Karajan of shallowness having heard this swirling descent into annihilation is beyond me.

I remain attached to the tauter Mravinsky set but the early 60\x27s sound is hissy and brittle compared with the sumptuousness here; for individual recordings of the Fourth and Fifth, a young Abbado with the VPO and Shipway with the RPO remain first recommendations but Karajan\x27s Sixth is in a class of its own.

product_title: The Night God Slept
review_body:
Silent Planet is another entry into Solid States ever-growing line of talented metalcore bands. Though the genre itself can be a bit tired and not nearly as impressive as some of the genres perfected in Europe, few brands of metal give us the always exciting guitar riffs with aggressive growls and clean singing. Silent Planet sounds a lot like the typical SS band, but they take everything a good metalcore band needs, and does it to near-perfection.

Silent Planet\x27s debut record is bolder than most would expect, and so its the music. Vocals are aggressive, and the album\x27s themes are sharper and clearer than many metal records. XX deals with pornography, and Native Blood inspects the impact of religion with the Native Americans. Darkstrand addresses the fallout with Japan after WW2.

My favorite tracks include the aforementioned songs, along with Tiny Hands, and Wasteland. This band is very good at storytelling, and this is as good a debut as any in the metal scene. Silent Planet is already one of Solid State\x27s top names.

product_title: Fritz Reiner - The Complete Chicago Symphony Recordings on RCA
review_body:
I got the Fritz Reiner set as a most welcomed Christmas present. I had a few of the LP and CD reissues of a few of the 63 discs in the set but the overwhelming majority are new to me. The discs are issued with the original LP covers, down to the comments, in extremely fine print, on the back cover. The CDs reproduce the look of the original LP down to the side 1 label. The sound quality is clear and crisp as anyone who heard the original Living Stereo recordings will remember. The only time I heard some minor distortion was in the Rhapsodie Espagnole and one of the Rossini overtures. There is much to like and far more than I can mention here. I had not heard Fritz Reiner conduct any Mozart and Haydn and the performances came as a pleasant and welcome surprise. Some highlights of the set.

\xE2\x80\xA2 Respighi: Fountains of Rome, Pines of Rome. Arguably, the best recording of the Pines and Fountains.
\xE2\x80\xA2 Beethoven: Concerto for Piano and Orchestra No 5 (Emperor). Van Cliburn is superb in this performance.
\xE2\x80\xA2 Mahler: The Song of the Earth. Beautifully recorded with Richard Lewis and Maureen Forrester.
\xE2\x80\xA2 Beethoven: Symphony No.5, Coriolan Overture. A magnificent no nonsense recording if the famous 5th.
\xE2\x80\xA2 Berlioz/deFalla: Nuit d\xE2\x80\x99Ete, El amor brujo. Fabulous performances by the young Leontyne Price.
\xE2\x80\xA2 Bartok: Music for Strings Percussion and Celesta, Hungarian Sketches. Still the standard recordings of this music.
\xE2\x80\xA2 Festival: Kabalevsky\x27s Colas Breugnon, Tchakovsky\xE2\x80\x99s March Slav and Miniature Overture and Glinka\x27s Russlan and Lyudmila Overture. A magnificent disc of Russian music with the odd title Festival and cover of a Chinese dragon. Presumably the Cold War was responsible for not calling the disc Russia, following the trend of Spain and Vienna.
\xE2\x80\xA2 Hovhaness/Stravinsky: Mysterious Mountain, Divertimento. Legendary performances.
\xE2\x80\xA2 Spain: de Falla: The Three-Cornered Hat: Dances; La vida breve: Interludeand Dances; Albinez: Iberia: Triana and Fete-dieu a Seville, Navarra; Granados: Goyescas: Intermezzo. For me, the Albenez orchestrations are the highlight of this disc.
\xE2\x80\xA2 The Reiner Sound - Ravel: Rhapsodie Espagnole, Pavane for a Dead Princess; Rachmaninoff: Isle of the Dead. A beautifully played account of Rhapsodie Espagnole and the Pavane and an atmospheric account of Isle of the Dead.
\xE2\x80\xA2 Prokofieff/Stravinsky: Lieutenant Kije, Song of the Nightingale. Two classic records of these works.
Arguably, the most important composers for Fritz Reiner were Richard Strauss and Bela Bartok. The earliest recording in the set is the fabulous Also Sprach Zarathustra and Ein Heldenleben, both recorded in 1954. The recordings of Sinfonia Domestica and the Bourgeois Gentilhomme Suite are also not to be missed, while the Bartok Concerto for Orchestra, Music for Strings, Percussion and Celeste and the Hungarian Sketches are benchmark recordings. The collection includes a short bonus disc containing a never released Bach concerto and a brief comment by Fritz Reiner on Beethoven\xE2\x80\x99s Seventh Symphony.

If you enjoyed the Living Stereo recordings of Fritz Reiner in the past or you want to discover these fabulous recordings for the first time, this will be a wonderful set to have
