review_headline: Less than Half Noise Reduction compared to regular plugs but...
review_body:
These DUBS are cool, a great fit, and help take the edge off loud sounds.

However, the noise reduction rating (NNR) is 12dB.

It\x27s less than half of the 33 NNR of the best selling foam (cheap) earplugs available on Amazon.

Are these better than nothing? Absolutely. Are they cooler than sticking bright orange foam sticks in your ear? You betcha.

However, as far as actual protection of your ear drum, be advised that these just take the edge off the loud sounds.

Let\x27s get to some data (internet researched of course).

WebMD states that anything above 85 dB is harmful to your ears. The duration of the noise will determine the level of possible damage.

For reference, WebMD lists commons sounds at 85 dB to be \x5C\x22Heavy traffic, window air conditioner, noisy restaurant, power lawn mower\x5C\x22

A 12db reduction there would help bring down the sounds to safer (or even safe) levels.

However, subway noise ranks in at 90-95. We\x27ve now reached the edge of what these can protect against in terms of bringing noise down to \x5C\x22safe\x5C\x22 levels.

96-100 dB examples given are Boom box, ATV, and motorcycle noises.

A school dance is 101-105 dB.

So, 12 dB off 105 is 93. Not bad, but not in the \x5C\x22safe\x5C\x22 zone. Would you or your kids wear these to a school dance? Well, they\x27re certainly better than foam sticks in your ear, and the opening inside does help sounds in a certain range enter which help keep things clear instead of muffled. Who knows, maybe they\x27re the next rage at school dances.

Now a sports crowd, rock concert or symphony are listed as 120-129.

A 12 dB reduction doesn\x27t give you much there (reduced to only 117dB), but a 33 dB reduction from the standard foam plugs brings it down to 96 dB the high end.

So these provide less than half the noise reduction of regular plugs, and here\x27s the big ...ahem... but, I like them them (the DUBS that is).

I\x27ve found myself using them when using the foam sticks are just a hassle. We have a bunch of the foam plugs, but I don\x27t use them as often as I should.

The DUBS however, are easy to use, convenient, and they are...cool.

They take the edge off loud activity that yes, can hurt your hearing such as vacuuming, using power tools, etc.

These also fit well and remain comfortable to wear. They could easily be mistaken for a bluetooth earpiece (except for the fact that you have two of them).

So yes, while they only reduce the sound (or are only rated) by 12 dB, they\x27re better than nothing, and you might just find yourself grabbing these more, much more than the foam plugs.

We have bought a couple of these things and there\x27s a problem: In order to mount it, you "tip" the unit up and wrap it around the pole (e.g. mic stand) and twist it so it\x27s coil is wrapped around the pole. Easy enough. It stays in place by using gravity (as designed), meaning that the weight of the part that holds your drink is what keeps it from shimmying down the pole. So here\x27s the problem - as soon as you pull your drink out, inevitably you will lift that coiled part that holds the drink a little bit and then you stand and watch as this thing does some "slinky-style" shimmying right on down to the floor.

The only way we found around this was to use some gaffer\x27s tape, velcro strips, or the like to keep the unit from being tipped up and sliding down the pole. That works, but it looks like junk and kind of defeats the purpose of having a simple to use device it you have to jerry-rig it.

review_body: I\x27ve been using my work laptop for frequent live conference calls and got comments about the build-in microphone not working very well. So I tried a number of microphones with 3.5mm terminated cables that I could plug into the microphone jack on my laptop and, hopefully, improve the clarify and loudness of my voice to call listeners. Didn\x27t want the clip-on types, or the small units that plug directly into the microphone jack but require that I bend down close to them to be heard. I finally settled on the Frisby PC/laptop/VOIP microphone from Amazon (looks like a smaller version of a Shure mike), which has received very favorable reviews. Conference call attendees mentioned that my voice was much clearer and audible, but only if I spoke within a few inches of the Frisby microphone, which comes with a very small and lightweight plastic stand and holder. That small stand also forced me to bend over when I spoke, which becomes a chore and a pain in the neck during 2 or 3-hour meetings. Then I found the ChromCast CC-CGMIC-STAND at Amazon. The stand\x27s heavy and solid metal (bronze?) base actually takes up less desk space than most of the smaller, lighter, and similarly-priced plastic mike stands out there. The circular base and rugged and easily adjusted gooseneck with attached mike holder raises the Frisby microphone (which fits snugly into the holder) up to 14 inches off the desk, so I can now position it within inches of my mouth without any need to bend forward or over to be heard. According to the Epiphone web-site, the electronics are supposed to be a shadow performer preamp with a nanoflex pickup.  The Shadow Performer line of pre-amps come in a variety of iterations, but the one epiphone shows on its web-site is the shadow performer tuner model, which includes a built in chromatic tuner.  The pre-amp actually installed on the guitar does not have the chromatic tuner, but rather what appears to be the "double-play" slider, which is supposed to be used to blend between a bridge mounted nanoFlex pickup and a fingerboard mounted nanoMag pickup.  Since I don\x27t believe this guitar includes the NanoMag pickup, I don\x27t see any advantage in having the slider, and would rather have the chromatic tuner instead.  I also kind of don\x27t like the "end-pin" jack, as it is a non-standard "button" size for attaching a strap.  I would prefer to have a standard strap pin button on the end, and have the jack mounted elsewhere.

product_title: Shure Sound Isolating Earphones with Quad High Definition MicroDrivers and True Subwoofer
review_headline: The best of the best 100% sound for 300% price.
review_body: This is a very interesting product for me. I think it is important to know my audio background before I can start talking about this product. I started listening to music on a pair of first generation Ipod Touch headphones. I then upgraded to a pair of V-moda ear buds which served me well for about a year. I then acquired a pair of Audio Technica ATH-mx 50 studio headphones that I used for studio monitoring, as well as a pair of Bose 2i2 earbuds for exercise. After several years my Bose buds broke due to a cable failure. With no option to replace the cable and an expired warrantee, I was forced to start perusing for a new pair of ear buds.  That is when the Shure earphones came to my attention.  I purchased them with the intent to use them for exercise and monitoring live performances and studio recordings. So far they have given me mixed results. First of all the sound isolation is really top notch; almost too much so. I recently used these in the woodshop while running a handheld power sander, I couldn\x27t hear the sander at all and the music was just as amazing. This is good because the music is all you hear no matter what, this is bad because it can be unsafe while exercising, walking, driving or doing anything where you need to hear ambient sounds for safety reasons. This is just something that should be noted before you decide wither or not to purchase.  The sound that these produce is absolutely stellar (as one would expect.) They provide exceptional clarity and all frequencies come through to provide an amazing sound signature. I have found some interesting attributes with some modern tracks that I am used to listening at a high volume. In the past I would turn the volume up rather loud to provide maximum awesomeness and a healthy dose of distortion. With these headphones, you can turn the volume up as high as you want and there will be absolutely NO healthy distortion. All of the sounds are crystal clear at all volumes, which is a good thing but something toget used to.  These earbuds are very comfortable. The over the ear cable provides an extra level of secureness on ones head.  If you are not used to in ear headphones you may experience some discomfort in the first few weeks but this discomfort will surely pass. They include two different cable lengths that come in very handy for different applications in the studio and on the go. If you can\x27t find a well fitting set of tips from the selections included, you have bigger problems. Huge variety of tips that provide different acoustical qualities and different feels. These headphones are highly customizable.  Another note: ya\x27 know that hair raising tingling sensation that goes from your head all the way to your toes when you are listening to the best part of one of your favorite songs? Yeah, that happens at least twice as often when I\x27m listening on these earbuds. It\x27s really weird, I keep thinking there is something wrong with me. But day after day, repeat after repeat I keep achieving the same results. Shure has clearly done something very right here.  Overall there is diffidently a time and place for these headphones. If you\x27ve got the cash and you are willing to spend it these are definitively the best of the best; these are the 100% sound. If you are the average consumer looking for a 90% sound for everyday use I would go with the Bose 2i2. The only reason I gave it four stars is because of the price; sorry I forgot to mention that. This is a perfect product for certain applications, with in an imperfect & elitist price tag.   Hope you found this review helpful, I am happy to answer questions to help you decide if these are for you!

product_title: Audio-Technica ATH Professional Studio Monitor Headphones
review_headline: Excellent pair of headphones. Great sound, great noise-canceling (no batteries!) and great price.
review_body:
As a radio DJ, I used a set of these headphones in my studio for four years and loved them. I recently picked up a pair for personal use.

Pros:

I\x27ve had these headphones for about six months. They are extremely comfortable, even on long plane flights, and I find that they have impressive canceling characteristics as well, with the added bonus that there are no batteries or battery compartments to fool with since this is a direct consequence of their over-ear design. That means no annoying background buzzing. They ship with an elegantly designed screw-on converter so you can swap quickly between a quarter inch connector for amps or a studio sound board and a standard-sized headphone connector for your mobile devices and laptops. I spend about as much time practicing my electric guitar with these plugged into my travel amp as I do using them to listen to music.

The price is attractive as well. If you\x27re looking to upgrade your old ear buds and break into the quality headphone world, these are a really solid place to start and they will not disappoint you. I personally like their looks, comfort and sound much better than the $200-300 pairs of Beats that I\x27ve tried. Extreme audiophiles will probably want to consider something with a higher price tag that fits their exact tastes.

Cons:

There are very few. I will say that you should prepare yourself for a long, and I mean very long, cord. This is meant to facilitate ease of use in a studio setting, so you\x27ll appreciate it if that\x27s your intended use, but while at my desk or traveling I keep several feet of cord coiled up and secured with a zip tie. Not the most aesthetic solution but it certainly works. If that\x27s not up your alley then you should definitely consider the coiled cable model (though I can\x27t speak to the length of the coiled cord, as I don\x27t have it myself).

This sounds silly, but I can imagine that people with really large ears could find these uncomfortable since the ear cups are pretty snug (my father, for example, doesn\x27t find them as comfortable as I do). If this is something you have had trouble with in the past I recommend that you try them before you buy them.

product_title: Left Handed Black Acoustic Electric Guitar Full Size Thinline Cutaway Body with Case and Picks
review_headline: Excellent value at twice the price.
review_body: It was extremely hard to choose a guitar sight unseen.  Had I not been looking for a left-handed guitar at the last minute, I would have researched it much more in person in my area.  That said, I got an excellent deal and a great guitar.  I waited to leave a review until I had had it a month so I could give a fair account of the guitar.  It keeps tune quite well (according to my electronic tuner) and I rarely have to adjust the tuning.  I am just learning to play, so I keep the electronic tuner on the headstock and check the tuning every time I pick it up to practice.  Approximately every third day or so I need to adjust about half the strings less than a quarter turn of the peg.  Once I left the house when it was warm and left windows open and the heater off, and when I got home it was 30 degrees colder--that time every string had to be re-tuned by about a half-note.  I bought a walk-around size amp and am perfectly pleased with both the acoustic and the electric sound of the guitar.  I went back and forth whether it would be possible to find a good quality, left-handed, 3/4 size guitar for a decent price the day before Christmas, and I decided to go with the full size Jameson.  It is _almost_ too big for me, both for my hands and for my body (I\x27m five feet tall full grown).  It\x27s a reach between notes on the first and third frets and if I\x27m not paying attention my hand drifts towards one fret or the other and the next note at the opposite fret sounds off.  It\x27s difficult to find a sitting position that is both comfortable to hold and play.  I\x27m confident that as I become more practiced and proficient these will become less of an issue.  I assume that as I become a better player, I may want a fancier or more expensive guitar, but this is ideal for a learner.  I think it would be a steal at even twice the price.  It came with an amp cable, several picks, a gig bag and a great info sheet with tuning and chord info, plus info sheets on registering the guitar and customer-support info.  I bought separately a tuner, several extra sets of strings (I broke three strings before I got it tuned properly the first time--haven\x27t broken another since), a pin-winder, the belt-amp, and a lefty beginning guitar book.  All together this was under $120.00 including shipping, and makes an excellent learn-to-play setup.  As I was prepared to pay at least $120 for a basic acoustic guitar, I found it a great deal and the excellent quality above and beyond what I expected for the price (or even twice the price) a wonderful surprise.  After I had already paid for it but before it arrived, I read a bunch of scary reviews where people described it as a piece of junk that wouldn\x27t keep tune and as a cheap toy, so I was relieved when it arrived and I found it to be a serviceable and well-made beginner guitar.

product_title: Guitar Effects Pedal Boogie Master Simulation Mesa Distortion Speaker Simulation Effects Pedal
review_headline: Returned - unacceptable hiss and noise even with all controls set to minimum
review_body:
I own several Joyo products including the JP-02 power supply, JF-10 compressor, JF-11 6-band EQ, and two cab simulators, the JF-14 American Sound (Fender) and JF-13 AC Tone (Vox AC30). They are all great and quiet.

After watching a few YouTube videos of Joyo Ironman pedals, I was stoked to try them out - super practical small size combined with supposedly higher end sounding yet still cost-effective pedals. The first one I chose was the Ironman Boogie Master (to be used mostly at cleaner, subtler settings).

When I tried the pedal out, I played with lots of settings for use with a basic Strat and Telecaster. Strat tones were basically a bust - nothing very interesting. The Telecaster tones were better and more useful but less than I hoped. The irritating deal-breaker, however, was how much self-noise (hiss) that was generated. This was very unexpected because all my previous experience with Joyo pedals had been positive. I tried inserting this pedal before the JF-14 and then after (testing both active and bypass). The noise problem was the same before and after. Even setting all Boogie Master controls to minimum, there were unacceptably high hiss levels.

This is the first time I bothered to return anything that I got from Amazon.

This pedal was either an example of poor quality control or just a dud.

I will be wary of other Joyo Ironman pedals based on this first experience.

review_body:
Full disclosure: I received this product free to review.

This is the first regular LED light bulb I\x27ve used and I\x27m already quite impressed. It does turn on to full brightness instantly and fills the room with a lot of light. This bulb puts out fairly "warm" light as far as color temperature is concerned. I currently have it in an adjustable, dimming desk light. Initially it remains cool to the touch, but have it on for a few hours and it will get hot, not near as much as a regular bulb, but you won\x27t want to grab it barehanded. I was disappointed that the lowest brightness you\x27re able to get with this bulb is quite a bit higher than what you can do with an incandescent.

product_title: Undercover Canopy Aluminum Instant Shelter - 100 Sq.ft of Shade (10 x 10- Feet, White)
review_headline: WILL NOT COMPACT UNDER FIVE FEET IN LENGTH!
review_body:
My order was for model: UC-3P10W

I guess I was SPOILED by my cheapie E-Z Up canopy...
Let me warn you now: this thing is NOT compact!
Yes, it does say 62-inches "for easy storage"...
Yes, it does say "65...inches" on the Product Dimensions...
Yes, it\x27s my fault for not comprehending all the details, but with phrases like "easy storage" and "ease-of-transport"...
Then you\x27ve got this sentence: "Women and senior users in particular tell us they absolutely love this shade."
I\x27m 6\x27 and easily over 200lbs., and I cannot see an elderly or "women" handling this easily?!?!
This one tops the cake: "backpack ready wheel-bag"
Since when backpacks were FIVE FEET LONG???
I\x27m no midget - see above - and I found the canopy packed in it\x27s "bag" to be cumbersome at best!
You really need a truck to haul this thing around!
My Toyota sedan will NOT be able to transport this at all; at least my cheapie E-Z Up compacted down to 3 - 4 feet, so it fit ACROSS my rear seats which can accommodate up to 4-feet across, or dump it ACROSS my trunk.
I measure this canopy in it\x27s bag as 9-inches square and a smidgen (~2 inches) over 5-feet in length!
Yes, the bag does have integral "backpack straps" sewn into it, but you like you\x27re hauling a coffin!
Most hatchbacks - even with the rear seats folded down cannot handle this length...
This is primarily why I took off a whole star.
Another minor point is that the holes for the "stops" were pretty rough; it would\x27ve been nice if they could\x27ve finished the holes better.
In fact, some of my holes still had the plugs inside the square tubing, so it looks like they used a punch?
I chamfered the holes myself with a drill, and the stops worked a whole lot better.
I wished they could\x27ve used smaller holes, as I could see the stress marks on the walls of the square tubing;I\x27m sure this is where the legs would eventually fail as a weak spot.
The canopy is a shade - you can easily see the pinhole spots in daylight.
If you want waterproof, use 3M Scotchguard, Thompsons Water Seal, or equivalent - it\x27s not going to stop rain.
When I first removed the canopy, there was one large spring covered in a brittle plastic wrap.
No where in the instructions ("UC-3 User Handbook") was this spring mentioned.
I figured out that you remove the brittle plastic wrap and stuff it inside the "Peak Pole" - which is the center pole, which is technically two nest square tubes, top and bottom
Even with all of that, it is worth the ~$200 if you\x27re tired of the cheapie canopies that you can get under $100, IF you can deal with the 5-foot length!
The aluminum tubes should hold up better and does shed a lot of weight.
For those wondering about dimensions...
This thing stand very tall, with the canopy almost 1/3rd of it\x27s total height.
At it\x27s lowest setting (of 3), I get 68" of clearance in the corners - the centers of each side is actually 2.5" more clearance!
I measured the canopy corners at 16.5" inches from the horizontal seam, which the centers was only 14.0", so it\x27s a slight curve.
This is hard to tell from some of the pics, as the canopy overhang looks even across.
The adjustment holes are 5" apart from center-to-center.
As I said before, I\x27m 6", so I graze the corner edges on it\x27s lowest setting, but barely clear (68" + 5" = 73" or 6\x271") at the middle setting.
Set at the highest, and it feels like a cathedral ceiling at 78" of clearance in the corners - that\x27s a 6 and a half feet!
To the lady with the 6\x274" husband...he should have no problem with the canopy set at it\x27s highest.
The description does state: "Head Clearance 72\xE2\x80\x9D up to 82\xE2\x80\x9D", but I find that optimistic...
Surprisingly, the lowestpoint of the canopy is not the corners - it\x27s the center adjust knob on the center pole, by an inch or two.

product_title: Cabeau Air Evolution Inflatable Travel Neck Pillow - The Best Travel Pillow Built for Maximum Comfort and Portability
review_headline: Still needs design work but it\x27s the best on the market
review_body:
Pros:
Very comfortable, once it is in place. This cradles my head almost perfectly and provides great neck support.
Extremely compact and can fit easily in a small purse or carryon.
Soft cover is machine washable.
Can be inflated to accommodate your pressure preference.
Air does not escape quickly when inflating.

Cons:
Difficult to get in place. I can imagine myself elbowing people next to me trying to get it into place if I were on a plane. I also have long hair so that did not make it any easier, might be easier for short haired people. Thankfully I don\x27t usually travel alone so I will have a second hand to help me get it in place.
Extremely difficult to zip, I\x27m hoping this gets easier with practice and use.
Took much longer than I thought it would to inflate and also a lot more effort than I was expecting. No, I\x27m not elderly and I do not have respiratory problems.

Overall I would recommend this because it is the best product on the market for traveling pillows. If size were not an issue I would recommend going with the non inflatable version because inflating this was a pain.

UPDATE: I purchased the memory foam for comparison. In my opinion the inflatable is more comfortable, the memory foam was too stiff/dense for me and hurt my ears when resting my head to the side. The memory foam pillow was much quicker and easier to use, rolling it up into the provided travel bag took me approximately 90 seconds. Deflating the air pillow took me almost 15 minutes! I finally went on their website and looked at their Q&A\x27s \x5C\x22To deflate the inflatable air core, face the valve away as you simultaneously squeeze the base of the valve and slowly roll the pillow up\x5C\x22 once I figured out that you have to pinch the valve base it went SLIGHTLY quicker but I still don\x27t think I could get it to deflate in under 5 minutes even if I was well practiced. The valve on this air pillow narrows into a tiny funnel, making itdifficult to get air both in and out. Now that I have both, I will probably chose to travel with the air pillow and let my boyfriend use the memory foam because he prefers a firmer pillow.

product_title: Mini Expresso Maker by GSI Outdoors
review_headline: Surpasses my machine, and, no more instant while camping
review_body:
Finally found something I can enjoy while camping. I\x27ve been bringing a large-jar of instant Espresso I\x27ve been getting at the local grocery (Krog...). Only place around with such a product. Decent but not like at home. Then while on a trip to N.J., found this little gem in Ramsey Outdoor. Unfortuantely, did not buy it at the time, but, did think about it a lot.

Couple weeks later, decided to bite-the-proverbial-bullet and get one. Oddly, had to go back up to NJ from GA for a trip. Should\x27ve waited because Amazon got this from, who else, Ramsey Outdoor. Oh the irony.
Anyways, this lil\x27 rascal is waiting for me to try out. Soooo, unwrapped, cleaned-out for the first-time (per instructions), and gave it a shot over the kitchen stove.

Wow! I haven\x27t had espresso like this since living overseas, and, nothing like it since being in Italy. It was even better than what I usually have each morning at home from my counter-top machine. Thicker (viscocity-wise), tastier, and a little more than 1-cup. I tried a couple cups to iron-out the amount of water and espresso-grounds. Granted, the water & grounds do play into it, but, having the same water & grounds from my machine, this lil\x27 bugger is amazing. And quick. Within 60-secs, not on super-high but about a medium flame, had my cuppa.

The only unfortunate part is I\x27ve heard & seen others state a cup came with theirs. I was expecting the same. No such deal. Not a prob since I\x27ve gone back and seen its not part of the original advertising. I initially used a Frangelika cup but any 4-5 oz will do. Recently, went to the "Beyond" place and found a nice metal one for a couple bucks.

But, I\x27m going camping in a couple weeks and can\x27t wait to try this one on an open propane-stove at a lower flame. Even experiment over coals, hoping the maker & cup are level. No more instant stuff that takes-up a lot of room in my pack.

product_title: CatEye K-Edge Handlebar Mount
review_body:
Well-made & well engineered but expansive

I have used various computer mounts before this one and this is by far the best. Extremely well build and a great product.

I am using this with a CC-RD420DW Strada Digital Wireless and a CC-RD200 Strada Cadence (wired) after swapping my 2nd unit with the wired bracket. It\x27s a great out front mount for a wired Cateye computer too!

Compared to Cateye out-front mount from Cateye & Bar Fly:
1) K-edge puts the computer further out
2) The computer bracket can be changed
3) It\x27s more elegant to look at
4) It\x27s a bit heavier 28 gm vs 12 gm for the Bar Fly version.
5) The package does not provide a shim for \xC3\x98 26.0/25.4 mm handlebars while Cateye provides a rubber shim (no shim provided by Bar Fly either) . This is easily fixed but they should provide one for such a premium product.
6) Uses 2x M4x12 mm bolts, while Cateye uses a M4 bolt.
7) More expansive.

BTW, the red matches my Cane Creek 110 headset! :)

Lastly, in terms of angle, up/down adjustment, K-edge\x27s range is very limited when compared to other generic mounts like the BM-Works Extender.

product_title: Canada Goose Citadel Parka
review_body:
Chances are most of you shopping for a new Canada Goose jacket aren\x27t planning to spend 6 months in Antarctica.
Many of you (like myself) are simply looking for the best possible coat/parka money can buy that will keep you toasty during a rough cold patch.

If that\x27s the case, the Citadel jacket is probably a good bet.

There has been mixed opinion from critics about just how good a Canada Goose jacket is when the high price tag is taken into account in relation to other, less-expensive (but still pricey) parkas. I can say that if you simply ignore that debate and have the cash to burn, you can\x27t go wrong with the Citadel parka.

In short - the Citadel is a more form-fitting (and slightly less toasty) version of their signature Expedition parka. On CG\x27s heat scale, this parka will technically keep you warm up to -25C. Again, that\x27s less coverage than the Expedition - but that jacket was also designed for scientists who spend half a year working on science projects in Antarctica - not for people who live in New York, Michigan, Maine or Minnesota.

Just for comparison purposes I tried both the Citadel and Expedition at my local sporting good shop. I can tell you this.

1. Both parkas are ridiculously toasty. I mean if you\x27re indoors, if you have this coat on, anything more than a T-shirt will have you sweating profusely in minutes. When you\x27re outside, both parkas make you feel absolutely fine (unless it\x27s -30C outside, which is more than unlikely 99% of the time). On a day when the wind chill was 9F, I had my Citadel on and I didn\x27t feel a thing (I was wearing a shirt and tie underneath). The Expedition will surely be the same, if not warmer.

2. The Citadel is definitely more form-fitting. When you put it on, you don\x27t look like you\x27re wearing a huge tent. Again, if you\x27re going to be hanging out with Polar Bears for months at a time, the Expedition will probably be better and wherever you are you won\x27t really care if you look like the Michelin Man. However, for other folks the slimmer cut of the Citadel is much more appealing.

3. Sizing is different for the Citadel vs Expedition. We all know Canada Goose sizes run large but there is a difference between those jackets.
For the Citadel I took it one size smaller than my usual size (XL). For the Expedition I had to drop two sizes, and even dropping a third was still tolerable. I\x27m 6 feet tall with a 34 inch waist. For the Citadel the L was a perfect fit. The M was a bit too tight in the chest area (due to the form fitting nature of the parka). With the Expedition the M size was still pretty big. S felt a bit snug so M was the better option even if it still felt like I was wearing a big warm tent on my body.

4. The Citadel has plenty of pockets (like the Expedition) though you can take off the fur lining on the hood of the Citadel (You can\x27t on the Expedition, unless you buy the PBI edition of the Expedition parka, which has that option).

In short - if you\x27re looking for the ultimate hardcore cold weather Canada Goose jacket but don\x27t want to look like a huge marshmallow .. the Citadel is your best choice. Again, I emphasize that unless you\x27re going to be working in the Arctic or South Pole, the Citadel will do fine. Frankly if you\x27re prone to getting hot, this parka might be too hot for you. But if you\x27re serious about staying warm and want something that still looks fairly stylish (and money is no object) then this is a great choice.

If I had to sum it up, I feel like I\x27m still in my warm bed when I wear this coat outside. It\x27s pretty cushy and comfy.

Think of it this way, this coat is solid (and Canadian made) and will last you like 10 years or more. Think of it as spending 85 bucks a year for 10 years to stay 100% warm and worry-free about any cold blasts that might come your way.n Man. review_body:
I love this little lantern! I have been dealing with a lot of power outages at the house lately and finally decided to get myself a decent light source that I could keep at the ready.

The things that are most important to me about this lantern are (in order of awesomeness):
Hand-crank to charge its internal battery
360 degrees of bright light (two levels). No complaints there
Auxiliary port to charge your mobile devices
Folds down and is compact (pack for camping / motorcycling trips or use around the house)
You can fold down the accordion-style light diffuser and use the light as a sort of puck-light

Things that would improve this product:
The power switch is flush with the body of the lantern. It doesn\x27t have much tactile feedback and I wish it were raised. Think of that when you\x27re fumbling to turn it on in the dark! Perhaps Version 2 could turn on when you expand the accordion.
The hanging mechanism they provide is a loop. IMO, a hook would provide many more options to hang this light when camping or working under the car.
Rather than incorporate a USB port in the device, they provide a barrel-style port on it side. You need to use the provided cable to charge your phone. If you leave it behind or lose it, you\x27re SOL :). They could have added some storage space to keep the cable with the lantern.
The hand crank assembly is sort of a light plastic, so I hope it holds up to regular use
They could have added fluorecent parts to the lantern so you can find it quickly when the lights go out

product_title: Giro New Road Insulated Vest - Men\x27s
review_headline: Good vest to keep a warm core during cooler cycling commutes
review_body:
This vest helps handle make commuting to work by bicycle in cold weather much more enjoyable. It\x27s designed to help add core warmth and visibility (at least the Glowing red version) while cycling.

The XL size I think is a true XL size; In comparison to the Chrome WARM vest size XL-- The Giro vest feels much more roomy without being loose in comparison to the Chrome vest which is waaaay to snug (borderline overstuffed sack) for being XL (to the point where I wished they had an XXL size for the Chrome vest).

The Giro vest is very lightweight and does a good job of keeping me warm enough in 45 - 60 degree weather without heating up my core too much, even while pedaling. It does come with a few pockets to help stow any personal items, but I prefer to use either my backpack, jacket, or pannier to hold whatever gear I have.

This vest is very good with layering and also pairs well with the Levi\x27s line of commuter jackets. I also wear a XL in the Levis jacket and their Commuter-series line of button-up line of dress shirts, and it all blends and works well together.

It is a very lightweight nylon-like shell that has a thin layer of insulation, which allows to vest to be quite packable. I can pack this down into the an accessory pocket on my backpack when the temps raise above 60 on the way home.

Pros:
- Fire Red version is quite bright. Good for being seen on the road but not so much while wearing in the office
- Keeps the core nice and warm without overheating
- Lightweight and packable
- XL doesn\x27t feel like a hipster-sized vest, styled like a skinny jean. It actually fits husky clydesdale cyclists
- Slightly stretchable, doesn\x27t feel constricting
- Pairs well with the Levi\x27s Denim Commuter jackets
- Vented, to allow some breathing in the back of the vest

Cons:
- Outer fabric is susceptible to static electricity. (Although this is easily fixed by being wipeddown with a dryer sheet)
- Expensive, but well constructed

In short:
This is a good investment for keeping warm without adding much bulk to your daily cycling commute. I would certainly buy it again.

product_title: SKS Raceblade 700x25-35 Mudguard 2016
review_headline: Good fenders where others won\x27t fit
review_body: These fenders work well on a road frame without mounts or clearance for proper fenders (in this case a \x2712 Trek Madone 5.2). Though not as effective as a full-coverage fender, they are helpful in keeping the bike and rider dry. Adjustment can be tricky, and it is odd that SKS includes the aero fork bracket with its Raceblade fenders but not the Raceblade XL. Once positioned properly, it is helpful to use the provided screws to make sure the fender blades stay in place within the bracket. For enhanced coverage it is best to forgo the small spoilers that are included (the longer ones shown in the product picture are not included) and opt for a set of Buddy Flaps. These will help extend the fenders and keep water and debris from wheels the out of the chainring and front derailleur, your shoes, and the face of the rider behind you. The biggest downside of the fenders is no coverage for the brake calipers or front half of the rear wheel, but they make your road bike rideable in less than perfect conditions even here in Seattle.

product_title: Ipow Portable Survival Flexible Pocket Wire Hand Folding Prepper Chinsaw with Fire Starter for Survival Gear, Camping, Gardening, Preppers, Backpacking, Bug Out Bag - Emergency Kit or Any Outdoorsman
review_headline: Good survival  / camping tools, but practice makes perfect!
review_body:
Summary: Good camping/survival tools, though be sure to practice fire starting! Note: free sample provided for evaluation

I have to admit that I\x27ve become a bit complacent with matches and a gas chainsaw. If you\x27re camping or out somewhere that you can\x27t really carry a full set of tools, the saw is suprisingly capable, while the firestarter works well - if you know how to use it.

The chainsaw took about 18-20 pulls to cut through a pine 2x2, and about a minute (I didn\x27t count pulls) for your average tree branch as big around as your wrist. If you were to add some heavy line to either side, you could very likely use this as a tree branch pull saw.

The firestarter puts out tons of very hot sparks, though I found I needed something more flammable than just dry sawdust. Shredded newspaper or paper towel worked better - you have to shelter it and blow gently on it to get it started. There\x27s a whistle and compass on it as well.

review_headline: Great construction, great price, looks much nicer in person.
review_body: This is a great boot bag. It doesn\x27t look at all like it does in the picture here, but this is the rare case where it actually looks a LOT better in person. The green is actually darker and more muted, and very nice. In general this is a very well constructed bag, seems like it will hold up for a while. Boots go in through the back, and there is plenty of padding to prevent the boots from sticking into your back. Other stuff goes in through the top. There is no "firm" barrier between the boots and the other stuff, just a flexible waterproof fabric, meaning the boots and the other stuff share the same space. This is a good thing, because it means the bag can accommodate any boot size, and whatever room the boots don\x27t use you can stuff with other things. If your boots are small, you get even more space. I had no problem fitting my boots, helmet, ski pants, 2 goggles, gloves, and all my other ski accessories in here. The bag is comfortable to carry, both on your back and by hand, thanks to thickly-padded shoulder straps and well-placed handles. Honestly, I could have paid twice as much for this bag (which is what similar bags go for) and still been satisfied.

Bought this product to see how it would work along with other repair products I purchased.  Needed the tent pole sleeve and it worked great. Everything else is so-so. I used the mesh screens and they worked well because I used my thread and sewing machine to stitch them on.  Used the seam sealer but had to use the entire tube because the cap did not fit right. Nylon ripstop patches worked OK, but tenacious tape has far superior adhesiveness. Used my own fishing line and knotted/taped it to the shock cord to get the cord thru the tent pole. Not enough shock cord (36\x5C\x22?) to do much with. Thread & needle were worthless and used my own. I would not purchase again. I would go to online outfitters to get the tent mesh and purchase other items in larger quantities.

product_title: Smart Air Beds Diamond Top Elite Queen Raised Pillowtop Air Bed, Blue
review_headline: Only Good for a few Uses - Very Poor Qualtiy
review_body: This was a major mistake and a complete waste of time and money.  I purchased this bed a couple years ago and used it one time soon after I received it from amazon.  It seemed to work fine that night and my guest reported it was comfortable.  Now a couple years later, needing a bed to sleep in while remodeling a condo several hundred miles from home, it seemed like it would be perfect for my needs, saving a hotel room for a couple weeks .  The first night the bed seemed to work okay but lost some air and had to be reinflated.  The next night it seemed to loose air as soon as I got on it and was flat within a few minutes.  being in the middle of the night I had no choice but to sleep on the floor.  I tried the patch kit but it was dried up, so the next day I went to Lowes and picked up a kit designed for pools and air mattresses.  I found the hole (not an easy task) which was located in the middle of a seam about 3\x5C\x22 from the top of the mattress (not an easy place to patch), but seemed to have successfully patch it .  After spending another night on the floor, I reinflated the bed and the patch seemed to work.  The next morning I woke up laying on the floor with the air mattress bubbled up around me.  It had leaked all night.  I again searched for the air leak and found another hole on the same seam as the first!  It seems like the quality control of the bed manufacturer is non existent, with defective seams getting weak and holes forming.  Since any vinyl can be easily punctured, I have always been so careful making sure no sharp objects were around the bed or on the carpeting.  I never thought the bed it\x27s self would develop holes regardless of how well you care for it.  Now I have been on the floor more than on my air mattress.  I am extremely unhappy with this product as it has caused me several very uncomfortable nights both on the mattress and off.  I weigh under 200 lbs and looking at the other seams on the bed it seems like they are separating internally, leading me to believe the basic construction of the bed is faulty.  My recommendation is that this mattress may not be suitable for more than a few uses, if you are of average size and weight.  Another reviewer basically said it only lasted one day but was cheaper than a hotel room, well I am not that rich when I purchased the bed I expected it to last for years with occasional use and proper care.  If the bed is disposable I still think the cost of use is very very high.

product_title: Hydration Pack with 1.5 L Backpack Water Bladder. Fits Men and Women with Chest Sizes 27" - 50". Great for Hiking - Running - Biking - Kids
review_body:
So after a few trail runs I have finally sat down to give my review of the Camden Hydration Pack. While I have not used it for more than 20 miles at a time I have used it on three separate trail runs of 12 miles or more. I also am no expert on hydration packs since this is only my second one but as a runner/biker I can lend my point of view from that aspect of the product. So without continued rambling lets us begin.
Upon receiving the package I opened it and inspected the product. The Hydration pack was packaged neatly and in a manner that should not be damaged during shipping. I pack itself was incredible light when I picked it up and that concerned me some. The shell of the pack has several pockets that are convenient to access and useful in size without adding a lot of extra material or weight. The bladder was wrapped up neatly inside the shell and ready to use after being washed (as you should with any new product).

Off to the trails we go. Once loaded up I began testing it on my runs. I noticed as most hydration packs do this one has the typical sloshing of the liquid of choice. I am use to it but it can be a little annoying for someone who isn\xE2\x80\x99t but again small matter there and not a performance issue at all. The pack when full balanced well and the straps did not bite into me at any point however I will note I wish the straps over the shoulders were a little more rigid maybe with some kind of dense foam insert but again that is personal preference. The mouth piece worked better than my pricier hydration pack I already have been using and I was able to get my water way easier and this was a very nice surprise. I had no leaks and pack performed exceptionally well on all three runs.

Conclusion. 4 out of 5 stars. Excellent pack for the price and worked well for my runs and would do well on hikes and biking I think. I am a little concerned about some places being single stitched and may wear so I would have liked to see possible wear spots and the zippers be double stitched for durability. The shell is also a material that will not take sustained abuse from harsh treatment such as rock climbing so with the durability concerns on rough outings I cut one star out.. Again though great pack for the price and for normal use. One deal not to pass up.

There is a flap of fabric designed to cover most of the zippers. Looks great. Problem is, the flap of fabric becomes "zipped up" in the zipper and ends up jamming when kids hurriedly zip and unzip. The result is zippers that cannot zip because they are clogged with fabric. Only by force can you get it open, and then the zipper teeth come apart.
My son say others in his school have had the same problem. Great backpack, lots of compartments, etc. But the zipper issue stinks. I tried cutting off most of the flap but it\x27s so close to the zipper that it\x27s practically futile. I ended up purchasing an OGIO and I guess I\x27ll use this one to carry around disc golf items or something. The zippers are shot. All this AFTER LESS THAN ONE MONTH OF USE.
Say what you want about user error, but the fact is that the users are kids in school, and if it doesn\x27t work for them, then what\x27s the use?

product_title: Razor Graffiti Chalk Scooter
review_headline: Chalk Pedal Removal Instructions - Easy with right tools.
review_body: I bought it for my kid because it was on deep markdown at half the price of a Razor A and with the intention of immediately removing the chalk pedal entirely.  It\x27s a standard Razor A (not A2 with the wheelie back bar and front shock absorber) scooter with a slightly longer platform by 2 inches in the back.  I know there is another review that says the chalk pedal is very difficult to remove, but it is fairly easy.    You will need a small screwdriver, small pliers, two (2) 5mm (metric size, not SAE) Allen wrenches - circle clip pliers are optional.  To remove the chalk pedal:    1) There is one pin and one bolt holding the chalk pedal together.  Remove the circle clip from the forward chalk pedal Pin.  If you have standard \x5C\x22circle clip pliers\x5C\x22 then this step is super easy.  I just used a small screwdriver to separate and bend one end of the clip up with a twist, then needle nose pliers to twist it completely off.  I used an index card on the metal frame to prevent scratching, but it is a kid\x27s scooter that\x27s going to be banged up and dropped anyway.  This is the most difficult part if anything, but about as challenging as bending a paper clip with pliers.    2) Two (2) 5mm Allen wrenches are required to remove the rear pedal bolt and rear wheel axle.  The rear wheel drops down and must be removed to get the inside black plastic spacers out.  Be aware there is a cylindrical crush collar between the rear wheel bearings.  It\x27s trapped between the 2 cartridge bearings and won\x27t fall out, just be aware it\x27s there for reassembly.    3) When both 2 bolts and 1 pin are out there are 2 black plastic spacer sleeves about 4 inches long each on either side inside the rails that just slide out backward with the chalk pedal; they are not glued in and should not be stuck in any way.  The whole assembly just falls out loosely.    4) Reassemble the black plastic spacers with the rear wheel being sure to line up the cylinder crush spacer between the bearings, or else the axle bolt won\x27t push through and line up.  The axle bolt longer female side with the washer goes on the rear wheel and the final assembly of the wheel should be tight with no lateral play or slop (this is what the internal crush cylinder is for).  The pedal axle bolt female side did not have a washer.    5) It\x27s your choice whether to just throw out the pin and chalk pedal bolt, they are not needed.  I personally just thought they just added unnecessary weight that would hit my kid\x27s legs and ankles so I threw them out.

review_body:
This \xE2\x80\x9Cportable shower\xE2\x80\x9D definitely serves its purpose. I\xE2\x80\x99ve had it a couple of years now, and though I really haven\xE2\x80\x99t used it a lot, it\xE2\x80\x99s held up. I took this to Bonnaroo in the summer of \xE2\x80\x9912, and I used it to freshen up and wash filth from my feet before going to bed each night. I didn\xE2\x80\x99t really notice a water temperature difference, but then again, the water they provide is already warmed from the sun. If you want to shower at \xE2\x80\x98Roo it\xE2\x80\x99s something like $5, so I used this shower instead. It was awkward because there weren\xE2\x80\x99t trees around, and I had to tie it to the top of my car and crane and position my body awkwardly to get it wet enough to lather soap on it. But at least I wasn\xE2\x80\x99t as stinky and sweaty as I could have been, so I consider that a win. I intend on camping more this summer, and I\xE2\x80\x99ll potentially come back and update my review if I take this little shower with me.

PROS:
Really good for quickly cleaning hands or rinsing off shoes/feet/legs.
Easily folds up to store.
Helped me save money, and kept me clean enough, which is all I can ask for at a Festival.

CONS:
You have to put it high up for enough water pressure to get a good stream. Being that the highest point I had was the top of my car, I have to squeeze the top of the bag with one hand and lather my hair up with another.
The little mechanism that pinches the hose so more water doesn\xE2\x80\x99t flow still allows for a trickle. This could probably be solved by utilizing another clasp, like a clothespin.

THE VERDICT:
You get what you pay for: a cheap, lightweight way to stay relatively clean. It beats being covered in dirt and filth, especially if you\xE2\x80\x99re going to be outside hiking or working up a sweat at a Festival. That being said, I could see myself coming back and buying another one, once that one I have now wears out.

TIPS:
You\xE2\x80\x99ll want to clean it before storing it, with some kind of disinfectant. I made the mistake of forgetting to do that, and it grew some mold in the container.do that, and it grew some mold in the container.

product_title: Planet Bike Superflash Micro USB bike tail light
review_headline: Small & bright, but lower runtime than advertised
review_body:
The Planet Bike SuperFlash Micro USB Tail Light is a tiny red light that is quite bright. It comes with hardware that allows it to be mounted to a bike seatpost or seatstay and a clip for mounting it to a bag or clothing. I used several zipties in combination with the clothing clip to attach the light to the back of my helmet.

The light\x27s packaging makes wildly optimistic claims about runtime. Like pretty much every LED "blinky" on the planet, this light can be set run in either flash or steady modes. Some folks are find flashing lights very annoying and various randonneuring events and some European countries require lights be run in solid modes. I tend to favor the steady mode of light myself, so I figured I\x27d test the runtime to see how long a charge really lasts with the light set to solid. When blinking, the light is effectively off about half the time so naturally the light burns longer since the battery gets to rest between each light pulse.

The package claims a 2 to 4 hour charge should give 36 hours of runtime. Experience has taught me that such claims are inflated and I figured they were basing this on flashing times, so I ran a couple of tests on the light. The charge times were accurate.

I plugged in the Mini USB cable and charged the light. I ran the test a couple of times, charging the light fully until the blue LED stopped flashing and burned solid. I then let the light run in solid mode up until the battery depleted to the point it switched to the flashing low battery warning flash mode. In both my trials, the results were the same.

The charge time was about 2.5 hours. The solid burn time was nowhere near 36 hours. After 7.5 hours, the light switched to the flashing mode. 55 minutes later, the light would go out. Obviously, this is far short of the claimed runtime.

On the plus side, the light is well made and seems nicely weatherproof. It retained full brightness for the 7.5 hours and the low battery warning flash is still plenty bright to get most commuting cyclists home on a dark night.

Since I never believed the 36 hour claim, I\x27m not too disappointed in the short runtime. For my purposes, as a helmet light, I appreciate the light weight and with my current, brief commute I won\x27t have to charge the light all that frequently. But randonneurs or others looking for a light that can reliably shine steadily through long dark nights should look for something larger with more proven battery life.low battery warning flash is still plenty bright to get most commuting cyclists home on a dark night.

product_title: Mudder MT-CT09 Clip Design USB Rechargeable LED Bike Tail Safety Light
review_headline: A very good rear cycle light
review_body:
This is a really good little rear cycle light. The manufacturers sent me one for review and I am very impressed.

The light comes simply packaged in plastic with a charging lead and instructions, which are a bit sketchy and in eccentric English, but largely adequate. (They don\x27t tell you how to turn the light off, though, which you do by pressing the on/off switch for about 3 seconds.) The charging lead is a standard micro-USB lead; it is 1m long which is long enough to charge the lamp from a power bank while riding if you need to.

The lamp itself is compact (about 7cm long and 7cm wide at its widest point) and light enough to carry easily in a pocket or bag when you leave the bike. It has a good, strong grip with rubber pads to hold it firmly onto the frame and it works just like an old-fashioned bulldog clip so it\x27s dead easy to put on and take off. (That does mean you can\x27t really leave it on the bike unattended because it is so easy for someone else to remove it.) The light is very bright red and the design means it is visible in a 180 degree arc at the back of the bike. It has three modes: high, low and strobe, and it flashes briefly every minute to warn you when the power is low.

Time alone will tell, of course, but this has the feel of a solid and robust product which is built to last. It is well-made and properly waterproof, and I expect it to give years of good service. (I will update this review if I encounter any reliability problems, but I\x27m not expecting any.)

In short, this is a neat, practical and well-made light and I can recommend it warmly.

I was soon shredding though the pebbles and rocks, not that I still didn\x27t bail attempting the most rudimentary of tricks, I just bailed at a significantly lower rate. These served me for around a year and half and now sit collecting dust as my skating tastes have refined and I retired from street skateboards after realizing I was a TERRIBLE skater.

These handled the abuse admirably. they get my stamp of approval.

product_title: Scrubba Portable Laundry System Wash Bag, Light  Green
review_body:
[[VIDEOID:2ba5a26bb7f6c216ef9ab3b98a055b6c]] I use this when traveling. It saves me a ton of time and money, having to find (and wait) at the local laundromat.

With all the money I\x27ll be saving, I estimate this thing will pay itself off in 15-20 washes.

Pros:
- Cleans very thoroughly.
- Easy instructions that printed right on the bag.
- Relatively fast to get a \x5C\x22load of laundry done.\x5C\x22
- Easy to use--not too hard physically.
- Lightweight yet surprisingly tough.
- Packs down small into a tiny package.
- Innovative: remarkable how they took old fashioned technology and made it accessible.

Cons:
- Difficulty breathing when placed over my head. On the plus side I felt like an astronaut with his helmet on.
- I wish they\x27d put a little loop on the inside end of the bag. That way when you\x27re finished with the Scrubba you could hang it upside down to dry. Right now it\x27s rather awkward to hang to air dry, which is a must to ensure it doesn\x27t get moldy.

HINT: This is best for very small \x5C\x22loads\x5C\x22 of laundry. It\x27s not designed to wash huge amounts of clothes. Think \x5C\x221 or 2 people\x5C\x22 who are traveling, not entire families with kids. Unless you\x27re very devoted.

HINT x2: I would not suggest washing \x5C\x22delicates\x5C\x22 (e.g. bras, lacy things, etc). The little nubbins are designed to really scrub (hence the name) your clothes clean, so don\x27t be surprised if the life of your clothes degenerates faster than usual when using this guy. Best for traveling but probably not daily use.

HINT x3: It will be tough trying to wash something large, like a pair of jeans or a especially a jacket. If you have clothes that are too bulky, it will take forever (unless you\x27re okay with being patient), but you\x27d probably be better off finding a laundromat for those bulky items.

5/5 stars. An absolutely beautifully engineered product. This is a must-have gadget for anyone who travels, especially to third-world countries or places where you don\x27t really want to spend the day at a laundry facility.specially to third-world countries or places where you don\x27t really want to spend the day at a laundry facility.

product_title: The StingRay-Stops Your Goggles From Snapping Off of Your Helmet
review_headline: Affordable and Effective Solution to a Frustrating Problem
review_body:
When goggles aren\xE2\x80\x99t being used, it\xE2\x80\x99s a habit to pull them up and rest them on the front of the helmet. The problem is that the elastic strap sometimes causes the goggles to slide backwards until they snap right off the helmet. Nobody wants to risk losing or scratching their goggles that way.

What I love about the StingRay is how easy it is to use and how successfully it solves the problem of goggles snapping off a helmet. Simply peel off the adhesive backing, fit the StingRay onto the helmet and press down firmly to secure the device in place. It\x27s just that simple. The next time I used my goggles, the stopper prevented the goggles from sliding off the helmet when I wasn\x27t wearing them. And so far it\x27s stayed secure even in our minus 30 temperatures.

Since a good pair of goggles can cost hundreds of dollars, it just makes sense to protect them and the StingRay does that with ease. I also appreciate the one-size-fits-all design so that when my boys hit the slopes with me, they can benefit from having a StingRay as well. Best of all, it\x27s affordable!

review_headline: Surround Sound At A Fraction of the Cost
review_body:
This was easy to set up with the sound bar going under my TV & the subwoofer/2 Speakers behind me and to the sides. You can connect to Bluetooth and seamlessly switch between that and other channels like Optical, USB, etc. and still be connected to Bluetooth, which I liked.

One thing I\x27ll add about the speakers is that they don\x27t seem to play music when you are connected to bluetooth, but I may have to mess with the speakers to make sure.

If you want a surround sound system, buy this. You get the sound bar plus a subwoofer that wirelessly connects behind you, although the 2 speakers are connected to the subwoofer. The cable connecting them, however seems to be about 10 ft long so you\x27ve got full range with this. Even the power cords for the sound bar & subwoofer were different lengths, which saved me when I connected the bar to my TV. BUY THIS!

product_title: Slingbox 500
review_headline: Fantastic Product....when you know the tricks
review_body: This works awesome.  I didnt give it 5 stars because of reasons that are beyond slingbox controls.  I have directv and what I learned is, and as stated in other reviews, it just wont work with the Genie and HDMI.  The new Genie\x27s dont even have component out anymore.  Just HDMI.  And with the HDCP Directv uses, you will be able to watch NOTHING.  The work around was to buy an S-video to component out converter cable, only $7 on amazon.  But that defeats the point of having this.  You can get a much cheaper slingbox version if you are going this route.    What I did find is a simple splitter works.  I am not sure how.  But if you install a POWERED HDMI splitter between the Genie and the Slingbox 500, it somehow tricks the HDCP.  The caveat is you need to have the slingbox setup.  So hook it up, get it setup, then add the splitter. I used a 1x2 splitter, with the second output empty.  The cableing goes from the genie to the splitter, to the slingbox, then to the TV.  You cant hook up the slingbox to the 2nd output.  It wont work.  Trust me I tried.    Hope this helps someone and saves a tremendous amount of frustration.

product_title: Tablo DVR for HDTV Antennas with Wi-Fi
review_headline: Cut the cord and go green, too - Finally a feature-loaded DVR for the masses, no required monthly fee.
review_body:
I spent a lot of time searching for a DVR and always came up empty save for the few offerings that required satellite or cable service to get them, or those few that were made but not well supported because so few bought them. Why would I want to pay a monthly fee, hundreds of dollars a year, for the right to record OTA TV? Or IU was finding stuff that when I clicked the link I found the company stopped making them for some reason or got a lot of "no longer available". I had given up - until I had trouble finding DVDs for our DVD recorder and decided to look into DVR again. This time I got results - I kept seeing the word "Tablo" pop up on Amazon.com and on tech review sites. Most had "good" reviews, some said "young product" or "not mature" but they all loved the concept. So did I. It was what I had been hoping for without realizing it.
Even better than expected this used an external drive, had multiple tuners, and no need to tether it to just a single TV if you have 3 or 4 or 5 TVs in the house. I read all I could and decided with Amazon\x27s return policies I couldn\x27t lose.
Thanks Amazon but I won\x27t be needing your return policy.
The really good:
This device is LIGHT,
small, low power requirements (it uses a small external transformer or power supply, proving how little power it really consumes. One could call it going green AND cutting the cord to those crazy cable fees.),
For location or placement of your Tablo that is limited only by where your existing antenna needs to sit, where your roof antenna cable terminates or where you have room for a new antenna. (by the way, *free TV has never gone away*, it\x27s always been there, free over the airwaves regardless of what the cable and satellite companies would love you to believe. It\x27s not because of any mandate or law like the makers of that antenna sold on TV commercials try to convince you, it just never went away, only converted from analog to digital. Those roof antennas aren\x27t just for show.)
Mine sits on a small shelf on the bottom of an end table in the front room. Antenna cable, short USB cable to slim drive for the recordings, Ethernet to my Netgear 2200D router, power supply.
The connection to the TV is over Wi-Fi using a Chromecast device plugged into one of the 3 HDMI ports on my TV. (I could watch on other TVs by buying other devices such as more Chromecast, or move this one to a different TV. The Tablo can stay put, no need to even look at it.)
It\x27s also Wi-Fi equipped (more on that later)
Their support is quite good, responsive and cares.
They listen to suggestions and requests and are willing to look at customer input or ideas.
They keep adding features where and when possible.
It can broadcast live TV and/or recorded shows to multiple devices (depends on number of tuners and other things)

Here is the "more on that later" part - Wi-Fi. It can utilize Wi-Fi to connect with "control devices" which mean a tablet, Android phone, PC, iPad, etc. and to the receiving device - Chromecast, Rokue and other things - the list keeps growing.
HOWEVER, Wi-Fi success depends on YOUR network, your home layout, walls, etc. Wi-Fi is fine for convenience and data but isn\x27t always the best thing for streaming media like TV shows at a decent resolution. There are a lot of "what-ifs" involved there. I strongly suggest using the Ethernet port the Tablo is equipped with and wiring it to the core of your network - your router or a good switch next to your router in your network configuration. This way your Wi-Fi is used only to get from router to streaming device.
In full Wi-Fi mode the program has to traverse Wi-Fi from Tablo to router, then from router over Wi-Fi to the control device (iPad, phone, computer and from there to Chromecast, etc.
If you wire the Tablo to your network, the Wi-Fi is used for only the last parts and it\x27s much faster/better.
That\x27s not the fault of Tablo or the device, that\x27s just networking 101, Wi-Fi as it is.
There\x27s a bit of a learning curve - setup is SIMPLE and fast. You can record without reading a thing, but playback can require some thought or reading because you aren\x27t popping in a disk and hitting the play arrow. But on the other hand, it\x27s mostly intuitive and is well supported by Tablo and by a growing community of Tablo fans who know these things inside and out. As General Zod said "you are not alone" - if you buy a Tablo there\x27s a wealth of information and support out there.
Oh, on the topic of monthly fees - there is one but only if you want to pay. It\x27s for their guide. It\x27s CHEAP, and it\x27s wonderful and I absolutely DO recommend it. Click to record. Otherwise you can skip the fee and manually program shows to record like we used to do before DVRs (for any of you old enough to remember VCRs or DVD recorders)
If it\x27s this great and still so young, it can only get better and smoother with age.
Buy a Tablo right here on Amazon. You can\x27t lose with their return policy.
Buy directly from the Tablo web site - they also have a good return policy.
They will also strive to be sure you are happy with it.
If you have questions, shoot Tablo a message or ask on their online community.
It\x27s hard to go wrong!

product_title: VIZIO E-Series, Smart TV
review_body:
I have had this HDTV for about two months. I wanted to give the product a fair period of time to better evaluate. I chose a four star rating due to a problem I experienced and a concern on available controls "on TV". The problem experienced was that the remote stopped working and the TV had to be unplugged a couple of times to get the TV and remote to work again. On all other TV\x27s owned in the past there was always on/off, channel up/down and volume up/down "on TV" controls. The only button on this TV when pressed brings up "input" menu. After about 1/2 hour with Vizio on line Chat support I finally found out you could turn off TV with same button if you hold the button in. product_title: Roku LT Streaming Media Player (Old Version)
review_headline: Easy to Set Up, Fun to Use
review_body:
The Roku is a nice, convenient, and cheap way to turn your TV into a Smart TV. The Roku connects to your wireless internet and to your TV. This allows the TV to do many things. You can watch Netflix (with a subscription) as well as numerous other TV/movie channels. Some you have to pay for, of course, but many are free. You can play games with it, watch news or sports programs, watch Youtube, or music videos. It\x27s pretty neat.

The Roku works with WatchESPN and HBOGo, which is nice if you have those subscriptions. I have yet to discover a channel that I have wanted which is incompatible with the Roku.

The reason I got a Roku instead of something like a Chromecast is that you can connect it to your TV via HDMI or the old 3 colored cables system. This means that you can connect to even old TVs, which is nice. An HDMI cable is not included, but the colored cables are. It also comes with the remote. No additional purchases are necessary to use the Roku.

This particular version of the Roku does not have an ethernet port. This means that you do have to have wi-fi in order for it to work. It detects your wireless network automatically, all you have to do is enter the password once, and it will remember your network and automatically log you in.

The Roku is simple, intuitive, and practical. I got one for my parents, who are not technology people, and they have not had any troubles using it. Plus, Roku customer support is pretty good.

The device itself is fairly small and slim, it will sit next to your TV without being distracting in any way.

When you first set up your Roku, you will have to have some other internet-enabled device handy. You\x27ll register your product, which includes adding credit card information. However, you can delete this information once you\x27ve created a Roku account. The fact that you have to enter credit card information is a little annoying, but it\x27s only temporary.

Set-up ispretty easy, everything is guided and happens automatically. All you really need to do is follow the instructions. Once the set up is complete, you can add channels to the Roku. These channels can be anything from Netflix to card games. Think of them as like apps for the Roku. The channel store is well organized, extensive, and most things on it are free.

I\x27ve had my Roku for 7 months, and have had no problems with it whatsoever.

Overall, the Roku is easy to use and much cheaper than buying a Smart TV. It\x27s major selling point for me was its ability to connect to TVs that don\x27t have USB and solid customer support. Definitely worth the buy.

product_title: Nest Learning Thermostat - 1st Generation T100577
review_headline: Forced into Nest thermostat  - now I love it!
review_body:
A year ago I began looking for a remote thermostat and naturally the Nest was a candidate. Based on some of the reviews I decided to purchase a different (Radio-thermostat) model. I installed that unit in our second home because we needed the ability to monitor and control the heat remotely. The installation and setup for the other thermostat was a grueling experience and required several hours and several chat sessions, but I finally got it working satisfactorily. I intended to purchase a second unit for our primary residence, but the thought of a second installation put that off for a while. In the interim, we received a Nest unit as a gift from someone unaware that we already had a remote thermostat. I didn\x27t want to disappoint the gift giver and decided to install the Nest unit and live with it in spite of what I believed were shortcomings. I was wrong about its shortcomings. It is astounding how easy the installation and operation of the Nest is in comparison. The unit is clearly superior to our Radio-Thermostat model. I am now contemplating removing the other unit and replacing it with a Nest.
A case in point - we occasionally need to run the fan only to distribute heat from a heat producing fireplace. The Nest allows me to turn the fan on for a specific amount of time rather than turn it on and try to remember to turn it off. (which frequently happens) I am so pleased with our Nest thermostat, that I find myself walking by it and waking it up just to see it work.

product_title: Kitchen Cooking Timer Digital Sets 1 Second to 100 Hours Easy To Use
review_body: My Radio Shack kitchen timer finally gave up the ghost. I\x27ve had that thing since college, so dating myself, that would be 30 years. Not happy that it doesn\x27t work anymore. The little guy served me well.    So began the search for a new kitchen timer. Most people\x27s complaints about kitchen timers were concerning entering in the time with only one button available. For example, if you want 22 minutes, you would have to hold down the button and watch the display count up to 22. If that was too slow, you could, of course, press the button 22 times. The bad part is if you accidentally overshot to 25 minutes, then you have to clear the display and start over. If you have time, no problem. If you\x27re in a hurry, like I always seem to be, then it\x27s frustrating.    The other complaint was that on some of the timers is when the display was counting up, it would beep each time. ANNOYING!    I have none of these problems with this kitchen timer from epowermall. Because it has the full complement of buttons, I can enter in the desired time. If I want 1 hour and 32 minutes, I simply type in 01 32 00. That\x27s it! To make it even simpler, I could type in 92 00 (for 92 minutes). This timer let\x27s you do it either way!    The beep is not as loud as I would like, but it is not annoying. I just make sure that I\x27m nearby so that I can hear it.    This timer also uses just one AAA size battery so I don\x27t have to scramble to find one those \x5C\x22watch\x5C\x22 type batteries. I have AAA batteries all over the house.    And the price was right for this timer.    The only thing that I didn\x27t like about this timer is the mushy feel of the buttons. What I mean is that when you press the buttons they don\x27t click to give you tactile feedback. You have to pay attention to the display to make sure that your entry is correct.    *  *  *

product_title: Bulbrite Q75CL/MC 120-Volt Halogen JD Type Mini-Candelabra E11 Bulb, 75-Watt
review_headline: Beautifully bright light, but they burn out fast -- expect 200-300 hours, not 2,000 hours, as stated!
review_body:
These bulbs are bright and beautiful. But they barely last 1/10 of the advertised life expectancy. I bought this 10-pack just one year ago and I have already burned through all 10 bulbs. The first 2 bulbs burned out within 2 weeks of installation. I figured they must have been a few bad apples. But 10 bulbs in just 1 year? That\x27s pretty bad!

My light fixture holds 5 bulbs at a time, so each bulb lasted me 6 months. This lamp doesn\x27t get much use: maybe 1 hour a day on very busy days. So at 2,000 hours of life expectancy, each of these bulbs should have lasted me at least 5.5 years. Instead I got 6 months.

If the product description had said "lasts 200 hours" I would have rated these bulbs 5 stars. After all, they DO light up fast and they\x27re nice and bright. But to overstate the product\x27s life by 900% is just unforgivable. Go with a higher rated product. In the case of Bulbrite halogens, you get what you pay for!

product_title: 1st Generation August Smart Lock - Silver
review_body:
I eagerly awaited the August Lock from the day I saw it online and immediately signed up for a pre-order. I was impressed with their customer service throughout the wait as they were always responsive to emails, even if only to reply that they didn\x27t have a definite shipping date yet (I am also still on the \x5C\x22pre-order\x5C\x22 list for Lockitron, though I think I have lost all hope of actually seeing that product, and at this point, with their lousy customer service and continued broken promises, I don\x27t care if I ever see it, especially now that I have the August Lock installed). I have rated the lock at 4 stars for two main reasons: 1) being bluetooth only makes for limited functionality as you must be within sight of the lock to interact with it, and 2) the time it takes for the app to connect to the lock and allow me to open the door is probably longer than it would take to pull keys out. Those drawbacks having been said, it is only fair to also say that I was aware of the limited functionality beforehand, and there was never a promise that the lock would be faster than using keys (indeed, you still can if that is an issue). Given that my main reason for installing the lock on the back door (besides that the front is incompatible and we are in a rental) is that almost always have my phone when I am out of the house, but sometimes don\x27t have my keys when I get to the back door, I can now unlock the back door without having to go around the house, and with a little foresight, I can be opening the app on the way to the door so that I can unlock it immediately and get my toddler inside to the potty before an accident occurs ;)

Now, the upside: drawback #1 is about to be obsolete given the announcement and impending delivery of August Connect (yes, I\x27ve pre-ordered) which will allow wifi interaction and the associated remote operation and access of the lock. And I believe that work is ongoing for the Android app to allow a phone to automatically connect to the lock when in range without having to have the app open, which would solve drawback #2 for most situations.

In all, is it a necessary item for the home? No. But it is a fun piece of tech that was well thought out and well executed as a product, and with future enhancements such as August Connect and compatibility with other home automation platforms, such as the Logitech Harmony Hub and the Nest products, it will continue to be a great product as well as becoming more useful. As it is, we plan on installing August Locks on all our exterior doors when we finally buy our next home. As for the 5th star, if August Connect delivers on its promise of remote connectivity, I will be editing this review.
Thanks for the great product!

product_title: SABRE Personal Self-Defense Safety Alarm on Key Ring with LOUD Dual Alarm Siren Heard up to 600 ft/185 meters Away. To Use, Pull Metal Chain from Base
review_body:
Although this personal alarm is not very attractive and a little bulky to carry on a key chain, it should be an effective tool to scare off an attacker. The manufacturer says that it looks like a USB stick -- maybe one made ten years ago because of its size -- and at first I couldn\x27t figure out why that would be something to tout. Because it\x27s pink, it can\x27t be an effort to make it unobtrusive. Then I realized that a potential attacker might try to keep someone from reaching for something that looked obviously like an alarm. The roughly 3" length (by a little less than 1" wide) makes it easy to locate and activate.

Having never using a personal alarm before, I was surprised by the effort required to pull the pin. I expected it to require almost no effort at all. But as I thought about it, I realized that you don\x27t want the alarm to go off by accident. I can lift my keys out of my purse by grasping the alarm only, and the siren won\x27t activate. You have to pull the body firmly away from the pin. The siren itself is not deafening, but I imagine it would seem so on a dark and deserted street. The object is (obviously) not to incapacitate an attacker but to startle him enough for him to flee. It draws attention to the act and the people involved. While it\x27s not a foolproof deterrent, it is still a valuable tool to have at the ready.

-- Debbie Lee Wesselmann
